title: An African man spent almost a year in Cambodia trying to go home
summary: In Cambodia, workers carried out online scams against people worldwide from inside massive fortified buildings they weren't allowed to leave
story: In Cambodia, workers carried out online scams against people worldwide from inside massive fortified buildings they weren't allowed to leave

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- The 33-year-old man, lured to Cambodia with the offer of a receptionist job, endured daily beatings for a month, locked in a dark room somewhere in the Southeast Asian country. He didn't know where he was, but he knew the price of his freedom: $6,000.

He had arrived from Ghana in November 2025 with the promise of a $1,000-a-month job — way more than he could make back home. At a training session he was taught to promote work-from-home “jobs” to people online, dangling the prospect of easy money.
He soon realized it was a scam, he said, and wanted out. That's when the beatings began.

“It’s not a joke the way they threaten you, they’ll beat you to your core,” the man told The Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution from the scam enterprise — which, he said, seized his passport — as well as the recruiter who got him into it.

For the next month, he said he endured beatings with fists, sometimes a bat and was shocked with tasers until the scam center was raided by Cambodian police in January as part of a nationwide campaign to shut down the criminal operations. Months later, he still cannot grip with his left hand after his wrist was broken during the abuse.

Online scam operations have flourished in Cambodia, as well as in Myanmar and Laos, since the COVID-19 pandemic, a multibillion dollar industry where workers carried out web-based scams from inside massive fortified complexes, living in dormitories they weren't allowed to leave. Some came knowing they were signing up for something illegal. But many, like the Ghanaian man, were baited with false promises of high-paying jobs through complex human trafficking webs. Cambodia was home to at least 182 confirmed scam locations, according to data collected by CyberScamMonitor, a watchdog that tracks them, though it has evidence of roughly 300.

Facing international pressure in late 2025 after the death of a South Korean student forced into such an operation and the U.S. indictment of the Chinese-born founder of a Cambodian conglomerate behind a massive cryptocurrency scam, Cambodia kicked its crackdown into high gear.

But even as it closed down dozens of scam centers, Cambodia has not prosecuted the criminal operatives behind the schemes or the elites who helped them flourish by providing financing, facilities and connections to the highest echelons of Cambodia's government — including senior politicians and relatives of Prime Minister Hun Manet, according to the U.S. Congress, which has called for sanctions.

After the raids ramped up in January, tens of thousands of former workers ended up in the capital, Phnom Penh, many sleeping in the streets. Some faced police harassment and arbitrary detentions. More than 10 months later, hundreds remain stranded.

“The government generally treats migrants found trapped in scam centers as offenders, and we have seen no evidence of adequate efforts to screen them for internationally recognized indicators of human trafficking,” said Li Ling, of the Eos Collective, a nonprofit dedicated to investigating human trafficking, which has helped 220 stranded workers return home.

Cambodia said in September, that it had dismantled all the larger compounds, and was prosecuting court cases linked to the scams. Last month, it said it seized assets worth $1 billion from one alleged scam network and called on Interpol to help track down 29 ringleaders. But it provided no evidence it was taking action against the Cambodian political and business elites behind the operations.

“They need to begin holding accountable evidenced elite perpetrators, not concocted, mid-level token investigations, but the ... Cabinet-level members, senators and members of the prime minister's family,” said Jacob Daniel Sims, a transnational crime expert and visiting fellow at Harvard University’s Asia Center.

Cambodian Information Minister Neth Pheaktra did not respond to detailed AP questions sent via Telegram for this report concerning Cambodia's treatment of scam workers, the calls for prosecutions of its senior politicians, or further information about any criminal cases it is carrying out.

In response to AP questions earlier this year about the treatment of former scam workers caught up in the crackdown, Pheaktra said Cambodia “rejects claims that it is failing trafficking victims or tolerating abuse linked to scam compounds.”

"All individuals are screened to separate victims from perpetrators, with victims receiving protection, shelter, medical care and assistance for safe return,” he said, without providing evidence of any such process.

The Ghanaian man, a university graduate who speaks English fluently, couldn't find a job in his special education field and, struggling to support his family of four, was working as a farmer. Then an acquaintance told him about what sounded like a dream opportunity: A Chinese company was looking for an English-speaking receptionist with IT skills in Cambodia.

“He told me I will be paid $1,000. The company is going to provide me with accommodation and with food,” the man said. He interviewed online and within days had a job offer, a visa and a flight paid for by the company.

There were early warning signs once he arrived in Cambodia: He was driven several hours from the airport to an unknown location, where he said his cellphone and passport were seized. He was given a two-year contract instead of one year like he'd agreed to. When he hesitated to sign, burly men threatened him.
He signed, and soon was training to be a “chatter.”

While scams differ from operation to operation, a “chatter's” job is to solicit as many people online as possible, with a simple text message like “hello,” or something more targeted, like “are you able to work weekends?” Then comes the pitch, often using a script.
Once the victim engages in a back-and-forth, a supervisor experienced in emotional manipulation takes over to build a relationship and entice the victim to hand over their money.
The Ghanaian man said he refused to work when he realized what the job was. But he didn't have the $6,000 demanded in repayment for bringing him to Cambodia.

After Cambodia's crackdown, workers who had money to buy a plane ticket home got out quickly. Others went on to find similar work in other countries. But thousands wanted to go home, couldn't afford it and got no help from their home countries.
The Ghanaian man headed to Phnom Penh, where he slept on the streets and went without food for two or three days at a time.
Henry Kyeyune, from Uganda, also slept on the street for months.

He eventually sought shelter at Caritas, a Catholic-run charity that was the only refuge for the ex-workers after the government issued a ban on providing them housing. It was full, but he slept on the ground outside in hopes of getting a spot.

While there are no comprehensive figures for how many workers left the compounds, reports from nearby countries provide a glimpse into the size and diversity of the workforce. China said in June it had repatriated more than 20,000 workers linked to scam centers, according to state broadcaster CCTV. One border province in Vietnam said it received more than 1,700 ex-workers in the first half of 2026. The Indonesian Embassy said in September it had received requests from 12,940 Indonesians for help getting home and that another 700 remain stuck in the country.

Betty O. Bigombe, Uganda’s ambassador to Malaysia, said she has helped more than 1,000 former workers navigate the complexities of getting out, mostly Ugandans like Kyeyune, but also Africans from other countries as more workers were lured into the operations from the continent.

Changing government policies were a major obstacle for the ex-workers. Many no longer had their passports and faced fines for remaining in Cambodia without proper visas. The government also started requiring interviews with immigration authorities to leave, said Li of the Eos Collective.
There were roundups by police in which ex-workers were taken to detention centers, where they'd be stuck until they could get a ticket home.

Kyeyune said he'd been sleeping outside the Caritas shelter for a week when he and others were detained. He was held for two weeks at a police station, then taken to a detention center known as Mango 2.
He spent another week there, sleeping on the floor, crowded with other workers before Bigombe helped him get a flight home.
“They keep it like a prison, we weren’t allowed to go outside,” Kyeyune said.
The Cambodian government did not respond to AP questions about why workers were taken into detention and the treatment they faced there.

The Ghanaian man was also detained in Mango 2. He was held for two weeks before he was suddenly removed by authorities in handcuffs and taken to the airport on Oct. 14. He boarded a plane to Ghana with a ticket provided by the Eos Collective.
Almost a year had passed since he arrived in Cambodia.

At times he'd thought about not going home, he said, so ashamed by what he'd gotten mixed up in and not wanting to face his family's disapproval. His father died while he was in Cambodia, and he said he failed in his duty to help bury him.

Now back in Ghana, he said he worries about how he will rebuild his life. He doesn't have the money to travel to his family's home, far from the capital. He can't even afford to buy data for his phone.
“I’m still not with my family yet, because I couldn’t transport myself there," he wrote in a text message. "I'm still not safe yet.”

title: 3 charged in scheme to use AI to impersonate CEOs and attorneys to steal $129 million
summary: Three people have been charged in a scheme to use artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million
story: Three people have been charged in a scheme to use artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million

NEW YORK -- Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, prosecutors said Thursday.

Over more than a year and a half, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies across the world in their AI scheme, according to the indictment filed in a U.S. District Court in New York.

Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida, according to court documents.
The defendants, from Spain, the UK, Israel and United Arab Emirates, were also charged with money laundering, according to the indictment.

Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment. It was not clear whether Hazan had an attorney. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York did not immediately respond to a voicemail left by The Associated Press.
The three were arrested between June and September. In 2008, Hazan was convicted in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office.

The trio, who have nicknames that include “Rocky Balboa,” “Superman Cash” and “Fat Boy,” often targeted the companies’ accounting departments. They would send an email purporting to be from the CEO and ask for help with a confidential financial transaction, according to court documents.
They would also coordinate a phone or video call where the defendants used AI to mimic the voice and sometimes the image of the CEO, according to the indictment.
The defendants would then tell them to contact an attorney at a major law firm, who the group was also ready to impersonate, according to court documents.

Soall mainly impersonated attorneys from the UK and had a “handwritten script titled ‘Lawyer Call’ that he utilized to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with and defrauding victims,” according to the U.S. attorney’s office.

The impersonated attorney would tell the employee to wire large payments to bank accounts across the world, according to court documents. The funds were then converted into cryptocurrency to try to conceal where they came from and then distributed to the trio and others involved, according to court documents.
FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle, Jr. said the case shows how advanced technology can be used to commit large-scale fraud.

“As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities," he said in a statement.
If convicted, each of the charges have a maximum sentence of 20 years, except for aggravated identity theft, which is two years, according to the attorney’s office.

title: Mexico bans cellphones in schools, despite opposition from parents worried about violence
summary: Starting Tuesday, Mexican schools will ban cellphones in classrooms to limit electronic device use among children and teenagers
story: Starting Tuesday, Mexican schools will ban cellphones in classrooms to limit electronic device use among children and teenagers

CULIACÁN, México -- Starting Tuesday, Mexican schools will ban cellphones from classrooms as part of a federal government effort to limit children’s and teenagers’ use of electronic devices, following similar measures taken by over a hundred countries in the last decade.

The initiative, spearheaded by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, has been supported by experts who see it as an opportunity to reduce young Mexicans’ exposure to technology and the resulting attention deficit, stress and anxiety.

Mexican authorities are also preparing to implement regulations this month that will require digital platforms to remove posts containing hate speech, abuse, sexual violence, harassment, cyberbullying and other illegal content.

However, the cellphone ban, which will take effect on Nov. 3, is already facing resistance in some parts of the country. Some parents fear being unable to communicate with their children amid ongoing violence, from which children and adolescents are not spared. According to the civil society coalition Network for Children’s Rights in Mexico (REDIM), in the first half of this year, one in 10 Mexicans between the ages of 0 and 17 were victims of crimes involving organized crime.

“I don’t think parents will accept not giving their children a means of digital communication, especially when those children … are spending so much time at home instead of at school,” said Francisco Ortiz, state representative of the National Union of Parents in Sinaloa, accusing the government of ignoring parents and approving regulations that “go against parental authority, against the rights of parents.”

The decree issued by Sheinbaum prohibits the use of cellphones and electronic devices inside elementary and middle schools throughout the school day, and only allows their use for educational purposes under the guidance of teachers or for personal emergencies, disability and health needs. Students can take their phones with them on the way to school.

Benigno Gómez, a father from Reynosa in the northern state of Tamaulipas, said that while he understood the educational authorities’ need to reduce students’ time on cellphones, he found it “a little difficult” that they weren’t allowed to have a cellphone to deal with a potential risk situation.
Mexican authorities have not commented on these concerns and have instead focused on the harm caused by cellphones.

During a recent address to the Chamber of Deputies, Mexico’s Secretary of Public Education, Mario Delgado, stated that the Sheinbaum administration seeks to “prevent addiction to digital platforms and the disorders they cause in minors.”

Just as the sun was beginning to rise, the residents of Escuinapa, the capital of the municipality of the same name located in southern Sinaloa, awoke on the morning of Oct. 22 to alarming news. A bus that regularly travels through the small town — which relies on mango and shrimp production — was shot at by a man on a motorcycle.

More than a dozen high school students were on board. A video recorded by one of the passengers circulated on social media, showing children on the floor and others hiding among the seats while one teenager asks another, “Do you have any credit (on your cellphone)?”
In the attack, only the bus driver was injured, suffering cuts from shards of glass shattered by the gunfire.
Upon learning of the shooting, one Escuinapa resident immediately called her teenage daughter, who had left early for high school in a car driven by her aunt.

“Just hearing my daughter’s voice and knowing she was OK calmed me down,” said the woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of the criminals plaguing her community — admitting that she didn’t hesitate to interrupt her daughter’s class to check on her.
The mother expressed doubts that parents will comply with the cellphone ban, fearing that violence could now reach schools in Escuinapa, and insisted that “the safety of our children comes first.”

For Israel Sánchez, president of the National Union of Parents, the Mexican government’s decision represents progress after years of struggle by the civil organization, which brings together hundreds of parents from public and private schools, mostly Catholic.
Sánchez argued that authorities must undertake an awareness campaign for parents and provide training for teachers to achieve the effective implementation of the regulation.

Dr. Lucía Magis-Weinberg, a neurodevelopmental researcher at the University of Washington who has studied the effects of technology on children and adolescents for years, said Mexico is joining the international movement to regulate cellphones at a very opportune moment.
Magis-Weinberg acknowledged the benefits of technology for socialization and accessing information but said it is “a double-edged sword.”
Regulations are needed to avoid cognitive damage, digital conflicts, and the risks of platforms that “are designed to maintain, to maximize our attention.”

The ban on cellphones in schools is already in place in 114 countries, according to UNESCO data. In Europe, restrictions have gained increasing traction, especially in France, where the ban was extended to secondary schools in August. Controls have also been implemented in some countries in Latin America, such as Ecuador, Brazil, Chile, Bolivia and Costa Rica. In the United States, bans are only maintained in some states.
Sánchez reported from Mexico City. Journalist Alfredo Peña contributed to this report from Ciudad Victoria, Tamaulipas.
Follow AP’s Latin America coverage at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Japanese online service company GMO apologizes for security breaches and promises compensation
summary: Japanese online service company GMO Internet Group has apologized for security breaches from cyberattacks, and promised to prevent a recurrence and compensate victims
story: Japanese online service company GMO Internet Group has apologized for security breaches from cyberattacks, and promised to prevent a recurrence and compensate victims

TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japanese online service company GMO Internet Group apologized Monday for recent security breaches from cyberattacks, while promising to prevent a recurrence and compensate victims.
Chief Executive Masatoshi Kumagai and other GMO executives bowed deeply repeatedly, as is the custom here, at a news conference in Tokyo.

GMO confirmed that unauthorized access to its cloud service called Onamae.com Desktop Cloud resulted in leaked information and transactions customers didn’t recall making, affecting dozens of securities firms and other businesses. It said there were more than 26,000 cases.
“I offer my deepest felt apologies,” Kumagai said, stressing the company took the problem seriously.
Tokyo-based GMO offers various internet services related to cybersecurity, online marketing and infrastructure systems, and support for robotics and artificial intelligence.
Kumagai, who founded the company in 1991, acknowledged GMO had been warned internally about a systemic weakness to such attacks, but failed to take proper action.

He apologized for recent social media posts, including a photo of him smiling, that he said may have hurt victims’ feelings. Kumagai is taking a 30% pay cut for three months, while other top executives are taking smaller pay cuts.
GMO promised to compensate for the losses and to pay 5,000 yen ($30) to all its customers to express “goodwill.” It will also switch to a new security system.
Recent Japanese media reports carried interviews with several people who said huge amounts of money went missing from a GMO service, although they had not initiated the transactions.
The problems at GMO have brought to light Japan’s cybersecurity vulnerabilities, which some experts warn have been brushed off for years and lack a sense of crisis.
The troubles at GMO come at a time of growing concern over cybersecurity.

Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has promised to beef up Japan's cybersecurity measures. The government has declined to comment on the GMO case, including possible suspects.
GMO acknowledged the attackers had deployed ransomware and said it refused to pay.

The company is offering $1 million for information that leads to identifying and arresting the attackers. It has set up a “GMO Cybercrime Bounty” site, where people can submit information in English, Japanese or Chinese. It said that as of last week, it had received more than 400 submissions.

At the news conference, the company’s first since the security problems surfaced, Kumagai spoke passionately and tearfully about how he and his employees were working hard to deliver the joys of the internet and other technology to customers.

The impact of the cyberattacks on GMO’s financial results is still unclear. GMO stocks, which have fluctuated over the past year, declined after news of the cyberattacks surfaced. The news conference started after trading closed in Tokyo. Its shares have fallen 17.5% so far this year.
Yuri Kageyama is on Threads: https://www.threads.com/@yurikageyama

title: Anthropic posts $17B quarterly revenue but losses continue in fresh IPO filing
summary: Anthropic reports quarterly revenue swelling to $17 billion but still posts a net loss for the latest three months
story: Anthropic reports quarterly revenue swelling to $17 billion but still posts a net loss for the latest three months

SAN FRANCISCO -- Anthropic's quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion but it still posted a net loss for the latest three months, the artificial intelligence giant said in an updated IPO filing released on Monday.

The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude chatbot also disclosed that it has committed to spend $895.4 billion on AI computing and infrastructure like data centers, including $70 billion that's due to be spent in the next 12 months.
The numbers were released about a week after Anthropic issued its original IPO filing in preparation for what's expected to be a blockbuster Wall Street debut later this month.
The document, like the earlier filing, shows the company's revenue is growing but — like its AI rivals — profit is still elusive.

Anthropic’s revenue grew by 13 times to $33.2 billion for the first nine months of the year, but it reported a net loss of $104 billion, including a charge of $94 billion for an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements.
On a quarterly basis, Anthropic lost $23.3 billion on revenue of $17 billion.

The filing gave no indication of how much the company ultimately expects to raise, or what the shares will be priced at when it goes public. Anthropic has previously said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

title: Apple posts strong Q4 revenue in first earnings report for new CEO John Ternus
summary: Apple Inc. posted stronger-than-expected revenue in the fiscal fourth quarter, giving new CEO John Ternus a positive start to his tenure that began in September
story: Apple Inc. posted stronger-than-expected revenue in the fiscal fourth quarter, giving new CEO John Ternus a positive start to his tenure that began in September

Apple Inc. posted stronger-than-expected revenue in the fiscal fourth quarter, giving new CEO John Ternus an upbeat start to his tenure, which began in September. The solid results bucked a downward trend for tech giants this quarter, as companies including Alphabet, Amazon and Intel had disappointing quarterly results.

The Cupertino, California-based company earned $30.71 billion, or $2.10 per share, in the July-September period. That's up 12% from $27.47 billion, or $1.85 per share, in the same period a year earlier. Apple said its earnings included 5 cents per share from tariff refunds.
Revenue rose 12% to $114.5 billion from $102.5 billion.
Analysts, on average, were expecting earnings of $1.99 per share on revenue of $113.4 billion, according to a poll by FactSet.

Apple recently hiked its prices partly due to a global memory chip shortage brought on by the artificial intelligence boom, which helped drive revenue. Compared with earlier generations, the iPhone 18 costs about $100 more and the price of Macs and iPads also increased in June.

“Apple’s strong earnings come in the wake of a recent tech sell-off, as investors question the enormous cost and uncertain returns of the AI boom driven by Apple’s Big Tech counterparts," said Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne, adding that record iPhone revenue and strong growth in China demonstrate the resilience of Apple's business.

While its rivals are facing investor uncertainty over massive investments in artificial intelligence, Bourne said Apple's “tepid approach" to AI infrastructure spending helps preserve its cash flow — while partnerships with companies like Alphabet could help Apple to strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers.

The iPhone Duo, Apple's first foldable phone that starts at $1,999, was not yet on sale during the company's fiscal fourth quarter, so it wasn't included in the earnings results. Demand has been strong for the pricey model, even though some users have reported problems that include cracked screens, which Apple is fixing or replacing. Apple is also dealing with supply constraints for the Duo, which went on sale in October, though current earliest shipping dates are for January.
Apple's shares were flat in after-hours trading. The stock had closed down 1.8% at $338.32 in regular trading.

title: European supermarket fridges got hacked. Again. Here's what to know
summary: Mysterious cyberattacks on European supermarket fridges have officials scrambling to understand what happened
story: Mysterious cyberattacks on European supermarket fridges have officials scrambling to understand what happened
LONDON -- Mysterious cyberattacks on European supermarket fridges have sent officials around the continent scrambling to figure out the cold, hard facts.

Supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).
One Swedish supermarket said its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).
It's a repeat of an earlier incident that struck refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.
Here's a closer look:
Supermarkets in at least half a dozen European countries, including Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, Italy and Estonia, reported problems on Monday.
It wasn't just big chains.

The owner of a butcher shop in Athens told private Greek Skai TV Tuesday that someone hacked into the temperature control of a refrigeration unit, raising the temperature to 150 degrees Celsius (302 degrees Fahrenheit).

George Boubas said his employees who start their shift at 4 a.m. at the shop in the Kifisia suburb first noticed the problem. It took a technician two hours to wrest back control of the unit’s temperature settings, although the meat products weren’t affected, he said.
Boubas said the technician told him that an area supermarket and a fast-food restaurant experienced the same issue.
He said they resorted to switching off the Wi-Fi connection to the refrigeration units to restrict outside access.
Experts said the cyberattacks were a reminder of the risks that come as more things get connected to the internet.

“This attack is a wake-up call. We have filled our homes and shops with devices that are really small computers, yet we still treat them like ordinary appliances," said Katerina Mitrokotsa, a cybersecurity professor at the University of St. Gallen, in Switzerland.
“A fridge doesn’t look like a security risk, and that’s exactly why attackers like it.”
The cyberattack mirrors one that happened weeks earlier that affected mainly French and Dutch retailers.

French cybersecurity investigators blamed problems with outdated remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland. Danfoss said most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, while Copeland identified a vulnerability in discontinued controllers.

“Supermarkets connect their fridges so they can monitor temperatures around the clock across hundreds of stores, get alerts before food spoils, cut energy costs and let technicians fix faults remotely," Mitrokotsa said.
"This saves money and reduces food waste, but every connected fridge is also an entry point that needs to be secured like any other IT system.”

Experts said many businesses are rushing to embrace trendy new technology while neglecting the vast network of connections that they rely on for their daily operations, from payment and ordering systems to warehouses, refrigeration and other building controls.

“Organizations are pouring budget into AI and digital transformation while the systems that keep food cold, water clean, and lights on often run on hardware that has not been funded since installation," said Nicole Carignan, senior vice president of security and AI strategy at cybersecurity company Darktrace.

“Nobody broke into these refrigeration systems with a zero-day," she said, using a term for a flaw that has gone undetected by the system’s creators and security reviews. "They got in through internet-facing controllers, end-of-life firmware, and default passwords. That is technical debt coming due.”
British cybersecurity officials on Tuesday shed little light on the latest attack, while pointing to what they called “legacy technology.”

“The cyberattack on French supermarkets was a result of exploitation of known vulnerabilities,” U.K. cyber minister Liz Lloyd said in a speech. “It’s a clear demonstration that poor cyber hygiene, like weak passwords, continues to put organizations at risk.”
Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Center, told reporters the French fridges were "connected directly to the internet with default passwords.”
A team from the center issued warnings and worked through Monday night contacting organizations that had “vulnerable technology exposed,” he said.

Advanced artificial intelligence systems from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have come under fire recently after a string of revelations that they hacked into organizations while evading human control.
Experts, however, said Tuesday that they didn't think these attacks were powered by AI.
“There is no evidence AI was used, and the techniques did not require it,” said Carignan.

“I think the key element of that is that this wasn’t an AI attack” said Paul Chichester, director of operations at the U.K. cyber center. “This is using vulnerabilities that absolutely have been out there for a long period of time. And that’s where we really need to sort of focus on.”
Investigations have so far failed to discover who might have carried out the cyberattacks and why.

France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, said it has been investigating refrigeration-system breaches since mid-October and coordinating protective measures with “all sectors that could be affected.”
In a statement to The Associated Press, the agency said it knew of compromised remote refrigeration controllers in Danfoss’s AK-SM and AK-SC ranges, as well as Copeland and Dixell xweb systems.
ANSSI said it was mobilized to assist “potential victims in France” and pointed to a security alert first published Oct. 12, which has been updated regularly.
Italian cybersecurity and intelligence officials were scheduled to meet Tuesday morning to discuss the incident, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
Officials at the European Union's executive Commission were also holding similar meetings.
European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier declined on Tuesday to comment on who might have carried out the hacks, saying that's up to the bloc's 27 national authorities to figure out.
Regnier told reporters the incidents “are not isolated” and that Europeans "have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents.”
Hadjicostis reported from Nicosia, Cyprus. AP writers Lorne Cook in Brussels, Lefteris Pitarakis in Athens and Thomas Adamson in Paris contributed to this report.

title: Argentina’s Milei pitches a regulation-free AI haven at the end of the world
summary: Data centers are facing a growing backlash in the United States and Europe
story: Data centers are facing a growing backlash in the United States and Europe
TRELEW, Argentina -- TRELEW, Argentina (AP) — Data centers have become one of the most polarizing issues in the world. Argentina’s president wants to lure as many of them as he can get.

As residents and policymakers in the United States and Europe fight the facilities that power artificial intelligence, President Javier Milei is pitching Argentina as a haven, promising a hands-off approach to draw foreign investment his crisis-prone country needs.
Like his ally, U.S. President Donald Trump, Milei frequently posts AI-generated images on social media. He has proposed creating “nonhuman corporations” run entirely by AI agents.
“We are not going to regulate artificial intelligence,” Milei told the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Washington last month. “We are going to leave it free.”

Visitor logs obtained by The Associated Press show a steady stream of tech figures meeting with Milei and his aides in recent months, from venture capitalist Peter Thiel to representatives of OpenAI, Amazon, Google, Oracle and data center companies. Foreign Ministry records show that data center developer Crusoe, which helped build OpenAI’s flagship campus in Texas, sought talks this year with Argentine energy officials about U.S. government-backed investments.

Milei’s hopes rest as much on geography as on ideology. Patagonia offers vast, open plains where noisy server farms can be built far from population centers, a chilly climate to cool the machines, powerful winds to generate electricity and one of the world’s largest shale deposits in Vaca Muerta to fuel power plants.

“In densely populated parts of the U.S. and Europe, there’s a lot of fighting over access to the grid and who should get the electricity,” said Marta Zlotkowska, head of international development at Green Capital, a Polish renewable energy company that plans to build a $3 billion data center in Patagonia to lease to big tech firms for AI computing, though it has yet to secure a customer.
“We compared potential locations for the project around the world and Argentina — well, Patagonia — came out on top in every category," she said.

For Argentina’s energy industry, already booming as the Iran war hikes oil prices, data centers represent a tantalizing new market. Pampa Energía, one of the country’s biggest power companies, has announced plans to supply immense amounts of gas-fired power to a data center near Vaca Muerta and is seeking developers.

“Being at the end of the world used to be a disadvantage,” said Rubén Etcheverry, a top official in Neuquén, the Patagonian province home to Vaca Muerta. “But today, faced with energy shortages and rising costs, investors are looking at us.”

To win over companies wary of Argentina’s chronic economic instability, Milei is pushing an incentive scheme that would slash the corporate income tax rate to 15% from 25% for projects of at least $1 billion in AI and other emerging industries. The measure is awaiting Senate approval.

The payoff for Argentines remains unclear. Data centers employ relatively few people. Milei’s proposed incentives don’t require companies to reserve computing capacity for local consumption or to disclose their energy and water use.

“We’re not talking about data centers designed to strengthen Argentine technological sovereignty,” said Alan Rocha Varsanyi, a researcher at Observatorio Petrolero Sur, an Argentine environmental group. “The computing capacity will be exported wherever OpenAI or the other companies need it.”

For all Milei’s hype, Argentina lags behind in the race to become a regional data center hub, as its neighbors tout cheap land, renewable power and expanding fiber-optic connections to U.S. tech giants.

Milei insists his calls for unfettered AI give Argentina an edge at a time when the European Union and a growing number of U.S. states have adopted new regulations. Critics warn he is pushing to deploy AI in Argentina without safeguards against risks ranging from mass surveillance to cyberattacks.

“Without rules, Argentina will become a laboratory — like when companies go to developing countries to test strange drugs they can’t test in major developed countries,” said Nicolás Wolovick, a computer science professor at the National University of Córdoba.
Milei may hear similar concerns next week when Pope Leo XIV, who has warned of AI’s threats to humanity, visits Argentina on his Latin American tour.

Even some in Milei’s own government acknowledge that his anti-regulation stance complicates efforts to build a clear legal framework, with one senior official not authorized to brief media saying companies are waiting for Argentina to settle rules on training AI with copyrighted works and sending personal data abroad.
Some investors are holding back until next year’s potentially tight presidential election, worried that if Milei loses, the next government could unravel his free-market reforms.

“One of our major challenges is getting foreign investors to understand that Argentina remains a friendly place for investment under different political parties,” said Andrés Arbeletche, cabinet coordination secretary for Chubut, a Patagonian province courting several AI mega-projects.

In remote ranching outposts across the treeless plateau of Chubut province, life revolves around tending flocks on steppes and shearing sheep in sheds. With the wool industry in decline after decades of drought, overgrazing and soaring production costs, some ranchers are betting on a different kind of shed — filled not with fleece but with blinking racks of servers.

“Sheep farmers are looking very hard at what alternatives can be found to bring in more income,” said Francisco Sáenz, an agricultural engineer and fourth-generation sheep farmer whose family is among 14 landowners who have leased a combined 130,000 hectares (about 321,000 acres) to Green Capital for its planned data center. The ranchers expect to keep grazing sheep alongside their colossal future neighbor.

Construction isn’t expected to begin until around 2028. If operated continuously at its projected peak demand, the finished campus would use about 2.7 times as much electricity in a year as the entire city of Buenos Aires consumed in 2025, according to an AP calculation.

Green Capital promises to generate all its own electricity from wind turbines, solar farms and gas-fired generators rather than strain Argentina’s congested grid. Provincial officials are counting on the project to deliver billions of dollars in investment, highly skilled jobs and a market for surplus wind power.
“For us, it is all a benefit, and we give nothing up,” Arbeletche said.

But some residents of Trelew, a dust-blown city near the proposed site, say they have no way to judge those assurances. Environmental studies are still underway, permits are pending and the company hasn’t specified how much water the project would need or how much of its power would come from gas.

“There’s just so little information,” said Cristina Gibón, 46, who fears the environmental toll of data centers. “Maybe we’ll have water until we’re old. But afterward, our children will still be here, and they won’t have those resources.”

Worries like hers are feeding a wider backlash against Milei's courtship of Big Tech. In Trelew, a small group of residents has rallied online and in the main square under the banner “Trelew Free of Data Centers.” In Congress, where lawmakers recently accused Milei of selling off the country at a hearing on billionaire Peter Thiel’s interests in Argentina, the opposition has forced the president to gut a bill easing restrictions on foreign land ownership and has stalled his plan to let AI agents control companies.
Back on his family’s farm, Sáenz sees a familiar Argentine reflex.

“Whenever a foreign company wants to make a major investment in Argentina, there’s a lot of criticism. Many people’s first reaction is to say, ‘No, they’re terrible people coming from the outside to take our resources,’” he said. “I’m not saying big companies are the best thing ever. I’m just saying that when I look at other countries, I see stable economies."

title: Meta delays new business terms after outcry over potential web scraping of news sites
summary: Meta is delaying new terms for business accounts after a backlash from media companies and open-web advocates
story: Meta is delaying new terms for business accounts after a backlash from media companies and open-web advocates

Meta said it was postponing the rollout of new terms for its business accounts after an outcry from media companies and open-web advocates who said the updated rules would allow the tech giant to scrape vast amounts of data and potentially build competing services.

The new rules, originally scheduled to go into effect Oct. 30, authorize Meta to use automated software such as web scrapers and bots to “index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs” associated with a business account.

The terms would have applied to all business clients, regardless of opposition, and without payment for the extracted content. Critics say Meta would have been able to use the content to potentially build products such as AI services that could compete with news publishers.
The new terms only apply to business accounts. Regular users of Meta's platforms, including Instagram and Facebook, can already have their posts scraped to train AI models as long as they are public.
On Oct. 28, a court in Norway granted a temporary injunction suspending Meta's new terms at the request of 180 Norwegian media companies, pending a full assessment of their legality.
Their case was supported by the Norwegian Media Businesses’ Association (MBL), whose member newspapers account for approximately 97% of Norwegian newspaper circulation.

“We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the new terms are unreasonable,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL chair of the board.
The U.K. Competition and Markets Authority said Oct. 30 it was starting its own investigation into the conditions.
“The CMA is concerned that Meta requiring news publishers and other content businesses to accept these terms could amount to an unlawful imposition of unfair trading conditions,” it said Friday.
Meta, however, says the terms don't change how the company uses web crawlers.

“This update is designed to make sure we’re able to pull accurate information about products for sale on third-party websites when making on-platform ad and content recommendations, not about scraping news sites,” wrote Meta spokesman Andy Stone on X on Oct. 16.

His comments came after a report by the Nieman Journalism Lab at Harvard University, which said that as written, “the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products.” Niemen Lab said it consulted three legal experts who reviewed the terms at its request.
While there do not appear to have been any lawsuits filed in the U.S., the Association of American Publishers called on Meta to drop the new terms.

“In putting forth these onerous terms of service Meta is implicitly acknowledging that permission is required for them to use creative works to develop and improve their products,” said Maria A. Pallante, AAP president and CEO in a statement. “But at the same time this mega-corporation is abusing its dominant market power by compelling such consent from any commercial user who connects to any of their platforms.”
At some point after Nieman Lab's report, Meta removed the word “train” from the updated terms. The company says the update is not about scraping news sites.
Meta on Oct. 29 said it was listening to feedback and said for now its existing terms remain in place.
“We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” Stone posted on X.
The Norwegian MBL said it wasn't satisfied with the postponement and Meta's assurances were insufficient.

“This is about people’s access to trustworthy and critical journalism,” Randi S. Øgrey, CEO of the Norwegian MBL, said in a statement. “When the financial foundations of independent news media are weakened, media diversity and the democratic public sphere are at stake.”

She said Norwegian media had three demands: Meta should commit in its new terms to respecting publishers’ reservations against scraping; using journalism in AI products should happen only after a separate, voluntary agreement and with payment; and publishers who do not sign the new terms should not be marginalized on Meta’s social platforms.
The Movement for an Open Web, the group which originally complained to the CMA, called Meta's move and the regulator's investigation a “significant win," but warned it was only the start.

“Unless the CMA and other regulators make it abundantly and quickly clear that this sort of anti-competitive landgrab is not acceptable, then we will continue to see the tech giants throwing their weight around in this way," said Tim Cowen from MOW.
The European Union executive body, the European Commission, confirmed it had discussed the proposed new terms with Meta and welcomed the postponement of their entry into force.

Spokesperson Sara Simonini said the commission was committed to ensuring that Meta’s practices comply with EU law, which prohibits a company from abusing its dominant market position and requires “gatekeeper” companies such as Meta to offer fair terms of use to businesses using their social platforms.

Simonini also said the EU executive had asked unspecified providers of AI models to give details about what training material they use, in line with the EU’s new AI Act adopted in 2024 and currently being implemented.
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland.

title: NASA space telescope plunges to Earth after two decades studying cosmic explosions
summary: One of NASA's premier space telescopes has plunged to Earth, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe's biggest explosions
story: One of NASA's premier space telescopes has plunged to Earth, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe's biggest explosions
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- One of NASA’s premier space telescopes plunged to Earth on Wednesday, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe’s biggest explosions.
The Swift Observatory’s demise came less than three months after a long-shot rescue mission failed.
The U.S. Space Force confirmed Swift’s reentry near Indonesia after tracking its sinking orbit, the result of intense solar activity the past few years.
NASA hired a private company to whip together an orbit-boosting effort, but Katalyst Space's three-armed robotic craft ran into trouble following its July launch and came crashing down in September.
It was not immediately known how much of the 1 ½-ton spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere. NASA anticipated some of the denser pieces surviving.

Swift rocketed into orbit in 2004 on what was expected to be a two-year study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars. It observed thousands of them over a mission that lasted 11 times longer than planned, serving as a first responder for other telescopes that could probe deeper.

NASA is gauging industry’s interest in mounting a rescue mission for another observatory whose orbit is being chipped away by solar storms: the Hubble Space Telescope. Launched in 1990, Hubble is expected to come crashing down by the mid-2030s, according to recent analyses.

The space agency is looking for input from private companies on whether and how they might boost Hubble’s orbit, upgrade its systems or guide it to a controlled reentry — or all three. Any such mission would need to happen by 2032.
Unlike the rush job with Swift, the space agency has more time to explore options for saving Hubble, said Nicky Fox, NASA’s science mission chief.

“Hubble still has important science ahead of it,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement, “and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible.”

title: Cyberattack hits French blood bank site but no blood products were compromised
summary: French authorities have reported a cyberattack on several blood banks that attempted to raise temperatures to dangerous levels
story: French authorities have reported a cyberattack on several blood banks that attempted to raise temperatures to dangerous levels

PARIS -- A cyberattack on several blood banks sought to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.

The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).

The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday.
“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” it said. The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites.
The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the statement said.
“Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.

title: El-Sayed: Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious'
summary: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed joins "This Week" after his historic victory against Republican Mike Rogers in the midterm election.
story: The Michigan senator-elect called the president "an unserious fool."

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said Sunday that Democrats will work with President Donald Trump to help the American people if "he wants to act serious," but if the president instead chooses "foolishness," the incoming senator said he will not find a willing partner in Congress.

"Let's talk about how he is an unserious fool. Think about this war in Iran that every single president had resisted fighting because, of course, it was a dumb idea," El-Sayed told ABC "This Week" in an exclusive interview. "Let's talk about the foolishness of a tariff war with Canada. ... Let's talk about the foolishness of gutting Medicaid to pass tax cuts for the richest people in America."

"So look, if he wants to act serious, we are happy to work alongside him to actually address these issues," El-Sayed continued. "He is the president of the United States. But if he wants to continue to fool, he will hire people like Stephen Miller to run the White House, and he gets to choose where he goes next."
President Trump on Friday said White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller would assume the role of chief of staff effective Monday, replacing Susie Wiles.

With his victory in Michigan's Senate race last Tuesday, El-Sayed is set to make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. During his campaign, El-Sayed said he focused his message on three issues: "to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for all."

But the issue that most defined both the contentious and close primary campaign against fellow Democrat Haley Stevens and the general election campaign against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers was U.S. support for Israel. El-Sayed has been a staunch critic of the Israeli government and U.S. military aid to Israel.
Asked on "This Week" if he's heard from his Republican opponent, El-Sayed said, "Not that I know of. I think he had a flight to catch to Florida."

Despite differences and his criticism of Trump, El-Sayed did say he would be willing to work with the president if it would help "advance the goals I ran on, to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All."
"I've said this, if he wants to pass Trump care for all, which will guarantee health care to everyone and put his name on it like he's putting his name on everything, I'm game,” El-Sayed said.

Karl also pressed El-Sayed on his past criticism of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. El-Sayed said that he and Schumer “figured out how to work together” during the campaign but he did not pledge to support a Schumer bid to become majority leader.
“The question to me is, who wants to be the leader who's going to make sure that we deliver on the mandate that we just got? I want to see who else is in the running,” El-Sayed said.

El-Sayed voiced support for Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who has not publicly announced intention to become majority leader. El-Sayed stressed that he is looking for a leader “who is ready to take action on day one,” adding that he has “not been impressed by what we've been able to do.”

“I want leadership who is going to deliver on the goal of getting money out of politics, put money in pockets, passed Medicare for all. As you know, a vote is a choice between two or more options. I don't know what those options are, but I am committed to making sure that we can deliver on the goals that we need, and we need action now,” El-Sayed said.

El-Sayed also reflected on his own journey to becoming Michigan’s next senator, again recounting a story from 2007 where he gave a speech to his graduating college class, and the commencement speaker, former President Bill Clinton, told him to run for office. El-Sayed said he initially dismissed the former president.
“I laughed in his face. I said, ‘Mr. President, I don't know if you saw my name. It's got 11 letters in it. People like me don't get to run for office.’”
El-Sayed said it was watching President Barack Obama get elected the following year that opened the path for him to run for office.

“[President Clinton] saw something in me I'd never seen in myself. And President Obama showed me something in me I'd never seen in myself. And 19 years later, I'm grateful to be the senator-elect from the state of Michigan,” said El-Sayed.

title: Iran live updates: Saudis say Houthi missiles targeted Riyadh, Aramco tower damaged
summary: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
story: The Houthis have been launching attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure.

Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.

Tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO says
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday night.

The unnamed tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz," the alert read. "All crew are safe and accounted for and there is no reported environmental impact at this time."

In another incident on Saturday night, the UKMTO said "military authorities" reported a tanker on fire in the Strait of Hormuz which resulted in the evacuation of the ship's crew. The incident occurred 8 nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, the UKMTO said.
Houthi attack damaged Aramco building in Riyadh, Saudi Energy Ministry says
Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry on Sunday confirmed that a building in Riyadh owned by the country's state-owned energy giant Aramco was damaged during a Houthi attack on the city.
"The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported," the ministry said in a statement posted to X.
Saudi Arabia says Houthi missiles targeted Riyadh

Saudi Arabian military spokesperson Col. Turki al-Maliki said in a series of posts to X on Sunday that Saudi air defenses intercepted three Houthi ballistic missiles, two cruise missiles and one drone launched toward Saudi regions.
Two of the ballistic missiles and both cruise missiles targeted the capital Riyadh, Maliki said.
Saudi Arabia issues safety warnings for Riyadh, Najran
The General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defense on Sunday morning issues safety warnings for the capital city of Riyadh and for the southwestern city of Najran.
Shortly after the warnings were issued, the directorate said the danger had passed in both areas.
The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have been firing missiles and drones toward Saudi cities and critical infrastructure sites in recent months.

title: 2 shootings at Winston-Salem State during homecoming weekend leave 1 dead
summary: It is too early to tell whether the shootings were connected, police say.
story: It is too early to tell whether the shootings were connected, police say.
WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. -- Two separate shootings during homecoming weekend at a historically Black college in North Carolina have left one person dead and three injured, police said Sunday.

Assistant Police Chief Jason Swaim of the Winston-Salem Police Department said both shootings occurred on Saturday on the campus of Winston-Salem State University, but that it was too early to tell whether the shootings were connected.
Authorities are investigating, and the campus is safe. An earlier lockdown has been lifted. He did not say whether any arrests have been made.
“At this point, the investigation is still very early in its preliminary stages,” Swaim said at a press conference early Sunday.

Chancellor Bonita J. Brown issued a statement Sunday morning, saying “this senseless violence” has shaken the community and that all remaining homecoming events were canceled. Instead, a local church planned to lead a call for prayers in support of the university.
Brown said additional law enforcement would remain on campus while the investigation continues and that counseling was available for anyone who needed.

“We also recognize the concern and anxiety these events have created among our students, parents, families and broader community,” Brown said. “We take our responsibility for campus safety seriously and remain committed to the well-being of everyone who is part of our university community.”

title: Election 2026 live updates: Trump says US took 'giant step back' through midterms
summary: President Donald Trump continued to criticize the results of Tuesday's midterm elections.
story: Trump blamed the results for last week's stock market sell-off.
Democrats won several key races in the high-stakes midterm elections -- with ABC News projecting that Democrats will take control of the Senate and the House.

10:57 AM ESTBlanche says 'there could be' investigations of Dems pushing oversight probes
Nov 07, 2026, 5:10 PM ESTTrump says DOJ should probe Dems for alleged threats, does not provide evidence

Blanche says 'there could be' investigations of Dems pushing oversight probes

Attorney General Todd Blanche suggested in an interview Sunday that there could be investigations of Democrats pushing oversight probes into President Donald Trump's administration, despite no evidence that such calls could amount to criminal threats.
"It depends on what's said. So, yes, there could be," Blanche said in an interview on CNN's "State of the Union" program, when asked if there could be such investigations.

"You have free speech in this country. You are allowed to be critical of President Trump, of me, of this administration. But when the threats become so vile and so dangerous that you are telling people in college that they better be careful if they want to work in the Trump administration because somebody will come after them, at some point, you have to draw the line," Blanche said.

Blanche's comments follow Trump's social media post on Saturday directing the Justice Department to investigate Democrats who have previewed plans for aggressive oversight probes into administration officials following Tuesday's midterms.
-ABC News' Alexander Mallin
Trump says US took 'giant step back' through midterm results

President Donald Trump continued to criticize the results of Tuesday's midterm elections, saying in a post to social media on Sunday that they represented a "giant step back in History" for the U.S. and blaming them for the past week's stock market sell-off.

"America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election -- Even the Stock Market, which has been a 'ROCKETSHIP' under 'TRUMP,' took a one day, 3 Trillion Dollar loss. But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!" Trump wrote.
-ABC News' Nicholas Kerr
Trump says DOJ should probe Dems for alleged threats, does not provide evidence

President Donald Trump is claiming, without providing evidence, that Democratic leaders are sending "threatening" letters and messages to Republicans and that he is directing the Department of Justice to investigate this alleged "criminal act."

"Threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat Political Leaders. By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" he wrote on his social media platform.

The president does not specify what "letters" he is referring to or how this would constitute a "criminal act." This allegation comes in a long post slamming Democrats for suggesting impeachment efforts of Cabinet members, with the president accusing them of "extortion" and insisting that his administration has not committed any wrongdoing.

"The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others, with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so, and there have been no impeachable acts committed, or even thought of, by the victims of this illegal process. This is extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable for this," Trump said.

This comes after Democrats reclaimed both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, prompting anticipation of new congressional oversight. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie is expected to reintroduce a privileged resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which could come as early as Monday.
Trump also claimed, without providing evidence, that Democrats are "threatening" Republican donors simply for their party affiliation, with the president referring to this as "weaponization."
-ABC News’ Emily Chang
Nithya Raman promises smooth transition of power
Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman made her first public appearance Thursday night, giving her victory speech after incumbent Mayor Karen Bass conceded the Los Angeles mayor's race.

Raman spoke to a gaggle of reporters and unsuspecting patrons at the Original Farmer's Market, saying she's made amends with Bass and City Hall over phone calls and is now focused on gaining public trust.

Raman also paid tribute to the mayor and thanked her for her service. She mentioned she and Bass have agreed to a smooth transition of power and went on to add that she's committed to working in tandem with city council.

"No matter what happened during the campaign, that is in the past now. And all of us, every single member of that city council and I are here because we love Los Angeles and we know that we need to work together in order to address the challenges that we have ahead," she said.
Raman added that her priority is instilling public trust in city government.

"I want to tell every single Angeleno out there, I am going to work so hard. And everyone behind me is going to work so hard to earn your trust, to earn you trust, and to earn the trust. To earn the trust of everyone across this city and to make people believe in Los Angeles again, to make believe in its City Hall again."
-ABC News' Clarissa Gonzales

title: Ron DeSantis hasn't made final decision on 2028 run: Sources
summary: In the days leading up to and after the midterms, DeSantis has ramped up his media appearances, reflecting on what went wrong for the Republican Party.
story: DeSantis said Florida fended off a blue wave in this year's midterm elections.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is keeping his options open for another presidential run, according to two people familiar with his thinking, after the governor said Florida fended off a blue wave in this year's midterm elections.

But the sources stressed that DeSantis is still watching the political environment to see whether he will perform well, whether there is a lane for him to break through, and whether he has something to offer the Republican Party and the country.
ABC News has reached out to DeSantis' office for comment on his plans.
In the days leading up to and after the midterms, DeSantis has ramped up his media appearances, reflecting on what went wrong for the Republican Party in this year's cycle.

The day after the midterm elections, DeSantis held a press conference where he described Tuesday's elections as a "meteor strike," arguing that even a "wave" fails to capture the scale of the Republican losses.

"Last night, we witnessed, to call it a wave, I don't think would be fully accurate. It's the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States, blue states, red states, everything in between, and the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida," DeSantis said Wednesday in Florida during a press conference.
DeSantis did not mince his words about the midterm election results for Republicans across the country, calling it "close to an extinction-level event" for the party.
DeSantis offered his analysis of what went wrong for Republicans, including what he said was a lack of positive messages from candidates to run on and messaging that didn't land with voters.
Prior to the midterm elections, DeSantis said in an interview that Republicans were "gaslighting" voters on gas prices, which have been impacted by the Iran war.

"Some of these Republicans are saying, 'Oh, well, the gas don't worry, you know, it's no big deal.' Like they're trying to blame Biden for it. No, no, listen, we just got to be honest. Gas is higher; it hurts people, working-class people, and it's higher because of this conflict. That's just a fact. If you can't admit that to voters, then you're gaslighting them, and they're not going to listen to you on other things," DeSantis said in an interview with Stephen A. Smith that aired on Monday.

DeSantis mounted an unsuccessful presidential bid in 2024, running against President Donald Trump and ultimately dropping out of the race right before the New Hampshire primary. He also finished a distant second behind Trump in the Iowa caucuses.
DeSantis' 2024 campaign was marred by political infighting that drew national attention and was complicated by overspending despite receiving immense donor support.

DeSantis has also taken lessons from his presidential campaign, including the need to do more media and that he cannot wait too long to enter the presidential race, a person familiar with DeSantis thinking told ABC News.
DeSantis' term as Florida governor ends in January.

title: Democrats flip statehouses in midterm wave
summary: The showing across the country that flipped Congress to Democratic control on Election Day also trickled down to the state and local level.
story: They're projected to control at least 10 more legislative chambers in 2027.

The Democratic wave that flipped control of Congress from Republicans on Election Day also washed through to the state and local level, with several legislatures seeing historic changes in their balance of power.

Democrats are now projected to control at least 10 more legislative chambers in 2027, with at least six states now having full Democratic control of the governor's office and both chambers of state legislatures, according to projections from The Associated Press as of Friday.
Those states where Democrats achieved "trifectas" are Arizona, Minnesota, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Wisconsin.

That could have major implications for policies in these states on issues ranging from abortion access to economic policy and congressional redistricting. In many cases, state laws and policies become the blueprints for federal laws.

"So it's going to be hard to get anything done at the federal level, so all the action and opportunities will be in the state," Leslie Martes, chief executive officer at Forward Majority, a super PAC focused on state legislatures, told ABC News.

Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, told ABC News, "I think without question, we affected generational change in our state capitals across the country. This is going to usher in an entirely different perspective of leadership in the states, and states are where things get done."
Here's a look at some of the states where Democrats either notched trifectas or broke Republican holds on state government.
Georgia

Democrats swept every race for statewide office, with Black women -- who have been hailed as the backbone of the Democratic Party -- winning races for governor, secretary of state and attorney general.
Democrats also won control of the Georgia House of Representatives for the first time in more than two decades and narrowed Republicans' majority in the state Senate.

Georgians are already beginning to see policy shifts in light of Democrats' victory. One day after the election, outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp announced he would not call a special session to redraw the state's congressional lines or limit Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms' power, saying, "The voters of our state have spoken. As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state."

At a post-election news conference on Friday, Bottoms indicated that expanding Medicaid in Georgia will be a priority for her and that she would consult with leaders in the legislature about possible steps they could take to change Georgia's six-week abortion ban.
Pennsylvania
Democrats had already been hoping to hold onto the state House and flip control of the GOP-held state Senate, a major goal for Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and the state Democratic Party.
They achieved that goal, with Shapiro winning reelection and by flipping four seats in the state Senate.
They're projected to have 26 seats in the state Senate to Republicans' 24, according to The Associated Press, while maintaining a comfortable majority in the state House.

As for what they'll do with the trifecta, Shapiro said Wednesday, "We will fund mass transit. We will raise the minimum wage. We will make sure that women have a right to reproductive freedom here in this Commonwealth. We will build more housing. We will allow survivors of abuse the ability to confront their abusers in court."
Nevada
In Nevada, Democrats retained control of both chambers and with Aaron Ford winning his gubernatorial race against outgoing Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, Democrats will secure a trifecta.
With all three branches of government in their control, Democrats could repeal Nevada's "right-to-work" law that lets workers get union benefits without paying dues, which Ford has pledged to do.
Texas

In the Texas gubernatorial race, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and became the first Democrat elected governor of Texas in more than 30 years. She also became the first Hispanic woman to be elected governor in the state.
Voters flipped the state House, breaking the trifecta Republicans have held since 2003. However, Republicans will still control the state Senate, according to The Associated Press.

Incoming Democratic Texas Attorney General Nathan Johnson told ABC News that he would scale back abortion law enforcement in the state, which comes after Attorney General Ken Paxton's office had aggressively enforced restrictive abortion laws.

"[Paxton's] been using the law to scare physicians, to scare women, to scare their families, to intimidate doctors out of providing, in some cases, life-preserving care or reproductive-preserving care. And I want physicians to know that I'm not going to interpret the law in a way that infringes upon their professional judgment or their relationship," Johnson said.
Wisconsin
Some Wisconsin Democrats warned ahead of the election that the gubernatorial race was flying under the radar and the blue wave may look more like a "ripple" in the swing state.
Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, defeated Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany to become the state's first Black governor.

And for the first time in nearly two decades, Democrats in Wisconsin flipped control of both legislative chambers. Democrats flipped three seats in the state Senate and eight seats in the state Assembly, according to The Associated Press.
The state government trifecta "would be a sea change," state Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein told ABC News ahead of Election Day.
Democrats told ABC News they would focus on addressing affordability concerns, public education funding, data centers and protecting voting and reproductive rights.
Halle Troadec and Clarissa Gonzalez contributed to this report

title: Trump says chief of staff Susie Wiles out, Stephen Miller will replace her
summary: Trump said his top aide Stephen Miller will replace her in the job.
story: Trump said his top aide Stephen Miller will replace her in the job.
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is exiting the White House, President Donald Trump said in a social media post on Friday.

Deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller -- a Trump loyalist, longtime political adviser and shaper of the president's immigration policies -- will take over on Monday, Trump said. Wiles will move over to the Trump political operation, he added.
The move marks a shake-up in Trump’s top advisers and comes after the historic midterm election earlier this week, which saw Democrats take control of both the House and the Senate.
In a social media post, Miller said that he is "honored beyond words" to have been selected for the role and thanked Wiles for her "devoted service" and "friendship."
"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic," Miller said.
As he departed the White House on Friday, Trump told reporters that he "wanted to make a change" with his chief of staff, adding that Wiles had done a good job.

But sources tell ABC News that Trump was privately blaming Wiles for his midterm's losses. Once that became clear, sources said Wiles made the decision to submit her resignation, which she did Thursday night.
Wiles confirmed that Friday would be her last day in the position in a statement on social media, saying that serving in her role "has been the honor of a lifetime."
"While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will," Wiles wrote.
Wiles was the first person that Trump named to his White House staff following his 2024 election victory, becoming the first female White House chief of staff.

"Susie Wiles just helped me achieve one of the greatest political victories in American history, and was an integral part of both my 2016 and 2020 successful campaigns," Trump said in a statement at the time appointing her to the position.
As questions previously swirled about Wiles's future in the administration, President Trump came to her defense as recently as three weeks ago.
"Susie is here, and she's going to be here for a long time," Trump said in October.

She was a key ally to the president as he sought to orchestrate his return to office in the aftermath of his 2020 election loss that resulted in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. Wiles, who served as campaign manager for the entirety of Trump's 2024 run, was known for running a tight ship and staying away from the spotlight and social media.
