It's not entirely clear when the Alien Throne came down, as poor road conditions kept Winters from visiting for a couple weeks. He had not seen any other posts about the feature's status until he rounded that corner Oct. 30 and saw it in pieces.
Social media posts ranged from those who were thankful they were able to see the formations and immortalize them with photographs to those lamenting that they never had the chance.
Condolences also were sprinkled in with debates about physics and the fragility of natural wonders.
“Gravity. It’s not just a good idea … it’s the law,” one joked.

For Winters and other Native Americans from the region, they’re more than just rock formations. They have served as waypoints, guiding ancestors along trade routes for thousands of years, and as connecting threads in stories handed down through generations.

“They are culturally relevant to our identity and our stories,” he said, adding that their legacies will be carried on through photographs, illustrations and in the stories people share about their time spent in this stretch of desert.
He called on people to let the sites “rest.” So no climbing on what remains, and certainly don't take any pieces home.

It's far off the beaten path down a rutted, washboard dirt road. But it's worth it, said Alan Studt of Parma, Ohio, who made his first visit in 2019 and then again last April as part of a 50-day road trip.

In looking back through his earlier photographs, he could see the formations were weathering. There were new holes forming in the throne and cracks along the wing's base, making it no surprise they would not last forever.

Studt spent hours exploring and photographing the hills and washes during this last trip. He described being drawn in each time he saw a new set of spires in the distance, marveling at the petrified wood along the way and the rainbow of colors in the soils.
“It is really so magical to be out there,” he said.

title: Grieving father of Learjet co-pilot defends his daughter's reputation after crash
summary: "She showed me what it is to be a hero," he said at a news conference.
story: "She showed me what it is to be a hero," he said at a news conference.

The father of the 20-year-old co-pilot killed alongside eight others in a Florida Learjet crash said Friday he has repeatedly listened to her final radio transmissions, searching for answers and finding pride in how she handled the crisis.
Allan Filgueiras, a pilot who helped teach Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras to fly, said he marveled at how “she's tough” even as the plane plunged straight toward the ground Sunday.
“I wanted to be by her side. Inside the plane, to help,” he said at a news conference, often holding back tears.

“She showed me what it is to be a hero,” he said, “because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys — military or whatever — they can’t handle. And she was the one over there to the last minute fighting.”

Nathalia Filgueiras can first be heard calmly telling air traffic control about ice buildup on the plane as it flew into a thunderstorm. Turbulence tossed it up and down by 700 feet (200 meters), but the situation quickly escalated as the aircraft fell at breathtaking speed. “Declare an emergency 722-Bravo-Delta. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute!” she said.

Her father and aviation safety experts have praised her composure as she called out updates while knowing the plane's fate was sealed. The captain, 55-year-old Jeff Gregory, is believed to have been at the controls.
“For the family — it’s like having the heart torn from my chest,” Allan Filgueiras said in Spanish. “I have to find a way to go on living.”

The family has challenged online criticism questioning whether she had enough experience to be in the cockpit of a high-performance business jet. She had more than 1,300 hours of experience and completed extensive training to earn her commercial pilot’s license and Learjet certification.
Her father's attorney, Stuart Grossman, said the news conference aimed to “preserve not just her memory, but her reputation.”

“She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years,” Grossman said, noting there were no immediate plans for any lawsuit.

The National Transportation Safety Board has not yet determined what caused the crash. The Learjet accelerated beyond its design limits as it fell, and pieces of its tail were found miles away from the crash site, which is a deep crater on the edge of a road. Investigators were still searching the area Friday after finding part of an engine a day earlier. The cockpit recorder remains missing.

Allan Filgueiras said he helped teach her how to fly after taking her aloft for the first time at age 12. Once she got a job as a pilot, she told him she couldn’t believe she was getting paid to do something she loved.
“It was her happiest moment, to fly,” he said.
Her mentor and instructor, Chris Kirk, said she earned her position through dedication and perseverance by putting in hard work and long hours.
During her Learjet 60 check ride in March, the examiner was so impressed he thought she had more than 5,000 hours of experience — nearly four times the amount of flight time she had logged.

Kirk said her professionalism was evident in those final radio transmissions, which gave the NTSB important information. Many members of the military special forces who Kirk worked with probably couldn't keep their wits in a similar situation.
“This was an incredible human being,” Kirk said, “who did a job that very few people would have been able to do under a duress that’s unimaginable.”

Retired airline pilot John Cox said earlier this week that his career began similarly to Nathalia Filgueiras', as he started flying professionally at age 19. He said she had done well to earn a Learjet co-pilot's seat.

“To be in the right seat of a Lear 60, she had to impress somebody, because that’s a good ride. I mean, that’s great. I know she loved it,” said Cox, who now runs Safety Operating Systems, an aviation consulting company.

The other crash victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family’s nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed. The other two victims were Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, who owned the Arca Boutique Hotel in Honduras.

title: Bank of England raises main interest rate a quarter point to 4% as Iran war stokes inflation
summary: Bank of England raises main interest rate a quarter point to 4% as Iran war stokes inflation
story: Bank of England raises main interest rate a quarter point to 4% as Iran war stokes inflation
LONDON -- Bank of England raises main interest rate a quarter point to 4% as Iran war stokes inflation.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates Thursday for the first time in more than three years in order to tackle the inflation shock caused by the Iran war.

With inflation predicted to rise further over the coming months, economists reckon the nine policymakers on the Monetary Policy Committee have little option but to increase the bank's key rate to 4% from 3.75%. The anticipated increase would be the first since August 2023.

The pressure on rate-setters has grown steadily over recent months, but the rise in inflation to an 11-month high of 3.5% in September — above their target of 2% — cemented market expectations of a rate hike this month and potentially more in 2027.

The main cause behind the spike in inflation this year has been the sharp rise in fuel costs as a result of the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz, which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies.

“We imagine that many committee members’ patience with the recent rise in inflation has worn thin," said Ellie Henderson, an economist at Investec. “The longer energy prices remain elevated, the greater the risk that a temporary price shock becomes more permanent."

Accompanying the expected rate hike will be the bank’s quarterly economic projections, notably those for inflation and growth. Higher interest rates cool the economy by making it more expensive to borrow, thereby bearing down on spending and inflation, but growth too.

Those projections are highly uncertain though — even more so than usual — because the economic outlook hinges hugely on what happens with regard to the Iran war. The heavy losses suffered by the Republican Party in the U.S. midterm elections have resulted in a sharp fall in energy prices.

If the falls in oil and gas prices are sustained over the coming weeks, then the upcoming peak in inflation will likely be lower, which could temper expectations of further rate hikes, not just by the Bank of England.

Others, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, have raised rates recently in response to the higher inflation stoked by the Iran war, and forecasts for their interest rate strategy are largely contingent on what happens to the price of energy.
Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.

title: Judge accepts ex-NFL star Brown's guilty plea to reduced charge, sentences probation
summary: Former NFL star Antonio Brown has pleaded guilty to aggravated assault with a firearm in connection with a 2025 shooting in Miami
story: Former NFL star Antonio Brown has pleaded guilty to aggravated assault with a firearm in connection with a 2025 shooting in Miami
MIAMI -- Former NFL star Antonio Brown pleaded guilty Friday to aggravated assault with a firearm in connection with a 2025 shooting outside a celebrity boxing match in Miami.
Judge Marisa Tinkler Mendez sentenced Brown to three years of probation during which time he will have to attend weekly counseling sessions and not possess a firearm, among other conditions.
He would not have any criminal conviction under the plea and could seek an early termination of probation at about the halfway mark of the sentence so long as all terms are met.
The plea to the reduced charge, which Brown entered in state court in Miami, allows the All-Pro wide receiver to avoid prison time.
Brown had initially been charged with attempted murder after police say he grabbed a handgun from a security staffer at the event and fired two shots at a man he had been in a fistfight with earlier.

title: World shares mostly gain after US midterm elections as AI-related stocks sink
summary: World shares are mostly higher though heavy selling of artificial intelligence-related stocks offset gains for some markets following the U.S. midterm elections
story: World shares are mostly higher though heavy selling of artificial intelligence-related stocks offset gains for some markets following the U.S. midterm elections
World shares were mostly higher Thursday, though heavy selling of artificial intelligence-related stocks offset gains for some markets following the U.S. midterm elections.

South Korea’s Kospi sank more than 5% and the Nikkei 225 in Tokyo lost nearly 2%. Oil prices were mixed after the Dow industrials jumped more than 3% on Wednesday following the Republicans' loss of control of the U.S. Congress.
In early European trading, the German DAX rose 0.6% to 26,598.03, while the CAC 40 in Paris surged 1.2% to 8,276.55. The United Kingdom's FTSE 100 gained 1% to 10,935.08.

The future for the S&P 500 was nearly unchanged, while that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.4%. On Wednesday, the S&P 500 jumped 1.6%. The Dow surged more than 1,500 points, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.4%.

U.S. stocks usually climb following midterms, regardless of who wins. But technology shares have taken a hit as investors mull the potential impact on the boom in AI from a Congress led by Democratic Party lawmakers from January.
The Kospi, which has gyrated through waves of selling and buying driven by the AI frenzy, tumbled 5.3% to 5,383.80.
Shares in Samsung Electronics sank 7.6%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix lost 9.4%.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 fell 1.8% to 61,077.90. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group shed 6.9%, while computer chipmaking equipment company Tokyo Electron skidded 9.5%. Testing equipment maker Advantest tumbled 15%.
Taiwan's Taiex lost 3.2%.
Asian markets less heavily exposed to the AI industry mostly climbed Thursday. Hong Kong's Hang Seng jumped 3.7% to 24,796.98. The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.1% higher, to 3,689.91.
In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 rose 2.6% to 9,065.10, while India's Sensex gained 2.8%.

“Global equity markets mostly welcomed the strong win by Democrats, with European and Chinese markets surfing on hopes that the Democratic shift in Congress could increase pressure to undo some tariffs and restore stronger trade ties with the U.S.,” Ipek Ozkardeskaya of Swissquote said in a commentary.

However, she noted, with regard to AI, “The Democratic victory is expected to become a potential obstacle to an investment story already facing questions over massive spending, future returns and financing.”
On Wall Street, stocks of hospital owners and dollar stores serving low-income Americans helped lead the widespread rally on Wednesday following the U.S. nationwide losses for Republicans.

Overall, the election may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. But investors generally prefer split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the U.S. economy.
But investors see risks ahead for U.S. President Donald Trump’s social media company, the AI industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.
Trump Media & Technology Group was one of the market’s bigger losers Wednesday, down 24.5%.
Since briefly touching a peak of $175 five years ago, it’s dropped to $4.49. Its main business is Truth Social, which is best known for Trump’s postings on the platform.
Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.3%, and SpaceX sank 3.8%. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress.

A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the Iran war, and that hurt stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the U.S. military. Lockheed Martin sank 6.9%; Northrop Grumman fell 4.5% and General Dynamics lost 2.6%.
The possibility of pressure to pull back on the war also sent the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, plunging 8.7% to $94.62.
Early Thursday, Brent crude rebounded, gaining 0.4% to $95.04 per barrel, while U.S. benchmark crude fell 0.3% to $87.86 per barrel.
In other dealings early Thursday, the U.S. dollar slipped to 158.22 Japanese yen from 158.41 yen. The euro rose to $1.1241 from $1.1228.

title: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns following bank collapse
summary: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns following bank collapse
story: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns following bank collapse
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay -- Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns following bank collapse.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.

Hours after Paraguay’s central bank seized Ueno Bank, a major digital lender that went from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, President Santiago Peña was facing impeachment, protesters were clashing with riot police and the bank's executives had been detained.
The swift collapse of a bank that claimed more than 60% of Paraguay’s adults as customers has sent shock waves through the country’s financial system.

By Thursday morning, a rebellion by several members of Peña's own conservative Colorado Party had become a party-wide revolt. Both of the ruling party’s main factions in the lower house pledged to back impeachment, with a debate scheduled for Thursday, after former President Horacio Cartes, the party’s powerful leader, withdrew his support for Peña.

Impeachment requires a two-thirds majority of lower house lawmakers present to send the case to the Senate, where another two-thirds vote would be needed to remove Peña, a 47-year-old former International Monetary Fund economist.

On Wednesday, before his own party turned against him, Peña had sought to move past the scandal in a video message, accepting no blame and promising to protect depositors’ savings. He also approved emergency payouts to depositors Wednesday and named a new central bank chief.
“Paraguay needs institutions that provide answers and protect our people’s resources,” he said.

The political upheaval and promises of relief leave a bigger question unanswered: how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno’s holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.

For many Paraguayans, the answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña’s long-ruling Colorado Party to the country’s regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.
“Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder.”

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno’s coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay’s giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees’ savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies.
Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank’s oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno’s loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno’s capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers’ accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what’s left.

Ueno’s app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks’ mobile apps, fueling public panic.
Officials appealed for calm and said they had begun repaying depositors, opening new accounts elsewhere for about 280,000 who had banked only with Ueno.
“The banking system is sound,” insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Peña’s request.

Authorities have detained eight senior Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud. Lawyers for several of the detained said they needed time to review the allegations before they could comment.

Hundreds of employees of Ueno Bank and other companies belonging to Grupo Vázquez, the bank’s parent conglomerate, protested outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages with their jobs in limbo and their salaries trapped at the failed bank. A day earlier, hundreds of retirees, depositors, university students and workers flooded the streets of Asunción, the capital.

“We want your head, Peña!” they shouted. Their signs demanded Peña’s impeachment, called him “the enemy of savers” and pleaded “Give us back our money.” Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber pellets to push back the crowds.

Many demonstrators saw Ueno’s collapse not just as the result of risky banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on the latest index of perceived corruption from Transparency International, a global watchdog.
“This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor,” said protester Belarmino Balbuena.
At the national stadium that once bore Ueno’s name, the bank’s logo had already been scrubbed away. But across the capital, fresh graffiti denounced politicians as thieves.
DeBre reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina.

title: Tesla’s Cybertruck heads for an exit after years of hype and division
summary: Tesla’s Cybertruck, the hulking, stainless-steel pickup that inspired devotion and derision with its science-fiction looks, will cease production next year
story: Tesla’s Cybertruck, the hulking, stainless-steel pickup that inspired devotion and derision with its science-fiction looks, will cease production next year
NEW YORK -- Tesla’s Cybertruck, the hulking, stainless-steel pickup that inspired devotion and derision with its science-fiction looks, will cease production next year.

CEO Elon Musk announced the model’s demise Friday with a curt post on X, his social media site, simply noting production of the vehicle “will be winding down” around the middle of 2027 at its facility outside Austin, Texas. Musk said the move was to allow increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi.
For the Cybertruck, a pet project of Musk who insisted it was Tesla’s best product, it marks an unceremonious end to one of the auto industry’s most ballyhooed debuts.

“Few vehicles in history have generated as much attention,” said Armen Hareyan, whose Torque News site covers autos. “The Cybertruck became a cultural symbol – loved, mocked and impossible to ignore.”

The Cybertruck rolled onto the scene in a dramatic unveiling in 2019, when a Tesla designer hurled a metal ball at the vehicle to demonstrate its supposedly unbreakable glass, only to see it shatter. He repeated the stunt on another window of the truck only to shatter that one, too.
Even as some critics scoffed, Musk was steadfast.

“I just wanted to make a futuristic battle tank — something that looks like it could come out of ‘Blade Runner’ or ‘Aliens’ or something like that but was also highly functional,” he told Automotive News. He called it “a better sports car than a Porsche 911” and “a better truck than an F-150.”
It struck some as the perfect vehicular reflection of the brash, convention-busting Musk.

“A really controversial vehicle unveiled by a controversial individual into a market where none of the electric trucks have been able to really capture demand,” said Spencer Penn, a former Tesla executive who left the company before the Cybertruck’s launch and now heads procurement software firm LightSource.

Penn remembered watching the unveiling and feeling initially revolted by the sight of the Cybertruck, calling its appearance “madness.” But the more he looked at it, the more his opinion changed. He signed up for a pre-sale reservation, though ended up not getting a Cybertruck when Musk’s promises of a price tag under $40,000 went unmet and the first trucks sold for double or more. Penn called the Cybertruck part of Tesla’s adventurous spirit that drives innovation.
“Some of these bets work and some of these bets don’t,” he said.
While the decision to end Cybertruck production may be driven by sales realities, it's also a reflection of Tesla’s shift to autonomous vehicles, on which Musk is betting the company’s future.

Musk once forecast he’d make 250,000 Cybertrucks a year. Kelley Blue Book estimated Tesla sold just 20,237 of the vehicles last year, down about half from the year prior. Sales through the end of September this year were down another 28%, according to Kelley Blue Book.

If the imposing, sharp-angled, dystopian appearance of the Cybertruck weren’t enough to turn many potential buyers away, Musk did so himself by allying with a panoply of right-wing figures, most notably U.S. President Donald Trump. He alienated some customers as his image morphed from eccentric innovator to polarizing force trading his billions for political influence.

Once-passionate Tesla drivers rushed to sell off their cars, or slapped stickers on the bumper declaring, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.” Organizers staged demonstrations outside Tesla showrooms and urged investors to dump shares of the company’s stock. Anger spilled into violence, with Molotov cocktails hurled at Tesla vehicles, charging stations set ablaze, and dealerships covered in graffiti.
Lovers of the Cybertruck became targets, too, subjected to shouts of “Nazi!” and extended middle fingers.
Ross Blankenship is one of them. When he first laid eyes on the Cybertruck, he felt transported to a world from his childhood, when he would play “Halo,” the sci-fi video game. He had to have it.

“I had that sort of child in me wanting to be part of something cool that would change the future of automotive,” Blankenship said in a call from his Cybertruck as he drove through Sunnyside, Colorado. Even as Blankenship found he agreed with Musk on politics, he hated seeing a vehicle he loved turned into a political symbol. “I never bought it for any other reason than the fascination with the future technology of trucks … so that was a little heartbreaking.”
He would buy another Cybertruck again in a heartbeat, calling its end “a sad moment.”

title: What to know about Pope Leo XIV's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
summary: Pope Leo XIV is returning home to the continent where he spent two decades as a missionary priest and learned to be a pastor, visiting Uruguay, Argentina and his second homeland of Peru
story: Pope Leo XIV is returning home to the continent where he spent two decades as a missionary priest and learned to be a pastor, visiting Uruguay, Argentina and his second homeland of Peru

VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV is returning home to the continent where he spent two decades as a missionary priest and learned to be a pastor, visiting Uruguay, Argentina and his second homeland of Peru.

The Nov. 6-17 trip marks the longest and farthest of his papacy and is coming just three weeks after Leo underwent surgery Oct. 13 to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Doctors nevertheless gave him the green light to make the trip.

Latin America still is home to around 40% of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, but the Catholic proportion of the region’s population has shrunk in recent year s and the decreases are especially notable in the countries Leo will visit.
The trip begins in Uruguay, whose secular identity and separation of church and state are so deeply entrenched that Christmas is officially “Family Day” and Holy Week is “Tourism Week.”

According to Vatican statistics, nearly 77% of Uruguay’s 3.5 million people are baptized Catholics. But more than half of all Uruguayans identify as religiously unaffiliated — the highest portion in Latin America – and only a fraction of those who identify as Catholic actually go to Mass regularly.

Leo’s itinerary includes a stop at a parish in Casavalle, a poor neighborhood on the outskirts of Montevideo plagued by drug trafficking and gang violence. The church works with national and municipal authorities on support initiatives, including housing construction and addiction recovery programs.

Leo will also celebrate Mass in Paysandú, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital and chosen because of its accessibility to those living north of the Río Negro, a river that crosses the country, and proximity to the Argentine city of Colón.

The visit begins with a welcome ceremony at the Plaza Independencia in the center of Montevideo, a symbol of Uruguay’s national identity and history. The plaza features a monument to independence hero José Gervasio Artigas.

But most significantly, Leo will mark an important Catholic feast day Nov. 8, which commemorates the Virgin of the Thirty-three, the patron of Uruguay and an icon deeply rooted in the country’s history and patriotism.

According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the small, wooden Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in the Uruguayan city of Florida on Aug. 25, 1825. It was to the virgin that the insurgents entrusted their faith.

By celebrating the feast day, paying homage to Artigas and celebrating Uruguay’s independence, Leo is expected to emphasize that Uruguay’s secular nationhood is intrinsically connected to its Catholic heritage. The goal is to suggest that there is still a place for faith today in even the most secular of countries.

Pope Francis’ refusal to return home to Argentina during his pontificate, and his polarizing tenure as both archbishop and pope, left a conflicted legacy that will dog Leo’s visit. But the American pope will formally honor his predecessor when he visits Buenos Aires’ cathedral and in a more symbolic way when he visits the federal prison where then-Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio ministered to inmates.
In the capital, Leo will also meet with libertarian President Javier Milei, who once called Francis “the representative of evil on Earth.” Milei later apologized.

Milei’s sweeping spending cuts, though, have strained relations with Argentine church leaders, who have criticized his government for cuts to disability funding and for putting economic orthodoxy ahead of the needs of the poor.

That flashpoint will be on display when Leo visits the Don Orione care home in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, a Catholic institution that houses more than 400 people with disabilities. The institution has reported facing extreme economic problems due to the spending cuts, outdated rates, inflation, and state payment delays.

Leo will also hear of economic woes when he meets with business leaders, trade unions, workers and social representatives at the Argentine Catholic University. Union leaders have said they intend to brief him on the crisis, including rising unemployment, poverty, and the erosion of household purchasing power.
According to official data, poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of the population during the first half of 2026, representing about 15 million people.

Another possible flashpoint between Milei and Leo could come over artificial intelligence. Milei, a Trump ally, has courted AI investment and data centers with promises of limited regulation, while Leo has warned about the threats to humanity and the environment of the AI race and called for strict, internationally policed safeguards on its development.

Leo will celebrate his first Mass in Argentina at Buenos Aires’ Monumento de los Españoles, where St. John Paul II led prayers for peace on June 12, 1982, during Argentina’s war with Britain over the Falkland Islands. John Paul, who also came in 1987, was the first and last pope to visit.
When Francis was elected, around 71% of Argentina’s population identified as Catholic, according to the Pew Research Center. That percentage has fallen to 58% in 2024.

And yet this year, in a prelude to Leo’s visit and despite persistent rain, a record of more than 2.8 million people took part in the annual pilgrimage south of Buenos Aires to the Basilica de Nuestra Señora de Luján, Argentina’s patron.

The highlight of Leo’s trip will certainly be his return to Peru and especially his diocese of Chiclayo, including the sprawling midsize city in northern Peru near the Pacific Coast. Leo will celebrate Mass in all his old stomping grounds including the mountain village of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.
Leo spent two decades ministering in Peru as a missionary priest and then bishop, and has credited the place and its people with shaping his view of the church and being a shepherd.

Because he knows the country so well, his speeches will be closely watched, especially one he'll deliver from the square in front of Lima's cathedral “on the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people.”

Peru, a nation of 34 million people, is beset by multiple challenges: the climate chaos of El Niño, violent crime, poverty and inequality. In 2025, 25.7% of the Peruvian population was living in monetary poverty.

Conservative President Keiko Fujimori came to power in July on promises of restoring order to a nation plagued by extortion and homicides. Illegal gold mining and the cultivation of coca leaves, the raw material used to produce cocaine, are affecting Indigenous peoples especially.
Leo will meet with popular groups in Cusco, in the Peruvian Andes, and will honor Peru's Indigenous peoples by travelling to Pucallpa, in Peru's Amazon to celebrate Mass.

Cusco was the capital of the Inca empire, an important city of Spanish colonial rule and today remains an important cultural destination, including the nearby ruins at Machu Picchu. He’ll celebrate Mass and pray in Cusco’s main square, where in 1781 the Indigenous hero Túpac Amaru II was killed following the most significant rebellion against the Spanish during the colonial era.

Huge crowds are expected to turn out to welcome Leo home, even though Peru has seen Catholicism fall in recent years. According to Pew, the Catholic population was at 76% in 2013-2014, but now stands at around 67%.

title: "The Altruists" actor Julia Garner on surprising herself
summary: In "The Altruists," the Emmy-winning star of "Ozark" plays Caroline Ellison, girlfriend of Sam Bankman-Fried and business partner in a multi-billion-dollar cryptocurrency fraud. Julia Garner talks about how, for her, the eyes truly are the windows to the soul.
story: Julia Garner has become known for her remarkable transformations. In the new Netflix series "The Altruists," she plays Caroline Ellison, the business partner and girlfriend of Sam Bankman-Fried, his accomplice in a multi-billion dollar fraud that led to the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX.

Her performance as Ellison has many mannerisms. Asked how she puts them together, Garner replied, "I notice everything. I do! I might look like I'm a little [whistling and gesturing like birds are fluttering overhead], but I'm not!

"You know, you can tell a lot with somebody's eyes," she said. "I look at photos, I obsess over photos. This sounds so crazy, but I'll cover half of their face and I'll just focus on their eyes. And I'm like, I want those eyes for that person that I am about to become."
Asked if she chooses characters based on complexity, she laughed, "Yes, but I feel like they also choose me!"
To watch a trailer for "The Altruists," click on the video player below:

Garner grew up in the Riverdale section of the Bronx, taking arts and crafts classes at the Wave Hill Cultural Center near her parents' home. Her father teaches art; her mother was an actress-turned-therapist ("Which is probably why I'm an actor," Garner said).

Describing herself as "deathly shy" growing up, Garner took her first acting class at 14. "Now when I look at my childhood, I think I was acting my whole life," she said. "Because I had lot of problems as a kid. I had a lot of, like, learning problems, and I always felt like such an outcast. And acting always protected me."

At 16, she landed her first film role in 2011's "Martha Marcy May Marlene." Garner's breakout would come in 2017 in the Netflix crime series "Ozark." Her performance as Ruth Langmore, a whip-smart hustler who runs a crime ring from a trailer park, would win her a Golden Globe and three Emmys.
"My life was so different before 'Ozark,'" she said.

Asked what playing Ruth taught her, Garner replied, "Not to be so scared. And then since then, for whatever reason, people are like, 'We're gonna hire her to play the most unhinged people. She's great for that!'"
She'd earn another Golden Globe nomination for "Inventing Anna" (2022), playing Russian-born Anna Sorokin, who conned New York society into believing she was a German heiress.
But the 32-year-old began to be unnerved by the attention she was getting: "I just didn't like the feeling of being watched all the time and it kind of got to my head," she said.
During the actors' strike in 2023, Garner signed up for a clown school in France: "I failed miserably at it, a lot of times. And you know what? It was the best feeling."

It was there she realized she felt ashamed of her own success – that she wasn't worthy of it. In class, her clown instructor called her out one day: "He's like, 'You are hiding from something, you feel a lot of shame, you are not comfortable. Look, let me see your eyes.' So, I had to open up."
What did she learn by opening up? "Not being afraid to fail," Garner said.
I noted, "I find it very interesting that he calls you out on your eyes, and you are someone who does so much with your eyes."
"But I didn't want someone to see my eyes, you see?" Garner replied. "I got a lot out of it. I'm still sometimes looking for my inner clown."
Aren't we all? "Well, I have a clown certificate!" Garner laughed.

Perhaps Garner's most famous role is in a film yet to be shot. Madonna picked her to play the singer in a biopic that was in development, but has since been shelved. Garner doesn't know if the film will get made: "Every hour it changes in a way," she said, adding, "It's not up to me. I would love for the movie to get made, obviously, but I also feel whatever happens, I made a great friend. I love Madonna, I think she's incredible. She works, like, she taught me properly, like, how to work."
The audition process required Garner to sing, dance, and act as Madonna. "I wasn't a trained dancer," she said.

Did she surprise herself? "Yeah, but I always try to," Garner said. "It's the same thing with the Caroline Ellison role. I really didn't want to recognize myself, like, at all. That's my goal. The thing that I'm concerned about always when I'm working is, how am I going to move people? How am going to affect people? How am gonna make people feel less alone? Because I remember growing up when I felt alone, and I watched a movie. It gave me this endless sense of hope, because I didn't feel alone. And that's the beauty of, you know, good acting."

title: With "Thrasher," Brandon Flowers returns home
summary: Smalltown Nephi, Utah, was where the musical sensibilities of Killers frontman Brandon Flowers started to take form, before finding success as a rock star in Las Vegas. Now his solo album, "Thrasher," is filled with country songs like those beloved by his dad.
story: The year was 2002, in Henderson, Nevada, and no one at the bar that night realized they were watching what would become one of the biggest bands in the world: The Killers. No one, that is, except maybe Brandon Flowers, who was barely 23 years old when The Killers shot to stardom with their first single, "Mr. Brightside," a story about being cheated on ripped from Flowers' own life, which became the anthem for a generation.

"I noticed early on, people would talk about the storytelling in Killers music, that they didn't always associate with young rock bands," Flowers said. "And I think that was when it first started to maybe dawn on me, where was I getting this from?"

Where he was getting it from turns out is Nephi, Utah, an hour and a half south of Salt Lake. It has one stoplight, and feels about as far away from rock & roll stardom as you could get. The family moved there from Las Vegas when Flowers was eight. "It's funny to look at it now, to say it was a culture shock," he said. "It really was, even though I was just a kid. My unit was my family, but there was something in me that still really felt planted in Las Vegas, and felt like that was part of my identity, you know? And it was something that I always wanted to go back to."

Flowers struggled to fit in, missing school to help his dad work on an apartment building, a family business. (His sister's name is still on the mailbox.) And to buy music in Nephi back then, he headed to the closest thing Nephi had to a record store: The Flying J Truck Stop. "They used to have these bins inside our Flying J that would just be full of cassettes, and you'd kind of mine through them," he said. "One particular treasure that I found was a Depeche Mode record there."

Another formative location in town? The local golf course. "This is the bar of the town," said Flowers. "This is where people can congregate and play a sport they love, but they can also drink. And so, there's sort of a subculture of guys that played golf here a lot. And so, that was my experience – my first cigarettes and my first chewing tobacco and alcohol was all here also." It was as close to Las Vegas as he was going to get in Nephi.
Flowers did end up back in Las Vegas for his senior year of high school, and it's where The Killers established themselves and rocketed to fame.

Btu these days, it's places like Nephi that actually inspire Flowers, which might be why his new solo album is country western, the kinds of songs his dad played on the radio. "It just really lends itself to the stories and to the characters and to detail," he said. "I was secretly absorbing it."
Gold and silvеr, God and glitter Lights that flicker on hubcap chrome On the road to Heaven In Strauss and Stetson Swimming pools of horsepower Take me back home-- From "The American Dream"
Brandon Flowers performs "The American Dream"

Flowers' latest solo project is called "Thrasher," filled with stories of his childhood. "One of my strongest memories, more so than getting beat up by a couple of country kids that were stronger than me, was [my dad] trying to teach me to fight," he said. "So, it's just an interesting thing to look back on. Now I have three sons, and I teach them to not fight."

Nine years ago, Flowers moved back to Utah with his wife and children, something he's glad he did now that they're leaving the nest. "They don't prepare you for this," he said. "You know, watching kids be young and that innocence and raising them was maybe the best, you know, felt like the greatest time for me. And now we just took one and dropped them off in Pennsylvania yesterday. It's just a tough thing to wrap your head around, letting them go."

Flowers, who's been a lifelong practicing Mormon AND a rock star, says he's looked to rock & roll's past for guidance on how to handle that balance. "One of the things I love about Elvis is, I see him as sort of like a spiritual progenitor and someone that, no matter what mistakes he made, you know – and we all know everything about Elvis – but just he was still deeply religious, and I think about that with Johnny Cash also, a couple of the people that always come to mind," Flowers said. "And they struggled with it, and so I'm able to learn from them and make my decisions based on, you know, you can read the books, you watch the documentaries, you watch the movie, you know how it would happen."
And sometimes it's learning from Elvis what to avoid? "Absolutely, yeah," said Flowers. "I mean, he was the first. He did everything. He did everything wrong and he did everything right."

To hear Flowers tell it, his true success wasn't found on the Vegas Strip or even on stadium stages. For him, his bright side has been found at home. "I mean, it's been a wild ride," he said. "I've been lucky. I have three sons, and me and my wife have been married for 21 years and it's just, those are the things you start to realize, what is success? I try to instill that into my children and show them I have a great time on stage, I love writing songs, it's fulfilling for me. But I am so happy walking down the street with you right now. You know, I have dinner, our routine, the things that we have implemented, like those are the things that feel like true success."

title: Judi Dench on an actor's life
summary: A film producer once told Judi Dench she had "everything wrong with her face." One Oscar and a Damehood later, she's had the last laugh. The actress, now 91, talks about her new memoir, "Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?"
story: Judi Dench has made a career out of delivering just the right words, such as ait ("It's an island in a river"). During a game of Bananagrams with a friend, we saw the 91-year-old is still very much in command. "Don't expect any vowels, because I've got them all," she laughed.
Although she can barely see the letters. "It's tricky if you're playing with an almost-blind person," she said.
Her eyesight is almost gone, robbed by macular degeneration, but there's no diminishing Dame Judi Dench.

She got her start on stage in 1957 as Ophelia in "Hamlet" at London's Old Vic Theatre. Her first starring role in film came 40 years later, in "Mrs. Brown." But her loyalties are clear. "Oh, theater, theater, theater, theater," Dench said.
Asked what she loves so much about the theater, she replied, "I love the fact of a group of people trying to get it better every night, whereas in film, they say 'Cut,' and you can't make it better."

A meeting with a movie producer early on was not encouraging: "'I'm sorry,' he said, 'you have every single thing wrong with your face.' So I said, 'Fine,' and I walked out and back to the glorious Old Vic."
She says that criticism didn't get to her: "No, because I didn't want to do films. But it must have stayed with me, and, I mean, I suppose my insides have dealt with it."

Her face would become one of the best-known in cinema. She has been nominated for eight Academy Awards, winning an Oscar for her portrayal of Queen Elizabeth I in "Shakespeare in Love"; and she's appeared in eight James Bond films as M, the steely MI6 boss, originally opposite Pierce Brosnan.

"Pierce came to lunch not long ago," Dench said. "When he got to the front door, what I'd forgotten was that I have a doormat which says, 'I've been expecting you, Mr. Bond…' He liked that. I think he thought I'd put it there for the occasion!"
What did they talk about? "Oh, everything, everything, of how frightened we were doing the first one together."
Why frightened of shooting a Bond film? "Well, the responsibility of the part," she said.

It's those sorts of stories that ended up in her new memoir, "Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?" Written with her friend of 30 years and fellow actor Brendan O'Hea, it's a series of conversations – the books reads like the two of them having a chat. "That is exactly how it evolved," Dench said. "He knows too much about me, and what he doesn't know, he makes up."

"Not true!" O'Hea interjected. "Working on this book has made me realize I knew Jude to be fun and generous and kind, and a fantastic, life-affirming human being, and a mischief-maker. But you realize all that was in embryo in her childhood. It was all there, and I think when you read about the childhood and your faith, your Quakerism, I think that is what's kind of probably shaped you."
"And being part of a happy family," she said. "How lucky."

At her home in England, she's planted trees in memory of friends and family, including her late husband, actor Michael Williams. She says it was friendship at first sight: "Yes, and a sense of humor, and daftness."
She planted a crabapple for Maggie Smith: "Well, because she was a terrific friend, and because she was unbelievably witty and funny. And I thought it actually suited her very well!"
Over the years, Dench has found herself in rather good company. She recalls a knock on her door and Sidney Poitier walking in. She felt 'completely dumbstruck" she said.
Does she really get starstruck still? "You are joking!" Dench replied.
But you're Dame Judi Dench! "Seth, that doesn't matter – Sidney Poitier!"
Yet, Dench doesn't believe that others might feel the same sense of awe when meeting her. "No, they don't," she said.

O'Hea said to Dench, "I think you mean that. I think that you are genuinely surprised when people come up to you and say nice things. You have no vanity. I think it goes back to that moment when that film producer said you have everything wrong with your face. I think something was lodged there."
"Did me a good service," Dench said. "I don't think I do have much vanity."
In her book, Dench is also very frank about aging. "There's nothing to be said for it, at all," she said. "I can't now read, I can't go to the theater."
And so, she says, she cannot take on roles anymore. "It's because I can't see, so there's nothing I can do."
But she does remember lines. "Oh yes, I can remember all sorts of lines," she said. "I could do an hour of Shakespeare for you now."
And so, we asked if she could give us an example. She recited from "Antony and Cleopatra," and did so flawlessly: Dame Judi Dench still has these lines deep in her.

I dreamt there was an Emperor AntonyO, such another sleep, that I might seeBut such another man …His legs bestrid the ocean, his reared armCrested the world. His voice was propertiedAs all the tuned spheres, and that to friends …For his bounty, there was no winter in 't …In his livery walked crowns and crownets;Think you there was, or might be such a man,as this I dreamed of?

title: Rob Sand's runway modeling past resurfaces after Iowa gubernatorial win
summary: Vogue asked on Instagram whether followers knew the Iowa governor-elect once modeled for Prada. A verified account for Sand, who was previously elected to the Iowa state auditor's office, replied affirmatively in the comments.
story: Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand, who won Tuesday's election, walked runways for Prada and other fashion houses while he was in college, according to Vogue.

Vogue asked on Instagram whether followers knew that Sand once modeled for Prada. A verified account for Sand, @robsandia, replied in the comments Thursday: "Yes, I knew that." The comment had more than 700 likes about 20 minutes later, and many replies were congratulatory.
"From runway to run USA ✨," one comment read, while another enthused, "THE biggest flex EVER for a politician plus 2 words: Italian Vogue. YES SIR! 👏 🔥"

Vogue reported that the modeling past surfaced on social media after his win, when a user reposted a video of Sand with a caption expressing disbelief that he once modeled. A Google search confirmed it, Vogue said.

The New York Times earlier reported, in a 2019 profile, that Sand briefly modeled in Paris and Milan while in college but does not like to talk about it. However, Sand's campaign confirmed to CBS News that he "did some modeling while in college in the early 2000s." And on X, formerly known as Twitter, Sand's campaign joked, "Audited: true." (Sand was previously elected to serve as Iowa's state auditor.)

Sand began modeling while attending Brown University, which Vogue described as a successful side hustle that took him to Milan. He walked for Prada, the Japanese label Number (N)ine and Giuliano Fujiwara, and appeared in editorial spreads, including a fall 2002 AnOther Magazine spread titled "Adolescents," Vogue reported.
Sand also previously told Newsweek that he missed a chance to caucus in 2004 in his hometown of Decorah, Iowa, because he was in Milan.
Sand defeated Republican Zach Lahn in Tuesday's race for governor earlier this week.

Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.
Choosing a Part
Have you always been in a position to choose which part you're going to play?

Of course not. And it's something I'll never take for granted. Mikey used to say, 'Always behave as if it's the last job you'll ever do.' I still carry the fear of not working. Or of never being asked again. You can't just expect to be employed in this business when there are so many terrific actors ready to step in.

I once knew an actor whose criteria for accepting a part depended on three questions: 'What's the billing? What's the money? What's the role?' In that order. I've also known actors who've turned down jobs because their character didn't say the last line of the play.

That's ridiculous. You'd never play Hamlet or Lady Macbeth. Was it Michael Caine who said he judged a script by its location, and if he fancied going to the place where it was being filmed, he'd accept the job? I know what he means. That's one of the reasons why I was so keen to do Mrs. Brown: a month in Scotland – bliss.
What are your own criteria for choosing a part?
I'm not very good at it, so I tend to leave it to others. When Mikey was alive, he would read any scripts I'd been sent and I'd totally trust his judgement.

I've never enjoyed reading scripts. I much prefer to be told the story – ideally by the director. When I met Stephen Frears to talk about the TV drama Going Gently, we went for a walk around Holland Park. It was lovely, being able to wander in the open air – no pressure, no expectations, nothing calculated – just listening to him tell me the story.

But some directors are more cunning – like Howard Davies, who came to the house to talk about Mother Courage and only told me the good bits. He didn't tell me that Mother Courage is in every bloody scene and doesn't shut up. I only found that out after the read-through. He also didn't tell me that she pulls a massive cart around the stage all evening while her mute daughter (played by Zoë Wanamaker in our production) sits perched on top, says nothing, and then steals all the reviews. [Laughs.]
Why do you prefer to be told the story, rather than read a script?

Laziness, probably. Or maybe it's the child in me, the memory of being read to when I was young. But I also think that when a director tells me the story it allows me to be more objective and I can imagine myself in the audience, experiencing it for the first time.
Is there a part of you that's also assessing the director's understanding of the story and how they're planning to tell it?

Not consciously but, now you say it, yes, probably. You want to make sure you're in safe hands, don't you? That instinctive response to a script is so important (and vital to hold on to) because once you've committed, and rehearsals have started, it's so easy to get lost in the weeds of a part. Holding on to that objective bird's-eye view provides a reminder of the overall story, and also your place in that story. It's a bit like being able to reference the picture on the front of a jigsaw box.
Somebody once said, 'You can make a good script bad, but you can never make a bad script good.'

I think that's true. That's why it's important to be alert to any little niggles when a director first tells you the story, because that's when you can spot if something's awry. Ultimately, you need to ask yourself: Is this story worth telling, and will it be arresting enough to make an audience sit and listen?
What's interesting is you've not once talked about the size of the role.

Because for me, it's the story that's important, and asking myself if I want to be part of it. The other thing I like to know is who I'm going to be working with. I had such a good time being directed by John Madden on Mrs. Brown that I wrote to him afterwards and said, 'If you have anything else up your sleeve – any old part, however small, even if it means just walking across the back of the shot – let me know.' He wrote back, saying, 'Well, funnily enough, I have got a small part which constitutes walking across the back of a shot,' and that's how I came to play Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love.

title: Case pitting "ER" against "The Pitt" can proceed, appeals court says
summary: A California appeals court has found that "ER" and "The Pitt" have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of "ER" creator Michael Crichton alleging "The Pitt" is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.
story: Los Angeles — A California appeals court has found that "ER" and "The Pitt" have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of "ER" creator Michael Crichton alleging "The Pitt" is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.

A three-judge panel from California's 2nd District Court of Appeal ruled unanimously on Wednesday that the trial court judge was correct to reject a motion to throw out the case from "The Pitt" production company Warner Bros. Television, which also produced "ER." But the judges dismissed Noah Wyle - the star of both shows and a producer on "The Pitt" - as a defendant along with two other producers who worked on both series.
The lawsuit is a clash between the makers of multiple Emmy-winning TV series that were each among the most important and acclaimed shows of their eras.

Crichton, the author of "Jurassic Park" and many other novels that became hit movies and TV shows, wrote the pilot script for "ER," the NBC show about a Chicago emergency room that redefined the medical drama genre and drew tens of millions of weekly viewers in its run from 1994 to 2009.

The lawsuit brought by Sherri Crichton was filed two years ago, before a single episode of "The Pitt" had aired. The HBO Max series that shows a real-time day in the life of a Pittsburgh emergency department has since become perhaps the most lauded series in television, winning two Emmys for best drama for its first two seasons and two best actor Emmys for Wyle.

Warner Bros. Television and CBS News have the same parent company following last month's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by the parent of CBS News, which was known at the time as Paramount Skydance and is now called Skydance.

Along with more technical legal issues, the judges had to decide whether the shows had at least the minimal similarity that would give the lawsuit enough merit to move forward. Their decision applies only to this early legal challenge and they did not rule on whether the plaintiffs had proved the "The Pitt" is derivative of "ER."

The court agreed with the plaintiff that "both shows provide commentaries on the healthcare system; they focus specifically on the emergency room and the difficult conditions under which the medical staff operates. Both shows take place, with little exception, in the emergency room, as opposed to other medical shows which track patients as they move out of the emergency room, or indeed never enter it."

The opinion also said that both feature "very fast pacing, and reactions to multiple overlapping crises. The fast-paced dialogue is (to a layperson) frequently incomprehensible shorthand and jargon, lending an air of immediacy and accuracy."

Warner Bros. Television said in a statement that "WBTV continues to maintain that 'The Pitt' is an entirely original series and that the claims against it are without merit. Nothing in the Court of Appeal's decision establishes otherwise, and WBTV looks forward to defending its position as the case proceeds."
The defendants argued in legal filings that the shows have "generic similarities" that would exist in "any dramatic story" that features "overworked doctors and staff."

The panel also unanimously dismissed as defendants Wyle, John Wells, who created "The Pitt" and worked on "ER," and R. Scott Gemmill, a "Pitt" executive producer who also worked on both shows. The judges found there was no evidence the three men knew the provisions of the Crichton contract that the lawsuit alleges they interfered with.
Sherri Crichton's lawsuit alleges "The Pitt" is a rebranded version of an unauthorized "ER" reboot that she had rejected.

Her husband had secured a coveted "frozen rights" provision in his contract for the series, prohibiting Warner Bros. from proceeding with any sequels, remakes, spinoffs or other productions derived from "ER" without Crichton's consent, or his estate's consent after his death from cancer in 2008.

After the production company could not reach an agreement with Sherri Crichton over a proposed "ER" reboot, the TV studio proceeded to develop and produce a series based on the same premise without permission, the lawsuit alleges.

title: Dolly Parton's estate moves to dismiss lawsuit against nephew
summary: The details of the resolution between Dolly Parton's estate and her nephew, Bryan Seaver, were not immediately known.
story: The estate of the late country music icon Dolly Parton has filed to dismiss its lawsuit against her nephew and former head of security, Bryan Seaver, following accusations he threatened to commit acts of violence and destroy Parton's brand.
The details of the resolution were not immediately known.

"Mr. Seaver is grateful to put this misunderstanding behind him so that the entire family can continue to grieve peacefully and ensure that the bright light of Dolly's legacy remains completely untouched," attorneys for Seaver told CBS News in a statement.
Attorneys for Parton's estate did not respond to a request for comment.

Seaver, who heads the private security firm Squadron Augmented Protection Services, had been tasked with announcing Parton's death in August. But in September, Seaver and SAPS were fired by She's Alive, which manages Parton's estate and business interests. Parton's longtime manager, Danny Nozell, who runs She's Alive, then filed for a restraining order against Seaver and SAPS.

Parton died of cancer at the age of 80. Seaver rose to national prominence when he announced Parton's death in a prerecorded video, in which he said it was "something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality."

She's Alive, or SAL, had alleged in its request for a restraining order that Seaver "made repeated, written threats to Ms. Parton's staff, partners, legal and business advisors, and others" and that he "sought to extract money from SAL and trusts through an obscene, deliberate, and escalating campaign of threats."

In one instance prior to Parton's death, SAL alleged that Seaver threatened to "destroy the entire brand" over a disagreement involving Dollywood, the theme park and resort opened by Parton in 1986. The lawsuit also alleged that Seaver repeatedly referenced his security business, which it described as a "heavily armed, paramilitary-style force capable of projecting threat and coercion against SAL's personnel and business partners."
Seaver made many of these alleged threats via text, according to the lawsuit.

Seaver, in a response to SAL's request to extend its restraining order last month, denied "each and every allegation." He said he and Nozell had been close friends for many years and that, until his firing, the two had never had an argument "apart from a minor disagreement years ago over a company logo."

While he admitted to using coarse and blunt language, he denied threatening anybody, including Parton or her estate's business partners, saying the text messages were "private messages" between himself and Nozell.

"They were sent in the course of private conversations between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving, and discussing strategy following Ms. Parton's illness and death," the court filing states.

He insisted the messages about the Dollywood disagreement were not threats of violence but that he was "privately warning" Nozell that he thought certain associates were "harming [Parton's] brand and imploring him to help."

Seaver also said in his response that Nozell didn't respond to the various texts cited in the lawsuit with any sort of pushback or alarm. In fact, Seaver claimed Nozell urged him to publicly play up his military and security history before trying to use those ties as evidence that Seaver was dangerous and threatening.

"I have declined to speak with the media about this case and have asked my attorneys to handle all media communications," Seaver wrote at the end of his affidavit. "I care about Ms. Parton, her music, her legacy, and her family. I do not want this dispute to harm her legacy."
This story published first on CBS News at 6:19 p.m. on Nov. 5, 2026.

title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
summary: Actor and comedian Russell Brand was accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
story: Actor and comedian Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three other women on Thursday at his trial in London. Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand will be sentenced to prison.

Brand, 51, was initially accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault. On Thursday, he was acquitted of two rape counts and the attempted indecent assault charge.

"You've been convicted of a number of offences including rape," Bennathan told Brand after reading Thursday's verdict, according to CBS News partner BBC. "The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I therefore have to remand you into custody."
Brand, who was denied bail and taken into custody, will be sentenced on Monday.
"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said, according to the Associated Press. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."
The allegations, made by six women, spanned a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

A jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days. They found Brand guilty of grabbing a woman's breasts during a party at a bar in London's Soho neighborhood in the summer of 2004, sexually assaulting a woman at London radio station Choice FM in 2004 or 2005, and raping a woman at his home in Hampstead in 2009.

Brand closed his eyes as the guilty verdict on the rape count was read but showed no emotion otherwise. When bail was denied, he gestured to his lawyers that he was OK and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken away.
During the trial, a prosecutor accused Brand of being a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator."

Brand, who pleaded not guilty to the charges, testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man. He said he once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will, saying he thinks that "consent is absolutely non-negotiable."
He said the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.
"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.

Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults, and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
During the trial, Brand suggested the reports were part of a coordinated attack because of his newfound prominence as an online wellness influencer and political commentator.

The women featured in the documentary said they only felt ready to share their stories after being approached by reporters, with some mentioning Brand's online fame as a factor in their decision to speak.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London's Metropolitan Police said the conviction was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," he said. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be."
Brand's father, Ron Brand, told the BBC after the verdict and that he was "bemused and shocked."
"I just didn't expect this - it's wrong," he said. "It's devastating."

Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" and "Get Him to the Greek" and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

title: Ronaldo retires from Portugal national team
summary: Cristiano Ronaldo says he won't play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record.
story: Lisbon, Portugal — Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he won't play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record.

The announcement marked the end of a lauded career that began more than two decades ago before Euro 2004 and finished with him walking out on the national team after a falling out with coach Jorge Jesus.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a long video message on social media. "I never felt it belonged to me alone but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.

"Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end."

While long-time peer Lionel Messi finished his career with Argentina after a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance with Portugal has ended up being on Sept. 24 in a 1-0 win over Wales in the Nations League.

Jesus kept him on the bench for the following match and said he didn't plan to start him in the next one, so Ronaldo decided to leave the team's training camp. Jesus later said Ronaldo would be welcome back and the decision to return was up to him.
The Portuguese soccer federation released a statement expressing "deep gratitude and immense admiration" for Ronaldo's service to the country.

"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" the federation said.
It said it intends to organize a tribute to Ronaldo "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much."
Like Messi, Ronaldo will keep playing at club level, and is expected to finish his club career at the end of this season with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.
He is in pursuit of his 1,000th career goal and has 985. Of those, a record 146 came in 234 appearances with Portugal.
Ronaldo became the first player in his sport to reach billionaire status, joining the ranks of the wealthiest athletes, Bloomberg reported in October 2025..

title: Seeking relief from chronic pain
summary: With about one in four American adults living with chronic pain, Dr. Jon LaPook examines some of the current treatments, from medications and surgery, to nerve stimulation, biofeedback and self-hypnosis.
story: Veterinarian Dr. Troy Hudnall enjoyed an active practice in Missouri. But in 2022, during an intense delivery of a calf, he felt a sharp pain, and heard a strange sound: "A snap or a pop, snap's probably the best way to describe it," he said.

Herniated discs and a pinched nerve in his neck caused numbness and severe muscle loss in Hudnall's right hand: "The first thing that I really remember is, I couldn't click my mouse on my computer. I started having trouble with instruments. Anything that required much agility in the fingers was almost gone."

Hudnall had multiple surgeries to help free up the nerves, but as sensation returned, he began experiencing severe pain … pain so bad, he says, he thought about amputating his own arm. Asked to describe how it felt, Hudnall replied, "For me, it's always been electricity. If you've ever touched an electric fence on a farm, or accidentally touched both prongs while you're plugging something in, it's that, but it's repetitive, it pulses."

That chronic pain has haunted Hudnall for three years now, forcing him to stop working. He treats it with a daily handful of pills, including opioids, and has tried red light therapy, physical therapy, electrical spine stimulation, and lidocaine injections. But despite all that, he says he experiences pain every second of every day. Rating his pain level from zero to ten, Hudnall says his "best days" rank at six to eight.
About one in four American adults lives with chronic pain, defined as pain lasting more than three months. Most are still suffering a year later.
"When you have chronic pain day in, day out, you're just inundated with this signal all the time; it's crushing you completely," said pain specialist Dr. Lara Crock.
A global problem

We followed Hudnall's care at one of the nation's top pain centers, the Washington University School of Medicine Pain Center in St. Louis, where, Crock explained, patients often end up trying many different approaches. "We throw medicines at it, we try different injections, we try different procedures," she said. "But really, we don't have a full understanding of why one person with the same injury continues to hurt while the other person heals and no longer hurts."

Treating chronic pain requires understanding the different ways a body can react to a painful stimulus. For example, when a person burns their hand, an electrical signal travels up nerves in the arm to the spine, then on to brain cells that interpret that signal as pain. In most people, once the painful stimulus stops, the sensation of pain stops. But not always.

Crock said, "The tissue that was injured before may be healed, or the injury that you had is recovered, but that signal continues to go and go." Why? "We don't know!" she said. "Your arm is totally normal, every scan, everything about your arm is completely normal, but there's an area of your brain that is affecting your hand that's damaged and causes your arm to hurt all the time."

Chronic pain is a global problem. Over the last 35 years, more than 900 journals in 86 countries have published thousands of articles about chronic pain. Approaches to treatment include using devices that stimulate the vagus nerve in the neck to lower pain in patients with rheumatoid arthritis or migraine headaches. And researchers are testing new non-opioid medications that block tiny gateways in nerve cells (called sodium channels) to keep pain signals from traveling to the brain.
Biofeedback

At Washington University, researchers are trying to lower pain by "retraining" the brain. Doctors Eric Leuthardt and Simon Haroutounian have come up with a headset, wearable at home, that uses biofeedback to train patients to increase certain brain waves that ease pain. "We have conducted a pilot in a small group of about six patients with chronic pain that was non-responsive to other treatments, like surgery, medications," said Haroutounian. "And everyone improved to some extent."

The positive assets of the device, Leuthardt said, include, "It's not a drug, it's got no pathologic side effects, it's not addictive, and in many ways, [it] empowers the patient to rehabilitate their own neural circuits for improvement."
Self-hypnosis

Still in early research stages, that headset isn't ready for patients like Troy Hudnall. But since last May, Hudnall has been trying hypnosis, in sessions conducted by pain psychologist Sarah Buday. "Clinical hypnosis is not your Las Vegas stage show; I'm not trying to make anyone cluck like a chicken or be under my control," Buday said. "The way I think of it is, I'm teaching somebody the skill of self-hypnosis. We are having them go into a very deep state of relaxation, at which point, I start to make suggestions about maybe the quality of the pain or the meaning of it, their emotions."
Several weeks ago, with the help of self-hypnosis, Hudnall endured another surgery. As for his future, he says he tries to remain positive.
And Buday is positive about Hudnall's outlook as well: "I think it's good. It's already getting better. And he is somebody that has a lot of optimism and hope."

And Lara Crock says, even if – despite all you throw at it – pain is only partially relieved, "It can be the difference from being able to get up and take your kid to school or eat breakfast or dinner with your family, versus laying in bed all day. So, that can be huge."

title: Americans wary of AI for medical care and insurance claims
summary: Most Americans have qualms about using AI in healthcare for tasks such as diagnosis and treatment, Pew Research poll finds.
story: How much artificial intelligence is too much when you visit your doctor? Although patients are generally open to healthcare professionals using AI to handle administrative and some medical tasks, they want humans wielding the stethoscope, a recent survey suggests.

A solid majority of Americans are comfortable with AI translating patient notes or scheduling appointments, either on its own or with some human oversight, according to the Pew Research Center, which polled more than 3,400 U.S. adults in June. More than half the respondents were also open to using AI to analyze medical scans and lab test results, provided a healthcare professional supervised the process.

But people draw the line when it comes to AI driving diagnoses or making insurance decisions, Pew found. Almost half of those surveyed said they don't want an AI model deciding whether to accept or reject an insurance claim, while 41% said they don't want AI making a diagnosis on its own.

Galen Stocking, associate director of science and society research at Pew Research Center, said people see value in applying AI to healthcare. Still, patients want to know when and how healthcare providers and administrative staff are using the technology.
"Overall, people say it's extremely important that their healthcare provider tell them if they are using AI," he told CBS News.

"There is a lack of clarity on the side of the public," he added, noting Pew's finding that 46% of the survey respondents said they don't know if AI has ever been used in the course of them receiving care.
Indeed, 60% of respondents said they are uncomfortable with doctors using AI for tasks such as diagnosis and treatment; only 30% are OK with that, while 10% are unsure.
"People are concerned about patient-doctor relationships and the security of their own health information," Stocking said.

More broadly, Americans are split over whether AI will improve the quality of medical care. Some 37% of respondents said AI will improve health outcomes, while a nearly equal share think the technology could reduce the quality of care.
