title: Spacewalkers complete space station solar power upgrade
summary: The eighth and final roll-out solar array installation caps a five-year effort to augment the space station's aging, original solar wings.
story: Completing a complex upgrade five years in the making, two spacewalking astronauts on Thursday mounted an eighth and final roll-out solar wing on the International Space Station, boosting the lab's power output to compensate for the age-related degradation of its original arrays.

NASA began the power-system upgrade in 2021 when two spacewalkers installed the first ISS roll-out solar array, or IROSA, at the base of one of the original eight wings. Six additional panels were attached during subsequent spacewalks, with the most recent installation carried out last week during a spacewalk by NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk.

The duo ventured back outside Thursday to install the eighth and final IROSA on the far right end of the station's power truss, beginning the extravehicular activity, or EVA — NASA speak for "spacewalk" — at 8:36 a.m. ET.

The final two IROSAs were delivered to the station aboard a SpaceX Cargo Dragon capsule earlier this month, with each one folded in half and stowed in the ship's unpressurized trunk section. The lab's robot arm mounted both rolled-up blankets on the left side of the station's power truss to await installation.

Attachment and extension of the seventh panel last week was relatively straightforward because the 58-foot-long robot arm could easily carry Menon, holding onto a new IROSA, to its nearby installation point on a fixture at the base of an inboard left-side solar wing.

But the Canadarm II does not have the reach to carry Menon and the final blanket directly to the far right end of the power truss as required, so he and Kutryk handed it off to each other leapfrog fashion to get it all the way out to a waiting support frame.

Once mounted on the base of the outboard array, Menon and Kutryk unfolded the new IROSA, bolted it in place, and connected power and data cables during orbital darkness when no sunlight was available to generate electricity.

As the station moved back into sunlight, flight controllers noticed one of the two still-rolled-up blankets did not appear to be generating a small amount of electricity as expected. The spacewalkers then waited for another night pass to double-check the connections. The problem was resolved, and the final IROSA blankets were extended to their full length of 63 feet.

"These solar arrays are incredible, half the size of the old ones. It's delivering 40% more power," Menon said after returning to the airlock. "It's really empowering all this research that we do and everything that we do to transform space and open the doors to the future."
The six-hour, 59-minute spacewalk ended at 3:35 p.m.
The IROSAs were designed to offset age-related degradation that has reduced the power output of the station's original arrays over more than two decades of use in the harsh space environment.
The new panels are smaller but more efficient, featuring state-of-the-art solar cells. Even though they shade portions of the arrays they are mounted on, they still provide a net boost in power.

Before the first IROSA was installed, the original arrays were generating about 160 kilowatts of power. The eighth and final IROSA was expected to boost the total power output to some 215 kilowatts, enough to sustain the lab through its planned retirement and de-orbiting in 2030, powering life support systems, computers, research and visiting vehicles.

title: Huge space telescope plunges back to Earth after 22 years in orbit
summary: NASA had previously said much of the observatory burned up upon reentry. The risk to people on Earth was low, the agency said.
story: The Swift Observatory, a 1.5-ton NASA telescope that was launched more than two decades ago, has crashed back to Earth after an effort to rescue the wayward instrument failed earlier this year.

The roughly 3,200-pound observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. ET over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, NASA said. Much of it burned up upon reentry. Some components are expected to survive reentry and may be found sprawled across hemispheres, NASA said.

The observatory's reentry path was tracked by NASA and the U.S. Space Force. NASA predicted its reentry time at around 3:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 4, with an 11-hour window of uncertainty on either side. NASA had previously said the "risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely," placing the odds at about 1 in 2,100.

The Swift Observatory was sent into low-Earth orbit on Nov. 20, 2004 — almost exactly 22 years ago. The telescope's mission was to search for massive galactic explosions, including gamma-ray bursts and supernovas. The telescope was named for its ability to swerve rapidly toward such events.

The telescope was initially designed to run a two-year mission, but continued its operations until last month. Solar activity eventually dragged the telescope back down to Earth. Katalyst Space was contracted by NASA to mount a rescue of the telescope in July. The company dispatched a three-armed robot named Link to push the telescope back into place, but the robot ran into trouble shortly after launching. It was not able to get within seven miles of the telescope. The robot fell back to Earth in September. In August, it was decided that the Swift Observatory would be allowed to plunge back to Earth.
The telescope continued to return observations until late October, when NASA determined it was too low to remain steady. Its systems were shut down at that time.

In addition to observing more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, the Swift telescope was a "first responder" for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes, NASA said. Swift would issue alerts to those and other facilities, which would then more deeply investigate those observations.

"Swift has broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system," NASA said in a blog post.
Scientists are still trying to figure out how to replace the work done by the Swift Observatory.

"We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team, said on Monday.
"Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe," Nousek added.

title: Data centers are unpopular — and a key motor of economic growth
summary: The political backlash against data centers is intensifying, threatening to choke off a critical source of U.S. investment, according to economists.
story: The shifting political winds surrounding data centers could buffet the entire U.S. economy, reducing investment in artificial intelligence and slowing growth, according to Wall Street analysts.

The historic tide of money pouring into AI, from data centers and frontier models to state-of-the-art chips and networking gear, has boosted business investment and financial markets in recent years. Federal Reserve researchers recently estimated that spending on data centers, power facilities and other AI-related tech equipment accounted for roughly 20% of U.S. gross domestic product over the preceding year.

In 2026, spending by "hyperscalers" such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — the companies racing to build data centers — is set to double to around $800 billion and is expected to reach $1 trillion in 2027, according to Capital Economics. Although slowing that buildout might well serve the public interest, given the widespread opposition to data centers, crimping that flow of dollars will have knock-on economic effects.

"Our economy is leveraged on this idea that AI will make us rich," economist Allison Schrager with the Manhattan Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, told CBS News. "There are risks to making it slower — it will mean slower growth."
"Detrimental effects"

Economists and investors now expect the Democrats' sweeping midterm election wins to both slow and increase the cost of data center development across the U.S. By contrast, those victories are unlikely to completely turn off the spigot, experts said, noting that political opposition to data centers isn't uniform, ranging from support for moratoriums on construction to more moderate proposals.
As a result, investment in data centers is likely to continue in the near term, both for projects currently underway and for facilities that have received permits.

For companies investing in AI, the bigger issue will be continuing such capital expenditures at the same pace even as the productivity gains and profits AI is expected to deliver remain largely unrealized for now.

"The high-level calculations essential to justify that level of CapEx, if sustained, we are talking $2 trillion in revenue for major AI companies by the early 2030s, which seems very unlikely," Capital Economics chief North America economist Stephen Brown told CBS News. "Our view is that because of that, there is likely to be some slowdown in data center construction. We are not saying it will stop altogether, but the level of investment is likely to ease. And that would have some detrimental effects on the U.S. economy."
Impact on stocks and consumer spending
Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi thinks investors are willing to continue pouring money into AI for the next couple of years, but said the long-term prospects are less clear.

"There are a lot of questions about whether that capital will continue to be there to fill that hole and, if not, AI companies will have to raise prices to cover costs. Then you won't see the same kind of investment," he said.

In 2025, investment in AI added roughly 0.3 percentage points to real GDP growth, according to Capital Economics, which expects investment in the sector to boost growth by roughly the same amount this year.

If AI investment were to fall in 2028, "It could turn into an outright drag on GDP," Capital Economics chief economic advisor Vicky Redwood said in a research note on Friday, estimating that a 10% annual drop in AI spending from current levels would knock around 0.1% off GDP growth.

If investment in AI slows, the greatest drag on growth could come from reduced consumption, Brown of Capital Economics told CBS News. Higher-income Americans who invested in AI stocks have seen their wealth grow sharply. With the S&P 500 up almost 100% over the past three years, such investors have driven increased spending.

"A big part of the wealth effect is coming from the strong rise in equity prices, and if data center construction slows, the likely weakness we'll see in the equity market is a sign of things to come," said Brown, who estimates that this "wealth effect" is boosting economic growth this year by roughly 0.5%.

If the S&P 500 were to lose 20% of its value, that boost would turn into a 0.5% drag on GDP growth, Brown said. "That would be a 1% hit to GDP," he said. "We would be talking about a sharp slowdown in GDP growth versus a recession."

title: Feds warn of potential cyberattacks on industrial refrigerators
summary: After a wave of attacks in Europe, U.S. officials are warning of "ongoing" cyber threats targeting refrigeration systems used in healthcare, agriculture and other industries.
story: The U.S. government encouraged grocery stores, healthcare facilities and other businesses that use commercial refrigeration to tighten their security measures on Thursday following a series of cyberattacks that remotely changed the temperatures of commercial freezers and fridges across Europe.

Five federal agencies issued a joint notice, warning of "ongoing cyber threat activity" that could target refrigeration systems used across healthcare, agriculture, transportation and other U.S. industries.
Bad actors globally are exploiting vulnerabilities and weaknesses in refrigeration systems that are "unpatched" or connected to the internet, the agencies said.

"If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system," the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said in a statement, which was issued in conjunction with the FBI, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Agriculture and Department of Transportation.

In a fact sheet, CISA said businesses that rely on industrial refrigeration should take precautions to protect their systems, including changing passwords, disconnecting system devices from the internet and making software updates to address vulnerabilities.

"Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,"  Chris Butera, acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity at CISA, said in a statement.
The agencies did not specify if any refrigeration systems have been targeted in the U.S.
Wave of refrigeration attacks

The warning follows reports of refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases in August. The Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, a U.S. federal law enforcement unit, has launched an investigation into the incidents, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News on Thursday.

Similar incidents have occurred around Europe in recent weeks, with hackers targeting fridges and freezers across numerous grocery chains. Food retailers reported unexpected temperature spikes in their refrigeration systems, causing food to spoil in stores in Luxembourg, Belgium and Sweden.

Officials in France, which has also been hit by grocery store cyberattacks, said on Wednesday that its national emergency blood supply network was targeted by hackers who tried to raise refrigeration temperatures at several blood banks.

Joshua Corman, executive-in-residence for public safety and resilience at the Institute for Security and Technology, a security think tank, said he expects more such attacks, warning that refrigeration systems used by medical labs, grocery stores and bulk warehouses in the U.S. could be compromised.
"There's only so many players that do industrial-level refrigeration, and they're likely also just as vulnerable," he told CBS News.

title: French blood banks hit by cyberattack days after European freezer hacks
summary: The cyberattack on several French blood banks comes after supermarkets across Europe reported their fridges​ and freezers​ were remotely taken over by hackers.
story: A cyberattack on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.

The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars.
The attacks have renewed wider concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure and the growing risks of internet-connected consumer "smart" technology.

In the most recent cyberattack, the French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said in a statement released late Tuesday  "temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels" on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma. Monitoring systems quickly detected the problem, allowing staff to take action in time so that "no blood products or samples were compromised," it said.

French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the cyberattack, said that the attack had attempted to reset temperatures that normally are at minus 22 Fahrenheit (minus 30 Celsius) to as high as 230 F (110 C).

The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites. The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the EFS statement said.
"No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost," the blood bank said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
The company supplying the refrigeration equipment, Coolworld, said in a statement it "is aware" of the cybersecurity incident.

"The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control," the statement said. The company said only a limited number of units were affected and it was taking "appropriate measures."
France's national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident. The ministry gave no indication of who might be behind the cyberattack.

This week's cyberattacks on refrigeration systems mirrored an episode in mid-October that targeted fridges and freezers at hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

One of the chains hit in that earlier incident, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize, said Wednesday that it expected the cyberattack to reduce its sales in the fourth quarter by as much as $281 million (250 million euros), and crimp its operating income for the period by over $112 million (about 100 million euros).

"While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations," CEO Franz Muller said. "As we all recognize, cyber threats are an increasingly harsh reality of doing business today," he said in a statement released with Delhaize's quarterly earnings.

The company had earlier blamed "malicious actions by others" and proactively took some of its systems offline, including websites and apps for its various brands in Europe as well as in the United States.

title: Hackers can hijack grocery store freezers. What about our homes?
summary: Large-scale hacks targeting grocery stores in Europe and France's blood banks are renewing concerns about the vulnerabilities of everyday "smart" devices.
story: London — Cyberattacks on grocery store refrigeration systems across Europe sent temperatures soaring on Monday, spoiling food and causing significant financial losses in the second such incident in less than a month. In October, hundreds of French stores were targeted in a similar attack that sent temperatures in some units soaring to 122° Fahrenheit, destroying a huge amount of food.

On Wednesday, France's health service said the country's national emergency blood supply network had also been compromised by hackers this week, though alert and backup systems prevented cold storage facilities from being shut down, and no supplies were lost.

The incidents have renewed wider concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure and the growing risks of internet-connected consumer "smart" technology. It is not just essential systems such as electricity grids, healthcare databases and grocery store chains' refrigeration, which can have multiple layers of security and redundancy built in, but everyday appliances that are now connected to the internet.
The concern among some experts is that devices pitched as time-saving conveniences for consumers could also create potential entry points for hackers.

CBS News spoke with several cybersecurity experts who warned that similar vulnerabilities to those exploited in the grocery store hacks could exist in our homes. From heating systems and smart TVs to security cameras, door locks and ovens, millions of household appliances are now online.
How vulnerable are our homes?

"Our homes may be more vulnerable than many people think. Smart fridges, TVs, cameras, and locks are small computers connected to the internet, and like any computer, they can have weaknesses," Dr. Manny Niri, a cybersecurity lecturer at Oxford Brookes University, told CBS News.
"Often the problem is simple: default or reused passwords, old software, or accounts with weak security," he said.

Professor George Loukas, head of the Centre for Sustainable Cyber Security at the University of Greenwich, said vulnerabilities in some mass-produced devices could potentially expose millions of households simultaneously.
"One flaw in a popular model opens the door to every home that owns it," he said.
What could hackers actually do?
The consequences could extend beyond hackers simply switching an appliance on or off remotely, to "anything the device is already allowed to do," Loukas said.

"If an app can turn off your heating, unlock your door or switch off your camera, so can a hacker. The physical harm comes from using the system as designed, just with malicious intent and controlled by someone other than you," he said.

"Unauthorized access to a camera or microphone could reveal when people are at home, what they are doing and, potentially, their conversations," said Niri. "A compromised device can sometimes give hackers access to other devices on the same network, potentially exposing personal or financial information. There can also be physical consequences, for example changing a fridge temperature, interfering with an alarm system, or opening a smart lock."

In 2025, U.S. cybersecurity officials identified a critical vulnerability in certain WiFi thermostats that could allow hackers to gain full administrative control of the units. Meanwhile, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission documented cases involving Ring security cameras in which hackers gained access to accounts and used cameras to spy on and harass homeowners.

Dr. Abdullahi Arabo, associate professor of cyberscience and network security at the University of the West of England, warned that a single compromised device could expose other systems within a household.
"A compromised device can sometimes give hackers access to other devices on the same network, potentially exposing personal or financial information," he said.
Could millions of homes be hacked simultaneously?
Experts say the greater danger may not be hackers targeting individual homes, but exploiting vulnerabilities across millions of identical devices.

In 2016, the Mirai malware infected hundreds of thousands of internet-connected devices, including household routers and security cameras, transforming them into a network capable of launching large-scale cyberattacks.
Artificial intelligence could make attacks like that significantly easier to pull off, Loukas told CBS News.
"With AI, an attack that once needed a skilled team working for weeks can now be run by one person," Loukas warned. "This lowers the bar for who can cause disruption at scale."
"When millions of homes rely on the same device, a single flaw becomes everyone's problem," he added.
How worried should we be?
The experts who spoke with CBS News emphasize that ordinary, individual households are unlikely to be deliberately targeted.

"I suggest awareness, not fear," Niri said, adding a warning that "comfort has a cost. Before buying a smart device, we should ask, 'Do I really need this to be online, and what happens if it is hacked?'"
He recommended changing default passwords on all devices, enabling two-factor authentication on those that allow it, regularly updating software, and retaining manual control over essential systems.

title: Google will block search access for schools that ban AI use
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other critics are accusing Google of trying to pressure U.S. schools to use AI.
story: Google said on Tuesday that it will turn off artificial intelligence in its educational apps for K-12 student accounts unless school administrators expressly enable it.
The Alphabet-owned search giant said that after surveying school administrators and teachers, it wants educational institutions to control students' access to various AI capabilities.

Access to Google's AI features — Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Classroom — as well as Google search will be automatically turned off for K-12 student accounts until "school administrators explicitly turn them on," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.
Schools that ban AI "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available," Phillips told The New York Times.
While Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will be turned off by default, schools can choose to turn on one, two or all three services, Google explained in a post on X Tuesday.
"We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach," Phillips wrote in the post.
New policy prompts outcry

Google's new policy immediately prompted criticism that it is seeking to pressure schools to use its AI apps. In a statement posted on social media, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused the tech giant of "trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."
"No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech," he added.
A Google spokesperson declined to respond to Mamdani's remarks.

Roughly 150 million students and teachers use Google Classroom, and many students use school-provided Chromebooks, according to Google. Google drew backlash in August when it activated its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.

In September, New York City schools said that AI would be banned until students reach high school and implemented a one-year delay on the use of generative AI for children in 2-K through eighth grade.
Lina Khan, who served as chair of the Federal Trade Commission from 2021 to 2025, said in a statement posted on X that Google is seeking to exploit its dominance in internet search.

"This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service," said Khan, who now chairs the board of the New York City Economic Development Corporation, a nonprofit group that promotes economic growth and investment in New York.

"Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened," she added. "As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don't fall in line."

Josh Golin, executive director of children's advocacy group Fairplay, said Google's attempt to "strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire." He said Google's technology in schools is not about learning but about "developing lifetime brand loyalty" for its products.

Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, accused Google of putting its business interests ahead of education. "Instead of working with teachers and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, it throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to the tools altogether," she said in a statement.

title: Snap settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
summary: Snap joins Alphabet, Meta and TikTok in resolving allegations that its social media platform was designed to encourage addictive behavior.
story: Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, reached a settlement in a social media addiction lawsuit on Monday, resolving claims before the case was set to go to trial this month, according to lawyers for the plaintiffs.

The teenage plaintiffs, identified in court documents as S.J. and K.D.B., had alleged in the suit that Snapchat was designed to be addictive and that using the platform from a young age contributed to their mental health issues.

"We are glad to reach resolution for our clients," Mark Lanier, founder of The Lanier Law Firm and lead counsel for the plaintiffs, said in a statement to CBS News. "We believe this jury would have found the companies' conduct reprehensible."

Snap was the last social media company named in the lawsuit to settle the case, which was set for opening arguments this week. Meta resolved claims last week, while Alphabet and TikTok, the other defendants, each also resolved the allegations.
Terms of the Snap settlement were undisclosed, according to Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan and attorney Emily Jeffcott, trial counsel for K.D.B.
In a statement to CBS News, Snap said that "the parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner."
The suit was one of several bellwether cases brought by plaintiffs who have alleged that social media platforms harmed their mental health and were designed to keep young users hooked.
In a landmark decision earlier this year, a jury found Meta and Google-owned YouTube liable and awarded $6 million to the lead plaintiff.

Meta also agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion and add child-safety measures to its social media platforms as part of an August settlement with dozens of U.S. states. The states accused Meta of deliberately designing its platforms to be addictive and of misleading users and the public about the technology's risks.

title: Meta settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
summary: Two plaintiffs alleged that Meta and Snap designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior.
story: Meta has settled a social media addiction lawsuit, resolving claims against the technology giant before the case was set to go to trial next month, according to a lawyer for one of the plaintiffs.

The suit was brought by an 18-year-old woman identified in court documents as K.D.B. who alleged that Meta and Snapchat parent company Snap, which remains a defendant in the case, designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior. Another plaintiff in the lawsuit, dubbed S.J., settled with Meta last week.
Terms of Meta's settlement were not disclosed.
S.J. and K.D.B. also originally sued TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube platform, which each separately settled before trial.
The plaintiffs claim that the social media platforms contributed to their mental health struggles.

"We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," Emily Jeffcott, the trial counsel for K.D.B., said in a statement.
Joseph VanZandt, an attorney with the law firm Beasley Allen who is representing S.J., said the plaintiffs will proceed with their complaint against Snap.

"Each plaintiff alleges that Snap designed Snapchat to maximize the time young users spend on the app, using features such as Snapstreaks, Snapscores, push notifications, and filters, and that their compulsive use of Snapchat caused and contributed to severe mental and physical health injuries, including depression, anxiety, an eating disorder, and self-harm," he said in an email.
Snap disputes the allegations and has defended the company's practices.
Jury selection began this week in Los Angeles, with opening statements expected to begin in early November. Lawyers for the plaintiffs have said they expect the trial to last into mid-December.
A spokesperson for Meta, which still faces similar litigation alleging that its social platforms harm users' mental health, said the company will continue to defend itself in court.

"Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception," she said in a statement. "We will continue to defend ourselves in court, and we stand by our record. We've spent more than a decade building protections for teens, and our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general goes even further with strict time limits, no access at night, and no notifications during school hours."

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to dozens of states that alleged the company used its social platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to hook young internet users while concealing the risks.

title: Binance resumes withdrawals for some cryptocurrencies after heist
summary: The exchange said it would resume withdrawals in phases, pending security checks.
story: Binance said Sunday it had resumed withdrawals for some major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum after more than $6 billion in assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
However, the company has offered reassurances it would cover 90% of the losses from the attack using company funds to buy tokens to replenish a large portion of what was stolen.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack but said they would be resumed in phases, the first of which began on Sunday.
"First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals," the exchange posted on X.

As of 5 a.m. Eastern Time, Binance said it had restored withdrawals for Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB, XRP, Base, Doge and Optimism, and that it would "continue to restore additional assets and networks in phases as security checks are completed."

The FBI accused North Korea of being behind the hack in a statement on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the statement said.

The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."

title: Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain
summary: Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China's most famous peaks, many carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organizers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.
story: Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China's most famous peaks Monday, many carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organizers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.
For hundreds of years, Mount Tai -- the tallest peak in China's eastern Shandong province -- was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors, and it features prominently in Chinese mythology.

But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.
The UNESCO World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.

Over a 2.4-mile course with more than 1,970 feet of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods such as fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.
A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology -- a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree -- completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.
Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.
The fastest humanoid robot -- belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue -- completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.
Organizers called Mount Tai's rocky terrain a "natural extreme testing ground" that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.
The race, organized by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

title: GOP Rep. Hill says he'll weigh whether Hegseth's actions merit impeachment
summary: GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas was noncommittal about whether he would support an impeachment push against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
story: Washington — GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas was noncommittal on Sunday about whether he would support an impeachment push against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as lawmakers are poised to return to Capitol Hill this week for the first time since voters delivered widespread rebuke in the midterm elections of the GOP — and the war in Iran.

"I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War," Hill said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Hegseth is expected to be under the microscope this week as long-brewing anger has come to the fore following the midterm elections, where Republicans saw brutal losses as many voters cited concerns about the war in Iran and its impact on the cost of living. Before lawmakers left town for the campaign trail, outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth. This week, Massie said he plans to push ahead with forcing the vote.

Hill acknowledged that he's not satisfied with how the war has been handled. And he added that, "The commander in chief has to take the responsibility for the strategy of conducting the war and how it's been conducted."
"But I'll tell you one thing: There's nobody in America that wants Iran to have a nuclear weapon," Hill said. "This has been a goal of the United States for five decades."
Asked whether Hegseth should be impeached, Hill said, "The question is for the president: Should he continue to serve as the Secretary of War."
Hill also drew a distinction between Hegseth's job performance and whether he's committed impeachable offenses. Under the Constitution, the basis for impeachment is "high Crimes and Misdemeanors."
"If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean per se that he's committed an impeachable offense," Hill said.
The Arkansas Republican said that if Hegseth isn't "conducting his mission in the right way," then "then the president ought to make a change there."
"The question is: Are we leading at the Pentagon in the right way or not the right way?" Hill said. "That's very separate from whether or not somebody's committed an impeachable offense."

title: Full transcript of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
summary: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and former Robert F. Kennedy health adviser Calley Means join Margaret Brennan.
story: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, moderated by Margaret Brennan:

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts Rep. French Hill, Republican of Arkansas Calley Means, former White House senior adviser and top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Rep.-elect Nancy Lacore, retired Navy vice admiral

MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm Margaret Brennan in Washington.

And this week on Face the Nation: In the aftermath of Tuesday's blue tsunami, Republicans regroup, President Trump makes a major staff change at the White House, and Democrats now face daunting challenges when it comes to getting stuff done.

Last week's decisive repudiation of the Trump agenda now puts Democrats on the spot. The pressure is on them to fix what voters say is wrong with the country. And that Democratic to-do list is a daunting one.
(Begin VT)
JOCELYN BENSON (D-Michigan Governor-Elect): Let's lower costs. Let's raise our wages. Let's end corruption.
SHERROD BROWN (D-Ohio Senator-Elect): We will fight to end these tariffs. We will end this war.
(CHEERING)
REP. CHRIS PAPPAS (D-NH) (Senator-Elect): It's expanding access to health care and childcare, saving Social Security.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Democrats may have won a healthy majority on Capitol Hill, but not a veto-proof margin. Can the two branches of government actually work together?
(Begin VT)
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): I will get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive. But I have to power of the veto.
(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will talk with two key players about the potential of bipartisanship when it comes to banking and financial legislation, Massachusetts Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and Arkansas Congressman Republican French Hill.
At the White House, the finger-pointing over what led to the devastating defeat for the GOP intensifies, as Susie Wiles departs and Stephen Miller becomes the president's powerful chief of staff.

We talked with former White House health policy adviser Calley Means, who's gone public with damning accusations against Wiles and other top White House aides, saying they put special interests ahead of the MAHA agenda before the midterm elections. Did Means' allegations lead to Wiles' ouster?
(Begin VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Was it your intention to get her removed?
CALLEY MEANS (Former White House Senior Adviser): Yes.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.
Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.

Voters on Tuesday were loud and clear. They want action when it comes to high prices, and they want it now. How will the president handle working with the legislative branch to get that action Americans are demanding?
We will hopefully get some insights tonight, when 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat's interview with President Trump, which was taped Friday just before news of Susie Wiles' ouster broke.
Here is a preview.
(Begin VT)
ROSS DOUTHAT: There's a "Forbes" story that said that your net worth – maybe it's changed with the stock market recently – but your net worth went up by $3 billion since you returned to…
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): Well, so did everyone. OK, you ready? So, here's…
ROSS DOUTHAT: Everyone's – my net worth did not go up by $3 billion, for the record.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Well, you should have had stock.
ROSS DOUTHAT: I should have…
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: You should have had stock.
ROSS DOUTHAT: I should have had stock.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Excuse me. So, I devote – I devote…
ROSS DOUTHAT: How did it go up by $3 billion?
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Well, let me explain.

I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lot of money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know. I have a son who's a very straight, good guy.
He watches over money. I don't even talk to him about it. He watches – he gives – they gave my money – I have a lot of cash. I have had a lot of cash long before I came in here.
ROSS DOUTHAT: Yes.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I don't take a salary, you know?
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: And you can watch that interview with President Trump on 60 Minutes tonight at 7:00 p.m.
We go now to Massachusetts Democrat Elizabeth Warren, the expected incoming Senate Banking Committee chair. And she joins us from Cambridge.
Good morning to you, Senator.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN (D-Massachusetts): Good morning.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you have written an outline here, an op-ed about what it's going to look like with Democrats in the majority.
You said: "Democrats won by being populist economic fighters who are unafraid to call out corrupt politicians and corporate interests who have rigged the system at the expense of everyone else."

That has echoes of President Trump's populist economic message, not what he said there, of course, but certainly what he has said to voters again and again. What specific policies do you think you can work with him on?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Look, President Trump himself said that he wants to reduce interest rates on credit cards to 10 percent. I got the bill. I'm ready to go.

President Trump says he wants to do more on housing. We're ready. We have the bills ready to go. And, besides that, we got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price gouging, on protecting our rural hospitals, on making sure that people have access to health care.

We have a lot of work lined out that we can do. In fact, one of the best parts of this election was how many Democrats stood up and didn't just say, I'm for the middle class. They said, here, I understand what is broken. Here are my specific plans to fix it, and I am committed to doing that.

So you end up with this situation where, in Michigan and Texas, you have got the candidates saying the same thing, break up big medicine. You end up with a situation where, in Kansas and in South Carolina, you have got the Democratic candidates saying, we love that ROAD to Housing bill, but we want to go bolder, bigger, more housing, a situation where, in North Carolina and Alaska, we have got candidates saying, hey, we need to break up the grocery monopolies and stop price gouging.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Iowa and Maine, where – where the Senate candidates there said, we're going to shore up Social Security and make billionaires pay their fair share.
And, you know, Margaret, those may sound like lots of different pieces.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: They're not. They're all about economic power.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well…
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: And people have told us that's what they want, and we have got the team to deliver now.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I mean, I don't have to tell you it's different to campaign than it is to actually legislate.

But President Trump has said he does want to work with Democrats on a few things here, immigration, tax cuts or – cuts or – quote – "maybe certain things having to do with taxes to make it more convenient, a lot of economic development initiatives."
Does that track with your expectations of how this White House will be able to work with you, run by Stephen Miller and, of course, President Trump?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Look, let's be clear. The American people are the ones who've really set the agenda here. They're the ones who have told us what they wanted.
And they didn't just tell Democrats. They delivered a message to the Republicans pretty loud and clear.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: And I just follow through on what happened in the – just this last summer. We put together a bipartisan housing bill that is going to expand the supply of housing and help bring down the cost of housing…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: … and, for the first time ever in American history…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: … going to ban private equity.
Donald Trump didn't even sign the damn thing, and yet it is now law. We have got a lot of ways to deliver for the American people, whether Donald Trump wants to be part of it or not.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because you got a veto-proof majority on that particular bill. That's going to be perhaps more challenging.
You have said you want to bring big tech CEOs, Wall Street executives, and giant corporations who may have broken the law to face consequences. To be clear…
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: … is your focus going to be legislation or is it going to be investigation?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Well, we have to do both.
But I do want to be clear. If you have been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you better get ready for some investigations, serious ones.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who do you have in mind there when you say that?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Anyone who's been cheating. That's what investigations are all about.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK. So you don't have a list of people you plan to subpoena yet, you – even though you're going to be in this chair?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: I – it is important that we go through the steps for investigation.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Because, look, the American people are just damn sick of this.
(CROSSTALK)

SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: They are sick of a White House that wouldn't enforce the laws even when they got cheated. They are sick of a White House that dropped investigations, that said, oh, if you make a nice contribution to Donald Trump's ballroom…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: … then there won't be any enforcement of the law when you have cheated millions of American customers.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I want…
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: That has to end.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Under – and we saw that in the polling, a concern about corruption.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Mm-hmm.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator Chris Coons, who is slated to take over Senate Foreign Relations in the new Congress, has said he wants questions answered about, it appears to be Nvidia, the chipmaker, and its CEO, Jensen Huang.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: "The New York Times" says he may have had a close relationship with a spy from China. Is there anything you can tell us about that? Is AI going to be a focus for you, and specifically this tech – this chipmaker?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Well, on the chipmaker specifically, this is an issue where we have actually substantial bipartisan support in the Banking Committee.
We have got – we have got Republicans and Democrats. I'm on bipartisan bills in order to put more restraints on the ability to export our chips to China.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: In fact, we have worked on a bipartisan basis to try to stop Donald Trump from encouraging Nvidia, permitting Nvidia to send these chips to China. And now we're seeing some of the consequences of that.
So we have got a lot of places where work needs to be done and a lot of different avenues to do it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well…
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: But the central part is going to be lowering costs for families and rooting out the corruption. It's not a long agenda.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, one of the things Democrats promised was to end the war with Iran. There are a few more weeks left in this Republican majority.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You sit on the Armed Services Committee. There are senators like Senators Bennet and Senator Mark Kelly who have said something to the effect of Democrats should cut off funding for White House operations in order to pressure President Trump to end the war.

There are people in the House making noise like that. I mean, what does this look like? Are we looking at cutting off all government funding? Are we looking at a government shutdown in the next few weeks?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Look, the pressure is building to end this war.

People have told us they want us to stop the war, a war that is illegal, that is halfway around the world, that to this day the Trump administration can't explain what their goals are and what their exit ramp looks like. They want us to stop it. They want us not to spend money over there.

They want to be able to buy gasoline and heating oil fuel, because they want this economy to work again. The way I think of this is, the wind is at our backs to end this war. We have got a lot of different tools on the table to get this done.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Leverage, you mean?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: But this is a democracy. And – yes.
And the American people have spoken. And it is time to listen to the American people. Democrats are ready to fight for that, and we invite the Republicans to join us.

NANCY LACORE: The things that I'm going to focus on, on day one, first of all, will be to end this war, because that has driven up costs extraordinarily high across the district and the country. We also need to look at repealing some of these tariffs that have driven up a variety of other costs, including those of building new homes. And the one big, beautiful bill. There are some great pieces to the one big, beautiful bill, but there are some very – pieces that have done a lot of damage and made things a lot more unaffordable. I'd love to talk about the fact that we're not paying taxes on tips or Social Security, and I think that's great, but we need to make that permanent because right now those are going to expire with the end of this administration.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Nine out of ten voters said government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their vote. They put it right up there with the cost of living.

Leader Jeffries, likely to be Speaker Jeffries, has said there should be accountability but, "the American people don't want us to get even, they want us to get things done because life is too expensive."
So, what does accountability look like? Do you need investigations or do you need legislation?

NANCY LACORE: It probably depends I think on what specifically we're talking about. We need to put some rules in place to make sure that our elected officials are not trading stocks. That is one area that we've seen I think extensive corruption there with insider information. But, you know, we also need to overturn, end Citizens United and make sure that we are getting that dark money out of politics so representatives can answer to their constituents and not, you know, insider interests.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, when we look at your bio, you will be the highest ranking female military officer ever to be elected to Congress. No female admiral or general has ever served before. You were chief of the Navy Reserve until you were relieved from your position by Secretary Hegseth in August 2025. He has said he's cutting the number of high-ranking officers by 20 percent, but he's also said he's ending diversity initiatives, or DEI. Do you have any idea why he targeted you?

NANCY LACORE: I don't. you know, I was never given a reason when I was removed from my position in August 2025. I don't think any of the other generals and admirals were ever given reasons either. And, frankly, at this point, it doesn't really matter. You know, it opened a door for me to do what I'm doing now and continuing my service in Congress.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Secretary Hegseth released a video Thursday arguing that attempts to oust him from office are about his rebuilding of the force Here's a clip.
(BEGIN VC)

PETE HEGSETH (Defense Secretary): Diversity is not our strength. Our unity is. Men and women, they're not the same thing, but in the military they must be held to the same standard. Strong young men who believe in something greater than themselves are admirable.
(END VC)

MARGARET BRENNAN: Went on to call being transgender a mental illness. He dismissed a reference to white rage. He said that seemed to be maybe about renaming military bases and taking confederate general names off of them.
Of all of these initiatives, what do you think the impact has been on the U.S. military?

NANCY LACORE: You know, I've said since I launched this campaign, Pete Hegseth is the most unqualified secretary that this nation has seen. He has caused significant damage to us as a country and put us at risk and really damaged the readiness of our entire military force. He is focused on the wrong things. He should be focused on strategy and readiness instead of these things that are down in the trenches.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, what do you think would be an impeachable offense? Because I know there is an effort underway in this Congress to do so. You've said you hope that gets taken care of before you come to Washington.

NANCY LACORE: Yes, I mean, I think there's probably plenty. And I do believe that this will be handled before I get there. You know, we can talk – we can tie this war as one thing that is extremely damaging to our country. Some of the things that we saw going on down – off Venezuela as well. But really it comes back to, you know, it's all a part of the problem with the corruption and the lack of strategy which is doing nothing but really driving up costs for people. And that's what people really care about. And so, that's what I want to focus on when I get to Congress.
(END VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll be right back.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's it for us today. Thank you all for watching. Until next week. For "FACE THE NATION," I'm Margaret Brennan.

title: ICE unlikely to scale back crackdown, sources say, citing Stephen Miller
summary: The Trump administration is unlikely to scale back its aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration following the results of the midterm elections, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, citing the elevation of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.
story: The Trump administration is unlikely to scale back its aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration following the results of the midterm elections, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, citing the elevation of immigration hawk Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

Republicans suffered huge losses across the country on Election Day, including in some historically red states like Texas. Exit polls indicated that immigration was one of the top issues, alongside the economy, among Texas Latinos, who swung heavily toward Democrats. And 58% of voters nationwide said the Trump administration's deportation crackdown had "gone too far."

In January, Democratic lawmakers will take control of both chambers of Congress and assume sweeping powers to investigate the administration's immigration crackdown and its most controversial policies.

Still, officials at the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have not received instructions to reduce immigration enforcement since the election, the sources said, requesting anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.

In recent weeks, ICE officials have been instructed to try to carry out around 19,000 arrests per week, or about 2,700 per day, an increase from a prior 2,000 daily arrest target, agency sources told CBS News. That target was set before the midterms.

The U.S. officials cited Miller's appointment to the top post in the White House as a clear indication the Trump administration is likely to continue ICE's deportation blitz, as well as its quieter yet far-reaching campaign to sharply restrict legal immigration.
Asked if the midterms would usher in a pullback in immigration enforcement, one of the officials responded, "I would count on the opposite" with Miller as chief of staff.

The sources also said the administration believes the stunning electoral losses last week were largely driven by concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran — not its immigration crackdown.

"This administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorize our communities. There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News.

Bis cited the Trump administration's efforts to bolster security at the U.S.-Mexico border, where illegal crossings have plunged to historically low levels after soaring to record highs under former President Joe Biden's tenure.
In a statement Sunday, DHS said ICE would not be "backing away or slowing down."
"Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation's laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets," DHS added.

Miller has been seen as a loyal foot soldier in Mr. Trump's inner circle for a decade, since his successful 2016 presidential campaign, when he promised to shut down Muslim immigration to the U.S. and dramatically expand deportations of those in the U.S. illegally.

During that time, Miller has solidified himself as the chief architect of Mr. Trump's hardline immigration policies. Miller was one of Mr. Trump's top aides during his first administration, when officials banned immigration and travel from Muslim-majority countries and separated thousands of migrant children from their parents as part of a "zero tolerance" crackdown that was abandoned after massive public uproar.
But Miller has greatly expanded his power — and his influence over federal immigration policymaking — since Mr. Trump's return to the White House.

In less than two years, with Miller as deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, the second Trump administration has effectively closed the U.S. asylum system; shut down refugee admissions, with a notable exemption for White South Africans; tightened access to different legal immigration benefits like green cards; and undertaken highly visible ICE and Border Patrol arrest operations across the country.

Those immigration enforcement operations have often triggered widespread community backlash, including in January, when federal immigration officials killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during a crackdown in Minneapolis that the administration scaled back following bipartisan outcry.

Miller has publicly floated the idea of suspending habeas corpus — the conditional right for people to challenge unlawful detention — for ICE detainees. Habeas cases have skyrocketed over the past two years, as the Trump administration has greatly narrowed other avenues for those fighting deportation to be released from ICE detention.

In addition to his immigration portfolio, Miller has also played an influential role in the Trump administration's crackdown on universities and legal groups, and its campaign to investigate allegations of fraud in Democratic-led states like Minnesota.

Theresa Cardinal Brown, an immigration official at DHS during the Obama and Bush administrations, said the Trump administration's deportation efforts are likely to face some obstacles next year. She expects congressional Democrats to use their new powers to try to rein in ICE, including by issuing a flurry of subpoenas, holding oversight hearings and passing measures to limit immigration enforcement funds.

Cardinal Brown also predicts that some communities and states with newly elected Democratic leaders, like Texas, may scrap or limit policies that allowed or required local law enforcement officials to work with ICE. Last week, Houston's mayor said he would direct local police to limit their cooperation with ICE, following the election results.

But Cardinal Brown stressed that Mr. Trump will likely veto any Democratic attempts to restrict ICE enforcement and noted the agency received $75 billion in funds through 2029 due to the "One Big Beautiful Bill" that the president signed into law last year.
"They're going to continue apace," Cardinal Brown said. "They have the money. They have the resources."

title: The SS United States and her final destination
summary: She was the fastest ocean liner in history. But the jet age took the SS United States out of service, and she wound up docked in Philadelphia for nearly 30 years. Now, she's scheduled to be scuttled off Florida, to become the world's largest artificial reef.
story: Even with her paint peeling and rivers of rust, the queen of the North Atlantic – five city blocks long, 12 stories high – still strikes quite a pose in the setting sun. The SS United States quickly became the fastest ocean liner in history. On her maiden voyage back in 1952, she reached speeds topping more than 40 miles an hour – a record for a transatlantic crossing that's never been broken.
But she was elegant, too – stately and refined. During her nearly two decades in service, she carried four U.S. presidents, countless celebrities, and tens of thousands of happy voyagers.

But what was once glamorous and spacious, the jet age did away with. Speed won out over starry nights at sea. By 1969, the SS United States was withdrawn from service, and that's what gets us back to her currently forlorn state. She wound up in Philadelphia, where for almost 30 years she sat with only spiders and sunbeams booking passage.
But she was still impossible to ignore.

"She still casts a spell; there's something about her," said Susan Gibbs, president of a non-profit called the SS United States Conservancy. "She has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together."

Gibbs knows every inch of this ship. Her grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the SS United States, with the U.S. military helping to foot the bill – a floating investment that could be converted in less than 24 hours into a troop ship to transport an entire division. "It may not seem that way now, but back then she was the space shuttle of her age," Gibbs said.
Only her bones are left, however – her once-grand staircase is bare; the indoor salt-water swimming pool is now just a ghostly abyss; the dance floor is still here, but nothing else.
And yet, there was still enough that Gibbs was determined to save. There were all kinds of ideas – museums, restaurants, event spaces – but no takers.

Our one-time flagship seemed headed for the scrap heap. Until that is, one man had a wild idea: return the SS United States back to the Atlantic, not to sail, but to sink – sending her to the bottom of the sea where nature, instead of the wrecking ball, will take its course.
"This will be the largest purposely-sunk artificial reef in the world," said Alex Fogg.

As the natural resources chief for Okaloosa County, Florida, Fogg has sunk a lot of ships – in fact, dozens of them, smaller ones off the coast of Florida as part of the county's artificial reef program.

The vessels have created habitats that are a delight for fish, fisherman and frogmen alike. But sinking the SS United States is something entirely different. Just one look at her two massive engine rooms and you realize the enormity of the task ahead.

For Jennifer Adams, director of tourism for Okaloosa County, what better tourist attraction could she bring? When she was approached about buying the SS United States, she said her response was, "'How much?' And he told me and I said, 'Go get her.'"
That price tag? A mere $1 million for the legendary ship, plus another $13 million to ready her for sinking. But then, the idea of sinking her suddenly became a little too real.
"I cried this morning when I walked on board," Adams said. "I just, I got overwhelmed."

Her county now owned a historic ship, but one full of 1950s environmental contaminants; that's problem one. Problem two was the SS United States still had plenty of fans on land, people like Linda Sylva, who made her first voyage as a teenager. "She was made in America, made from American parts, all over America," Sylva said.

Joe Beaman was just an eight-year-old kid when he set sail. All these years later, he's never forgotten it. "Oh no, once that ship has your heart, you never lose it," he said. "I mean, it's a part of me."
Even those who never sailed on her, like Jeffrey Smith, felt some kind of pull: "I drove in from Detroit yesterday because I wanted to say goodbye."
He and the others were on a farewell cruise of sorts, organized by the Conservancy, to give fans one last look before her last port of call.
In 2025, crews cast off her lines and began towing the SS United States south, her funnels barely clearing Philadelphia's Walt Whitman bridge.
Once at sea, she had all the majesty she always did, cutting the waves like a scalpel. She arrived almost two days ahead of schedule. "She's still breaking records, even today," Fogg laughed.

At a shipyard in Mobile, Alabama, she's undergone extensive remediation, from stem to stern, getting rid of those environmental contaminants. Holes were cut throughout to allow air and water to flow quickly and evenly during her sinking.
If all goes well, she'll be scuttled this week about 20 nautical miles off the coast between Pensacola and Destin/Ft. Walton Beach, Florida.

Her two funnels – some of the largest ever built – will become the bookends of a museum planned by the SS United States Conservancy that will eventually house one-of-a-kind artifacts, including the bar from the tourist class smoking lounge.
There will be plenty of salty tears when she's gone. Sinking seems contrary to everything she was designed to do. That said, the SS United States will remain a part of maritime lore forever.
After so many years alone, soon she'll become a place of life once again.

"She stood there year after year after year," said Linda Sylva, "waiting for somebody to say, 'Come here, you're welcome here.' And who is that welcome for? It's the ocean. What a perfect place for her to rest."

title: Villa Vie Odyssey "forever cruise" residents want their ship back
summary: Some residents of the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise are trying to reclaim the ship, which could potentially be auctioned off by its lender, CBS News has learned.
story: As the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship makes its way from Cambodia to Singapore, where it could potentially be auctioned off by its lender, CBS News has learned of at least two resident-led efforts to reclaim the vessel.

One effort recently failed after a lender denied funding to residents of the luxury "forever cruise." However, a second effort to buy the ship is still very much active, according to two sources familiar with the matter. It is led by another group hoping to buy the ship at auction, the sources said.
The second effort would not involve Villa Vie Residences' founder and executive chairman Mike Petterson, according to sources involved in the discussions.
Petterson said he believed he had an operational partner to rescue the ship, but that did not pan out, which led to the ship being taken by its lender.

Now, Petterson says he believes he could still get the ship back and is continuing to look for potential investors to take over the ship for good. Another option would be to raise the funds to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and sell the company. He no longer wants to be involved in company leadership.
"I'm not going to be the front face person of a company any time soon," Petterson told CBS News.

CBS News has also learned that a group of residents is considering legal action over fuel loans that were provided to the company in April — when residents said they raised more than $2 million dollars to keep the ship afloat.
The fuel loan program promised up to a 24% return if residents invested more money to help with the rising cost of fuel.
In a copy of an agreement obtained by CBS News, which appears to be from Villa Vie, the loan is described as "Unsecured" without "Collateral or Guarantees."

Craig and Cindy Voight were on board the ship from October 2024 when the Odyssey departed Belfast, Northern Ireland, for its voyage around the world. The couple said they spent more than $300,000 on their cabin and monthly dues, in addition to providing the company with $100,000 as participants in the fuel loan program. They said they plan to take legal action over that program.

"So we thought, alright, we're going to get 18% interest," Craig Voight said.  "First payment's supposed to start a month later. So between then and now they owe us over $113,000. They've never paid one penny."
Petterson acknowledged that some residents could potentially take legal action over the fuel loans in a statement that he shared with CBS News, saying "I take their concerns seriously."

In his statement, the executive also said financing for the loan program "was arranged during an urgent period for the vessel and was intended to support immediate operating needs, including fuel." The financing was structured through Villa Vie's parent company, Residential Cruise Holdings, "because existing financing restrictions prevented Villa Vie Residences from borrowing directly," he said.

"I recognize that residents want clear answers about how the loans were structured and handled," said Petterson. "Because legal action is being considered, I won't discuss individual claims or draw conclusions in the media. We will address the matter through the appropriate legal process and provide information through the proper channels."

title: 1 dead, at least a dozen hurt after car strikes cyclists in North Carolina
summary: One person was killed and at least a dozen others injured when a driver suspected of being impaired struck a group of more than 40 cyclists in North Carolina, authorities said.
story: One person was killed and several others injured Saturday morning when a driver suspected of being impaired struck a group of more than 40 cyclists in North Carolina, authorities said.

According to North Carolina State Highway Patrol, a little after 9:30 a.m. Eastern time a black Infiniti passenger car was traveling west on a road in Wake County when it crossed the center line and crashed into a group of cyclists who were biking east.
The driver did not stop at the scene, but continued for about a half-mile before crashing into a ditch on the side of the road, state highway patrol said.

Holly Springs Fire Chief LeRoy Smith said seven people were transported to a hospital with major injuries and 15 others sustained minor injuries. State highway patrol pegged the injury toll at about a dozen, however.
The deceased victim was identified by state highway patrol as 63-year-old Patrick Allen Turner of Cary, North Carolina.

The suspected driver, 76-year-old Donald Robert Morris-Jones of Apex, North Carolina, was arrested on multiple charges, including felony death by vehicle, felony serious injury by vehicle, felony hit-and-run involving serious injury or death, reckless driving and driving while impaired, according to officials.
He is being held on $1 million bond.
People at the scene told Smith the cyclists were part of a group that regularly gathers for weekend bike rides.
Wake County is located about 14 miles southwest of Raleigh.

title: Trump says he offered UFC's Dana White the press secretary role
summary: The role of the White House press secretary has been largely vacant since Karoline Leavitt stepped aside ​in August.
story: President Trump says he has offered the open White House press secretary role to UFC CEO Dana White.

The president said Saturday in a Truth Social post, "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States."

"I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris," he said in reference to UFC fighters. "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left."

It was unclear at the time of publication whether White has accepted the position, though he shared an image of himself at the White House press briefing room podium to his Instagram story with the caption, "On to the next chapter."
During a news conference for a boxing event in London Saturday that White was promoting, White was asked about Mr. Trump's social media post.
"I'm flying to Washington, D.C., right now," White said with a smile and a chuckle. "… I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday. So I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."
Reporting from at least one media outlet suggested that the post may have been made tongue-in-cheek. CBS News has reached out to the White House and UFC for additional comment.
The president's remarks come days after Democrats swept the midterm elections, taking control of the House and the Senate.

The press secretary role has been vacant since Oct. 16, when conservative commentator Katie Zacharia was removed from the job after just five days. Zacharia was Mr. Trump's pick to fill the role after Karoline Leavitt stepped aside in August, saying she wanted to spend more time with her young family.

As the chief of Ultimate Fighting Championship, running a global league valued at more than $15 billion, White has been a longtime supporter of Mr. Trump and attended his inauguration. The White House also hosted an Ultimate Fighting Championship in July on the South Lawn to mark the nation's 250th anniversary. The event coincided with Mr. Trump's 80th birthday.
"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" Mr. Trump said in his post.
In an interview with "60 Minutes" last September, White described his relationship with Mr. Trump, saying that when they get together for dinner, they "don't talk politics."
"We talk about … goofy guy stuff that all guys talk about. You know what I mean?" Dana said. "… We talk about 'Rocky' movies. We talk about different fights that have happened."

title: 2 licensed skydivers die after midair collision in California
summary: The two skydivers collided at approximately 150 feet above the ground, Skydive Elsinore said.
story: Two female skydivers who were taking part in an organized skydiving event in California were killed after colliding midair and plummeting to the ground.

The accident occurred Friday and involved two licensed, experienced skydivers at Skydive Elsinore, the company said in a statement. The Riverside County Sheriff's Department said deputies were dispatched late Friday morning after reports of an air emergency. The skydivers were taken to a local hospital with critical injuries.
They were pronounced dead at the hospital, the sheriff said.
The Riverside County coroner's office later identified the victims as 29-year-old Levi Pimentel of Aurora, Illinois, and 56-year-old Georgia Jean of Box Elder, South Dakota.

Skydive Elsinore said the free-fall portion of the dive and the opening of the parachutes were normal, but as they were preparing to land, the two skydivers collided at about 150 feet above the ground.

"The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground," Skydive Elsinore said in a statement.  The company said there was no evidence of equipment malfunction.
The skydivers were visiting from out of town to take part in an organized skydiving event, the company said.
Skydive Elsinore — which says they are the longest-running skydiving operation in North America —  is located approximately one hour away from both San Diego and Los Angeles metropolitan areas.
