title: Villa Vie Odyssey "forever cruise" residents want their ship back
summary: Some residents of the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise are trying to reclaim the ship, which could potentially be auctioned off by its lender, CBS News has learned.
story: As the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship makes its way from Cambodia to Singapore, where it could potentially be auctioned off by its lender, CBS News has learned of at least two resident-led efforts to reclaim the vessel.

One effort recently failed after a lender denied funding to residents of the luxury "forever cruise." However, a second effort to buy the ship is still very much active, according to two sources familiar with the matter. It is led by another group hoping to buy the ship at auction, the sources said.
The second effort would not involve Villa Vie Residences' founder and executive chairman Mike Petterson, according to sources involved in the discussions.
Petterson said he believed he had an operational partner to rescue the ship, but that did not pan out, which led to the ship being taken by its lender.

Now, Petterson says he believes he could still get the ship back and is continuing to look for potential investors to take over the ship for good. Another option would be to raise the funds to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and sell the company. He no longer wants to be involved in company leadership.
"I'm not going to be the front face person of a company any time soon," Petterson told CBS News.

CBS News has also learned that a group of residents is considering legal action over fuel loans that were provided to the company in April — when residents said they raised more than $2 million dollars to keep the ship afloat.
The fuel loan program promised up to a 24% return if residents invested more money to help with the rising cost of fuel.
In a copy of an agreement obtained by CBS News, which appears to be from Villa Vie, the loan is described as "Unsecured" without "Collateral or Guarantees."

Craig and Cindy Voight were on board the ship from October 2024 when the Odyssey departed Belfast, Northern Ireland, for its voyage around the world. The couple said they spent more than $300,000 on their cabin and monthly dues, in addition to providing the company with $100,000 as participants in the fuel loan program. They said they plan to take legal action over that program.

"So we thought, alright, we're going to get 18% interest," Craig Voight said.  "First payment's supposed to start a month later. So between then and now they owe us over $113,000. They've never paid one penny."
Petterson acknowledged that some residents could potentially take legal action over the fuel loans in a statement that he shared with CBS News, saying "I take their concerns seriously."

In his statement, the executive also said financing for the loan program "was arranged during an urgent period for the vessel and was intended to support immediate operating needs, including fuel." The financing was structured through Villa Vie's parent company, Residential Cruise Holdings, "because existing financing restrictions prevented Villa Vie Residences from borrowing directly," he said.

"I recognize that residents want clear answers about how the loans were structured and handled," said Petterson. "Because legal action is being considered, I won't discuss individual claims or draw conclusions in the media. We will address the matter through the appropriate legal process and provide information through the proper channels."
This story published first on CBS News at 8:28 a.m. on Nov. 8, 2026.

title: More than 600,000 left with no power in Ukraine after strikes, authorities say
summary: Ukraine has been bracing for Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
story: Hundreds of thousands of people were left without power after Russian strikes hit Ukraine's energy infrastructure, authorities said on Sunday.

In the central Dnipropetrovsk region, "more than 600,000 residents of the region have been left without power," power company DTEK said on Telegram after a "night attack has damaged important energy facilities".
It said the company was working to restore electricity but the task was "complicated by repeated attacks".
Ukrainian President Volodymyr previously accused Russia of ramping up attacks on Ukraine ahead of trilateral talks next week with Russia.
In another strike, a Russian drone hit "a critical infrastructure facility" in the northeastern Kharkiv region, the mayor of Zlatopil city, Mykola Baksheyev, said on social media.
"Nearly 250,000 customers in the Kharkiv region were left without power," Baksheyev said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the night-time strikes had triggered "widespread power outages across the country".
"In the Zhytomyr region alone, 140 apartment buildings were left without heating following a Russian strike," he said, as temperatures in Ukraine already hovered around freezing.
He also said Russia had launched a drone at Komyshuvakha, a village in the Zaporizhzhia region where Moscow had hit an aid distribution centre on Monday in one of the deadliest attacks of the war.
The death toll has risen to 55 people, Zelenskyy said. Emergency services previously put it at 50 killed.

"This morning, the Russians attacked Komyshuvakha with an FPV drone, where emergency rescue operations have been underway for seven days ... Unfortunately, more people may still be under the rubble," Zelenskyy said.

The strikes came a day after Ukraine's energy ministry said a massive attack on energy facilities had plunged residents in five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv.

title: Italy's leader blames pro-Russian hackers for personal data leaks
summary: Italy's foreign minister said he was targeted because of his country's support for Ukraine.
story: Italy's prime minister blamed pro-Russian hackers for leaking the country's foreign minister's data onto the dark web.

Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani said on Saturday he has been subjected to intimidation and that his personal data was leaked because of his support for Ukraine, but did not specify who was behind it.

In a post on X, Tajani blamed "cybercriminals" for posting his personal data on the dark web, a term used to describe a section of the internet only accessible with specialist software, commonly associated with criminal activities.
In a separate statement on Saturday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed "pro-Russian hackers" for the leaks.

Meloni expressed her "full solidarity" with the foreign minister over "what has come to light regarding the activities of pro-Russian hackers and the dissemination of personal data relating to him on the dark web."
"The sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination," Meloni added.

Tajani said the leaks have been going for days and expose him to threats and intimidation. He added that his family have also been targeted and the perpetrators are still looking for more information.

"Our position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted," the minister said. "Defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation's democracy and independence, is dangerous for these criminal entities."
Tajani said he would not be intimidated by the incident and vowed to continue his support of Italian allies.
"I will continue working to defend my ministry and Italy, and I will keep strengthening ties and cooperation with our allies so that we can protect ourselves together," the minister said.

title: Mass shooting in Polish market leaves at least 6 dead, 15 injured
summary: Krakow police said a man who had driven onto the square began firing at random people from his car.
story: A man drove into an open market in the Polish city of Krakow and opened fire from his car, killing at least six people and injuring at least 15 others, authorities said. Another three people were later found dead in the suspect's home. The suspected gunman was shot by police and taken into custody.

The shooting happened in the Main Market Square in Krakow around 3 p.m. local time on Saturday. Krakow police said the alleged shooter began firing at random people from his car. Police said the victims were four women and two men.
Two women and one man believed to be relatives of the suspect were later found dead in suspect's home, said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, according to The Associated Press.

Marcin Kierwiński, Poland's interior minister, said there were indications the suspect was fascinated by far-right ideology, according to Reuters. The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen, is fascinated with far-right ideologies and held "very radical" and "ultra-nationalistic" views, The AP reported Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Five foreigners were among the wounded victims, Kierwiński said. He said a foreign national was among those killed. A spokesperson from the U.S. State Department told CBS News they are not aware of any U.S. citizens being harmed at this time.

Police officers are also among the wounded. The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a confrontation with police a short distance away from the initial violence, and was taken to a hospital for treatment.
The death toll earlier stood at five, but the Malopolski regional government updated it to six in a post on X.
Kierwiński wrote on X that two police officers were wounded by gunfire and one is in serious condition.
"Police officers in Kraków risked their lives to intervene. Immediately. Thanks to their heroic actions, the attacker was quickly apprehended," he wrote.
In a social media post, Krakow police said the gunman acted alone.

Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, told TVN24 that the suspected gunman was wearing military-style fatigues and used a military-type long gun in the attack. Police found many pieces of other weapons, as well as ammunition, in his car.

"I am being kept informed by the Minister of the Interior about the situation in Krakow following the tragic shooting," Tusk wrote on social media, adding that "the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack."
He later headed to Krakow from the capital, Warsaw, a government spokesperson said.
Other details were not immediately available.
Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy.
"The square will belong to us again," Gibała said in a video posted to X.

"We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Krakow, a savage and murderous attack that's shattered the peace of Poland," Tom Rose, the U.S. ambassador to Poland, wrote on X. "America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow."
Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland, a European Union and NATO member of 38 million people.

"I saw a man shooting at people and walking around the square," Annette, a woman in her sixties, told news wire Agence France-Presse. "It's a tragedy for Krakow; we've never seen anything like this before."
Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said in a statement that the EU stands with Poland and offered her condolences.

"The tragic loss of life in the shooting in Kraków is a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland," she wrote on X. "Poland's strength lies in the resilience of its people. In this moment of grief, Poland does not stand alone."
Krakow is the second-largest city in Poland and roughly 155 miles from the capital, Warsaw.

title: Israel's president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government
summary: Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, ran against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but neither won a clear majority.
story: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27.
Eisenkot, a former military chief, ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leading a bloc of parties seeking to oust Israel's longest-serving premier.
"Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," Eisenkot wrote on X in his first reaction to the announcement of his designation.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu's party won a clear majority in the vote. But in marathon discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel's main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government.
Herzog's decision is a setback for Netanyahu, who has leveled allegations, so far without evidence, that some Arab countries interfered in the elections.

The acting director-general of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."

Herzog's announcement, which had been expected on Sunday, came shortly after Netanyahu called for a "national unity government" in a video statement and warned against "hastily swearing in a government with terrorist supporters" — an apparent reference to the Arab-led parties who have backed Eisenkot.

Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly portrayed the Arab-led parties as a threat to national security. Eisenkot, however, has indicated a willingness to partner with them as long as they meet certain conditions, including agreeing to refer to Hamas as a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed.

Eisenkot's party, Yashar, slammed the prime minister's video with a statement posted on X and urged members of Netanyahu's party, Likud, to disavow their alliance with "radical parties," which is seen as a reference to some of the settler-linked and ultra-Orthodox parties in his religious-nationalist coalition.

The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Netanyahu's bloc won 53, while Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 seats.

Because neither Eisenkot's nor Netanyahu's blocs won a clear majority of the vote, they would need some support from the Arab parties to form a coalition government. The heads of the two largest Arab parties said they would be willing to help Eisenkot's opposition bloc oust Netanyahu, though most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from the Arab parties to form a government.

Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on — Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament.

Netanyahu, whom President Trump endorsed enthusiastically, will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim.

title: Pope Leo calls for universal healthcare weeks after lung cancer surgery
summary: Pope Leo XIV spoke about access to healthcare on his first stop in Uruguay during his 12-day Latin American tour.
story: Montevideo - Pope Leo XIV drew on his own recent experience of illness and hospitalization after surgery for lung cancer on Friday to make an impassioned appeal for universal access to healthcare, greater social equality and a society that does not measure people's worth by their productivity or wealth.

"Recently I experienced firsthand the limitations imposed by illness and I received care for which I am grateful," the Pope said in his first speech after arriving in Uruguay, to the country's political and civic leaders.

Pope Leo XIV was released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital four days after removing a cancerous tumor from his right lung.  "The experience made me think of the many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis or receive the treatment they need."
"Ensuring that healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of their resources, is a duty that confronts every society," he said.

Uruguay is the first stop of a 12-day trip that also includes Argentina and Peru. Leo's doctors said he needed no further treatment after his operation and was cleared to travel. The trip schedule is the longest international journey of his pontificate so far, with 19,000 travel miles, 14 flights, 36 speeches and approximately 50 events.

Vatican officials told reporters ahead of the trip that the Pope would have a medical team travel with him, as is customary on papal trips, but that no special measures were being taken. "We're speaking of a 71-year-old person in good health," the Vatican spokesman said.

The Latin America journey is Leo's first return as Pope to the country and region that has profoundly shaped his vision, and where he spent decades of his life, first as an Augustinian missionary, and then as bishop of Chiclayo, Peru. The pope holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.
Leo's remarks on caring for the sick were part of a broad appeal for a society where the most vulnerable are protected, and where economic development benefits everyone rather than just the elite.
"The creation of wealth and economic initiative…must also translate into goods and opportunities that effectively reach everyone," Leo said.

While praising Uruguay for four decades of uninterrupted democracy, he stressed that a country's success is ultimately measured by how it protects human dignity and cares for the most vulnerable in society.
Leo also spoke in defense of children, including the unborn. Abortion was legalized in Uruguay in 2012, making it one of the first Latin American countries to do so.
"Their absolute dependence on their mother does not diminish the dignity to which they are entitled or the protection they deserve," the pope said.

Children, he said, must have access to quality education and opportunities to enter the workforce and achieve personal independence.  Touching on a subject close to his heart, he said that technological advances and artificial intelligence must serve human beings rather than replace workers.

Leo will remain in Uruguay until Sunday when he will continue his travels to Argentina and Peru. The Vatican spokesman said there, Leo would address a range of issues, including the environment, arms tracking and political instability.
The Pope will also hold meetings with survivors of clerical sex abuse, but no further details are available as of now.

title: Zelenskyy says Russia is stepping up attacks ahead of U.S. talks
summary: Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi for talks aimed at ending the war.
story: Missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media that Russia used 36 missiles to target critical infrastructure. Only four missiles were taken down, Zelenskyy said, highlighting a shortage of interceptors. He also said 172 drones were used in the attacks, which struck Kyiv and 12 other regions.
The president accused Russia of intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and the country's infrastructure ahead of trilateral talks.

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
"Russia has a very particular view of diplomacy – as a subtype of aggression," Zelenskyy wrote.
"We hope that the United States, like our other partners, will act on principle," he added.
Russian attacks target Ukrainian infrastructure
The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.
Zelenskyy said a kindergarten was "partially destroyed." Photos show rubble near the damaged building.
Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.

"The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It's very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren't sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. "I'm old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?"

Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 892-yard-long Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River. Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city's heating and water supply systems."

Ukraine's Energy Ministry said Saturday's missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.
The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.

Russia also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.

Zelenskyy said that at one energy facility, preliminary findings show Russia used KN-23 missiles "manufactured and supplied by North Korea." He called the use of the alleged North Korean missile "further proof that global sanctions regimes need to be significantly strengthened." Technical assessments at other sites are ongoing.
Recovery efforts continue after massive attack

Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.

"She went to get humanitarian aid, and a 3-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?" he said. "She didn't come home, and they didn't find her body there. She isn't in the morgue, and she isn't here alive."
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Russia reports drone strikes
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia's Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.

The head of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged "civilian infrastructure" and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

The head of Russia's Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.
Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol's Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.

title: Paraguay's president under house arrest after bank collapse
summary: The president was placed under house arrest after being removed from office following the collapse of a bank linked to the government.
story: Paraguay's president has been placed on house arrest on Friday after the collapse of a government-linked bank that locked nearly half the country's population out of their accounts.

Paraguay's Senate voted to remove Santiago Peña for misconduct in office, making him the second president ousted by impeachment since the end of Gen. Alfredo Stroessner's 35-year dictatorship in 1989.
Regulators had seized Ueno Bank just three days earlier, sending shock waves through the financial system and setting off the country's worst political crisis in more than a decade.

Peña was ordered to remain at one of his homes in Asunción until he appears before prosecutors Saturday morning on charges of breach of trust, influence peddling and using public office for personal gain, the most serious of which carry up to 10 years in prison. Lawmakers accuse him of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.
The Paraguayan president denied wrongdoing.

When regulators seized the bank, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say they can't reach their money.

The fallout has spread well beyond savers. A ride-hailing app that relied on Ueno shut down, leaving 3,000 drivers without work. The state power company says $21 million in loans from the Inter-American Development Bank and Taiwan, earmarked for public works, is trapped at the bank. Paraguay's bonds have posted some of the worst losses in emerging markets this week, and the guaraní has slid against the dollar.

Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaraníes (about $1,500). Deposits are insured up to about $35,000, which the central bank says covers 97% of Ueno's customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe.

title: Pope voted in U.S. election because he's "proud to be an American"
summary: Pope Leo, who is on a 12-day, three-country trip in Latin America, also said he credits God and doctors for his lung cancer surgery recovery.
story: Pope Leo XIV, who became the first sitting pontiff to vote in a U.S. election, said Friday he is "proud to be an American and to exercise my right" to vote.

His remarks, made to reporters en route to Latin America for a 12-day trip, come after the Vatican confirmed the U.S.-born pontiff had voted via mail-in ballot in his native Chicago. He declined to comment on the outcome of the midterm elections, which gave control of Congress to the Democrats in a repudiation of President Trump. Instead, he pointed to the statement released by the Vatican last week that cited his longstanding belief in civic participation.
The pope, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said in an Oct. 30 statement.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Vatican said in a statement.

The pope has a long history of civic engagement in the U.S., the Vatican said, confirming that during his nearly two decades as a missionary and then bishop in Peru, Leo voted whenever he was eligible. He holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.
The Associated Press reported Leo, as Robert Prevost, previously voted in five primary elections since 2000 — on the Democratic ballots in 2008 and 2019 and Republican ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
Leo said Friday that he hadn't been able to vote in Peru's recent election since absentee ballots "aren't possible."
"But I would have done it. It's a good thing," he said, according to the AP.
U.S. federal law allows American citizens, even those who work for foreign governments, to retain their citizenship.

The 71-year-old pope is on a three-nation, 12-day tour just three weeks after he underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. He was cleared to travel on Oct. 26 — two weeks after his surgery.

"I am very happy to be here myself. I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place," Leo told reporters when he greeted them in the back of the plane. "I confess that from the first day, I had no doubt. I was convinced that this trip had to go forward and very happy to say, praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistance, I am here today, I think, in fairly good shape."
He acknowledged, though, that he hadn't had a chance to play tennis yet.
"Not yet, but I will," he said.

On Oct. 13, doctors removed the lower lobe of Leo's right lung after discovering a malignant tumor. The cancer, identified as a lung adenocarcinoma, was discovered accidentally during a routine abdominal examination, his doctors said. The operation was successful, without complications, and Leo was discharged from the hospital on Oct. 17.

"Early detection is obviously the best way to go, and so regular checkups are a blessing," Leo said, crediting his recovery to "trusting God, good doctors, good surgeons, and overall I think a healthy lifestyle."

title: Thomas Markle Sr., Meghan's father, arrested in Florida
summary: It was reported in October that Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
story: Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday in Florida in connection with allegations he possessed child sex abuse material in storage units in California, the Justice Department announced.
The announcement came after three sources familiar with the matter confirmed the arrest to CBS News.

The Justice Department said Markle was arrested for allegedly keeping child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.

"These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.

Markle, who made his first court appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday, entered the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing black pants and a black T-shirt with an illustration of a cat drinking a tropical drink.

Markle was advised that this hearing was related to the items found in two storage units in California. Prosecutors said they have not made a determination on whether he stays in Florida or is transferred to California, where the charges originated.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Thomas Wilson ordered Markle released on personal recognizance and ordered him to submit to home detention and electronic monitoring. Markle is also not permitted to travel outside the Middle District of Florida and the Central District of California.
No plea was taken. Markle's arraignment date in the Central District of California is not yet scheduled, but likely won't happen for at least several weeks.
The Daily Mail, a British tabloid newspaper, first reported Markle's arrest.
Allegations in Philippines lead to U.S. and Mexican investigations

Last month, it was reported that Markle was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse material. Markle has denied the claims against him, calling them "sick lies."
"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the Daily Mail.

A spokesperson for the Philippine National Police told CBS News in a statement that they launched an investigation after Markle's personal items were turned over to law enforcement by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Jr. told the Sun tabloid last month that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.
"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him."
The Daily Mail reported last week that it alerted the FBI of a cache of child porn found inside a storage unit Markle Sr. had rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico.
In a statement on Friday, the Baja California State Attorney General's Office in Mexico confirmed to CBS News that a search was conducted on Oct. 29 after a report via the 911 emergency line.

"During the operation, three old magazines and VHS tapes containing child pornography were discovered," the office said in its statement. "The evidence and the associated case files were referred to the Attorney General's Office (FGR), which will handle the follow-up to the case."
DOJ's claims against Markle Sr.

According to an affidavit in the complaint filed in federal court, the investigation in the Philippines led law enforcement to investigate two storage units registered to Markle Sr. in the Los Angeles area that he had rented since 2008, with the most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Inside the units, agents with the FBI seized 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse materials. In one of the units, agents found at least 18 images that appear to constitute child pornography.
Two of the images found allegedly show an adult man — whom a witness identified as Markle Sr. — with a nude prepubescent girl, the affidavit said.

A third image allegedly shows a nude prepubescent girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Other photos allegedly show Markle Sr. with children in various stages of undress, the affidavit said.

"Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement, adding: "This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide."
If convicted, Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.
Meghan distanced herself because of allegations years ago

After the reports of the investigation were made public, Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News that she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.
She said it was based on that information that she and Harry decided to cut her father off from contact with their children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

Meghan also confronted her father last year about the child sexual abuse allegations leveled against him, according to CBS News partner BBC News. Video that the British tabloid the Daily Mail says it obtained exclusively shows Markle accepting a letter sent by his daughter in his hospital room in the U.S. in December 2025.
According to the BBC, in that letter, Meghan wrote that she and authorities "knew he had abused young girls," adding that he would never meet her and Harry's children Archie and Lilibet.
Meghan will not be commenting on the arrest at this time, sources say.

title: Ukrainian official sees hope for eventual Putin-Zelenskyy meeting
summary: Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for the first trilateral talks since February.
story: KYIV, Ukraine — Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine's Presidential Office, expressed "restrained optimism" there could be progress made toward an eventual meeting between Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin during trilateral negotiations next week.

Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for the first trilateral talks since February and the first since a heated back-and-forth over SpaceX's Starshield being throttled down. In an interview with CBS News on Friday, Budanov said the discussions would focus on postwar security guarantees for Ukraine and Russia.

"There are absolutely different situations at different times," Budanov said, referring to these trilateral discussions versus the ones in February. "Now, obviously, all parties wanted to hold this meeting. This means that there are certain prerequisites for this."
"These negotiations are not the last," he said.

Budanov, who led the country's Defense Intelligence service before taking over Ukraine's Presidential Office in January, will join the delegation led by Ukraine's top negotiator, Rustem Umerov. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to represent Washington. Russia's delegation will be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a Vladimir Putin aide who headed Moscow's team in earlier rounds of negotiations.

"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said in announcing the talks earlier this week.

The meeting follows several weeks of strain in the U.S.-Ukraine relationship. In October, President Trump announced a deal to allow Russia to supply diesel to the United States for the first time since 2022. Elon Musk's SpaceX also imposed limits on Ukraine's Starshield satellite networks, disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and some air-defense systems, before reinstating access weeks later.
Despite these developments, Budanov said he is optimistic about Ukraine's relationship with the United States heading into the trilateral meeting next week.

"Look, it's bad. It shouldn't be like that," Budanov said of the Starshield failures. "But along with that, we can remind you that this situation is resolved in one way or another. This gives optimism for the future."

The trilateral meeting comes as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Strikes this week hit energy facilities in 10 regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry, left hundreds of thousands of households without electricity and cut water to much of Kyiv for more than 16 hours.
Budanov, speaking from his office in the capital, said Russia was using the strikes to create political pressure on Kyiv.

Russia's goal is "to cause the maximum damage to our critical infrastructure," he said. "What they hope to do is to create a foundation for social dissatisfaction, for street protests, and to stifle the national interests. But this will not happen."

title: Grim details emerge after bear kills woman and daughter
summary: The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain and the grizzly bear's behavior.
story: Selah Reed's family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister.

When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia's central coast. Balcarras' car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found.

Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras' brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly.
When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found. The search was now a tragic recovery effort.

The killings of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 3 to 4 kilometers (1.8 to 2.4 miles) from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack.

Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials have set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend's attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. They also are not sure whether more than one bear was involved.
Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said the killings were triggering for the families who were traumatized by last year's attack.

"Our community is still healing," he said, adding that they've imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. "Our priority is to ensure they're safe and ensure our community is supported."
Bear attack complicated the search
The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain, even though it was close to the trailhead, and the grizzly bear's behavior.
Searchers found Jenny Balcarras first, then her daughter. The search was helped by more resources and a cadaver dog, Matt Balcarras said.

Searchers found his niece's remains in a bear cache — a place where bears stash food, sometimes by digging a small hole and covering it with branches and vegetation to keep other animals and birds away.
"Even though it was within 100 or so meters (330 feet), locating remains in a cache is difficult," he said.

By the time officials located his niece, she could only be identified by her clothing, he said. His sister was in a similar condition, but they knew who she was thanks to several tiny tattoos, he said.
"There's no obvious body to identify," he said. "The coroner's investigation will include DNA and dental work. But there is no doubt that the remains that were found are theirs."
Balcarras was comfortable in challenging environments

Grizzly bears are common in the area surrounding the Bella Coola community, officials said. Conservation officials maintain a hotline where people can report problem bears, but no calls had been received recently, Tyre said during a media briefing.

Balcarras, an art therapist, had moved to Bella Coola during the summer. She had previously lived in Alaska, where her children were born, and was "the central organizing person in our family," Matt Balcarras said.

"In classic, strong single-mother style, she scraped together a career and a life for herself and her kids," Balcarras said. She was small in stature but strong in character and physical abilities, he said.
She was comfortable living among the wildlife, he said.

"She lived in the Bush when her kids were babies," he said. "She and my niece were not naive or foolish or uninformed. They've lived in these areas and have been around animals of countless types for years and years and decades."
Other bear attacks in British Columbia

There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks. The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.

In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.

A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.

A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.

title: 'American Idol' star Justin Guarini endured dark spiral after Hollywood dream collapsed
summary: "American Idol" alum Justin Guarini opens up about the dark spiral after RCA dropped him and how embracing failure led to Broadway, "Wicked" and a whole new identity.
story: The first "American Idol" runner-up tells Fox News Digital about his rise and fall in Hollywood.
At the start of his career, Justin Guarini seemed to have it all: fame, fortune and a promising future in Hollywood.

After becoming the runner-up on the first season of "American Idol" in 2002, Guarini was thrust into the spotlight seemingly overnight. But when his Hollywood dream came crashing down, he found himself in a dark place that he would eventually come to view as one of his greatest blessings.

"I think it was one of the greatest things that could ever have happened to me," Guarini, who recently released his book, "Center Stage Confidence: How to Own Your Story and Command Any Room," told Fox News Digital. "Failure is the greatest teacher, one of the greatest teachers that we can have in any given situation because in that failure, you have one of two paths. You either give up or you keep going."

However, this mindset didn't sink in until much later.
Justin Guarini details the dark days following his Hollywood downfall. (Getty Images)
In his book, Guarini recalled the moment he learned he had been dropped by his record label, RCA, in 2003.

"I stared at the TV in shock as my entire world came crumbling down around my ears," Guarini, who said he learned the news during a "Weekend Update" segment on "Saturday Night Live," wrote in his book. "Every illusion of fame, fortune, and glory fell away in an instant — only to be replaced by the silence of loss. In that moment, the veil of my arrogance, my assumptions, and my entitlement were lifted away, and I saw my life for what it had become."

title: Bill Murray pours Guinness for fans at New York bar after admitting fame 'is not easy'
summary: Bill Murray played bartender on Halloween night, pouring perfect pints of Guinness for cheering fans at a bar in Yonkers and posing for photos.
story: Actor Bill Murray tried to make National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett briefly stop smiling during an interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Monday.
Bill Murray was spotted enjoying Halloween in Yonkers, New York, where he interacted with fans while working behind the bar.

The 76-year-old actor and former "Saturday Night Live" star was photographed sitting with Rory Dolan, the owner of Rory Dolan's Restaurant & Bar, and showing off his bartending skills by pouring Guinness for customers.
The actor looked like a natural behind the bar as fans cheered when he poured a glass of Guinness.

"He had a bottle of wine, a very nice bottle of wine, and he also had, he was drinking some beer, but he did pour a pint of Guinness," Dolan told Fox News Digital. "Three-part pour, which is good to see him doing it. It wasn't his first time to do it!"
Murray spent time on Halloween pouring Guinness for patrons at Rory Dolan's Restaurant & Bar. (Rory Dolan's Restaurant & Bar)
ACTOR BILL MURRAY STUNS TRUMP'S TOP ECONOMIC ADVISOR WITH BIZARRE QUESTION ON NEWS SHOW

According to Dolan, Murray arrived at the restaurant on his own. Murray kept it casual in a black outfit, with a navy blue button-up vest over a long-sleeved black shirt. In addition to serving drinks, Murray took time to pose for photos with other patrons at the bar.

"I think because he really was looking for the Irish culture," Dolan said. "He had been in Ireland doing this show. He has an excellent show out, but he was building on that energy, and he wanted to get behind the bar, pour a pint, and he wanted to know all about me and Rory Dolan's and whatever else. He was just very inquisitive, and he was very, very gracious to all, every one of the customers who went up and asked for photographs and spoke to them at length, and he was just, it was just great to have him."
Murray sits with the owner of Rory Dolan's Restaurant & Bar in Yonkers. (Rory Dolan's Restaurant & Bar)
Dolan also shared that the restaurant was celebrating another patron's 90th birthday the night Murray visited.

"The 90th birthday was that evening and then the crowd was in before the 90th birthday," Dolan said. "There was a big funeral, and they all came out to the bar, and it was just, the place was full and he was loving it."
Dolan said other celebrities, including Pierce Brosnan, have also visited the bar.

Murray got his big break when he was cast on "Saturday Night Live" in 1977, winning an Emmy for his work on the show's writing staff. He went on to receive an Academy Award nomination, seven Golden Globe nominations with one win, four Emmy nominations with two wins and a BAFTA Award.
Murray admitted that being famous doesn't always make him happy. (Rory Dolan's Restaurant & Bar)
In his new docuseries, "A Course Called Ireland," Murray discussed his relationship to fame and whether being a public figure makes him happy, answering, "In a word, no."

"It's not easy," he said, according to People. "I go through new revelations all the time about how I handle it and how to deal with it. It's not for everyone, but it has also brought me to this place, you know."
Murray also took time to pose for photos with fans. (Rory Dolan's Restaurant & Bar)
Despite it not being easy, Murray also admitted that being recognized in public has brought him joy on occasion, most notably when fans share with him how much one of his films means to them.

Meeting fans over the years has helped the "Lost in Translation" star realize there is "a lot of goodwill out there," although he also admitted that he's "not very pleasant."
Murray posed for a photo outside of Rory Dolan's Restaurant & Bar. (Rory Dolan's Restaurant & Bar)

"I think kind of famous people, they can decide that there's a certain way to play being famous, you know?" he said. When asked how he handles fame, Murray said, "Well, I’m not very pleasant. You can see that. I think just being nice-nice, I don’t go for nice-nice. If I were like an ordinary citizen acting the way that I do, I’d probably have a lot more cuts and bruises."

title: Pierce Brosnan backs 'Fantastic Beasts' star for next James Bond, predicts fans will be 'blown away'
summary: Pierce Brosnan singled out Callum Turner as a standout among the actors being considered for the next James Bond role in a Vanity Fair interview.
story: Former Bond girl Alison Papworth shares why she wants the next 007 to stay true to the books as speculation swirls over the role.
Pierce Brosnan is throwing in his two cents into the conversation regarding who should be chosen to play the next James Bond, nearly 25 years after he last played the iconic character.

During a recent interview with Vanity Fair, the 73-year-old actor said he is following along with the public as "an audience member," adding he is just as "eager" as everyone else "to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history." He did, however, give one actor a special shoutout.

"All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire," he said. "Callum, Callum Turner is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong. They all have a voice and a physique, and a presence on film. They all have longevity as actors, all of these young men."
While he doesn't know who will take on the iconic role next, Brosnan wishes whoever is chosen "the very best of life and strength and courage."
Brosnan wishes whoever takes over as the next James Bond strength. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)
FORMER BOND GIRL SAYS NEXT 007 SHOULD BE 'ANOTHER GORGEOUS MAN' AS JAMES BOND DECISION

Brosnan first appeared as agent 007 in the 1995 movie, "GoldenEye," having taken over the reins from Timothy Dalton. He appeared in his final Bond movie in 2002 with the release of "Die Another Day," and was replaced by Daniel Craig in the 2006 movie, "Casino Royale."
Craig starred as James Bond in six films, before hanging up his badge following the release of "No Time to Die" in 2021.
Brosnan began his tenure as James Bond in 1995 with the release of "GoldenEye." (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)
"You know, it’s hard to tell who it would be, but I eagerly await to hear the news and the celebration of the next James Bond," Brosnan said.
In addition to a new actor playing Bond, the film is also getting a new director in Denis Villeneuve, who will be taking over the franchise, which excites Brosnan.
Craig hung up his badge in 2021 with the release of "No Time to Die." (Greg Williams/Eon Productions via Getty Images)

When speaking with GQ about the mental and physical load of playing the character in September 2022, he nonchalantly explained, "You get chipped, you get nicked, you pull muscles, you get stitched up."
Brosnan also touched on the physical toll of playing James Bond. (Mike Marsland/WireImage)

title: King Charles' 'short fuse' on display in viral downpour as Queen Camilla gets umbrella first: expert
summary: King Charles III was left drenched after aides failed to provide an umbrella during a downpour in Antigua, while Queen Camilla was quickly sheltered.
story: The monarch got soaked during a celebration of Antigua and Barbuda’s 45th anniversary of independence at Sir Vivian Richards Stadium. Copyright: Thomson Reuters. Courtesy of ABS TV Radio.
King Charles III was left royally soaked — and his patience appeared to dry up faster than his suit.

The British monarch was caught without an umbrella as the skies opened on Nov. 1 during a celebration at Sir Vivian Richards Stadium marking Antigua and Barbuda's 45th anniversary of independence. Charles and his wife, Queen Camilla, were attending the parade during their royal tour of the Caribbean when the weather took a sudden turn.

As heavy rain pelted the royal couple, Camilla was quickly handed an umbrella and hurried toward shelter. Charles, however, was left exposed to the elements, getting more drenched by the second and appearing increasingly exasperated.
KING CHARLES’ ‘JUST GIVE US A RING!’ QUIP LEADS VIRAL MOMENTS FROM ROYAL US TOUR WITH QUEEN CAMILLA

King Charles III arrives in the rain for the annual Independence Ceremonial Parade, marking 45 years of Antigua and Barbuda's independence, at the Sir Vivian Richards Stadium on Nov. 1, 2026, in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda. (Aaron Chown - Pool/Getty Images)

After spotting his wife walking away beneath an umbrella, the 77-year-old threw his hands into the air and repeatedly waved at royal aides, apparently calling for an umbrella of his own as rain soaked his suit.
Help eventually arrived, but not before Charles was drenched. By the time an aide handed him an umbrella, the king was already soaking wet.

King Charles III walks in the rain as he attends a military parade marking Antigua and Barbuda's 45th Independence anniversary at the Sir Vivian Richards Stadium in Antigua and Barbuda on Nov. 1, 2026. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"King Charles has historically had a short fuse," royal commentator Meredith Constant told Fox News Digital. "What we see is that when he is under immense pressure and something seemingly small goes awry, like the pen incident, he loses his cool. In the situation with the umbrella, King Charles had every right to be annoyed with his aides. He's in his late 70s, living with cancer; his wife was immediately handed an umbrella; this was a downpour, not a light drizzle."
WATCH: KING CHARLES CAUGHT IN DOWNPOUR DURING ROYAL TOUR

"One of the reasons Charles and Camilla work is that she balances him out," Constant said. "She can laugh it off, share a funny aside; she has the ability to let things roll off her shoulders in a way Charles never has. Charles and Camilla function much more like a unit, particularly because Camilla never tries to compete for the limelight."

Camilla couldn't hold back her laughter when she rejoined her husband on the dais after the rain eased. The couple chuckled at the mishap. "I've started growing watercress on my trousers," Charles joked, according to the Evening Standard.

Queen Camilla gestures in the rain as she attends the annual Independence Ceremonial Parade with King Charles III at Sir Vivian Richards Stadium in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, Nov. 1, 2026. (Getty Images)

"The umbrella incident was in stark contrast to the public composure, restraint and emotional discipline demonstrated by Queen Elizabeth," British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "Yet 'all's well that ends well’ as the giggles King Charles and Queen Camilla displayed after the rain saved the day."
Queen Elizabeth II attends the Out-Sourcing Inc. Royal Windsor Cup polo match at Guards Polo Club in Egham, England, on July 11, 2021. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"The humor King Charles displayed at the moment, without any advice or counsel from courtiers, was immensely significant as it demonstrated he can handle challenges with grace, dignity and deflect with humor," she said.
But Constant said the soaking threatened more than Charles' carefully tailored suit.
King Charles III was in a stormy mood during the rainfall. (Getty Images)

"There's a lot of consideration as to what his legacy will look like," she said. "He certainly doesn't want images of him looking like a drowned rat in the archives, especially when there are large discussions happening about the future of the Commonwealth. Image is everything. This situation should never have happened."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
King Charles III is seen here with the umbrella that he was waiting for. (Getty Images)
Fordwich said the mishap became known as "Brolly-gate" in the U.K. "Brolly" is a common informal term for an umbrella.
"Queen Elizabeth II maintained a firmer distinction between her private reactions and her public responsibilities," Fordwich said, referring to the king's late mother.
Queen Camilla shelters from the rain under an umbrella. (Getty Images)

"She was from the generation which placed emphasis on public reserve. The immediacy of modern social media means unexpected incidents like this rocket around the world in minutes. The king is more visibly expressive, at times impatient, occasionally humorous and way more willing to let audiences see his immediate reactions than his mother."
Queen Elizabeth II attends a ceremony to mark her official birthday at Windsor Castle on June 13, 2020, in Windsor, England. (Toby Melville - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
Christopher Andersen, author of "The King," previously told Fox News Digital that sources had described Charles as having a short fuse in his younger years.

"He's very moody, very temperamental," Andersen said. "He has a volcanic temper. Camilla has always been a calming influence, and since he became king, Charles has mellowed considerably. That doesn't mean he's lost his edge entirely, by any means. When he is displeased by something, he lets his staff know it in no uncertain terms. They feel the royal heat."
King Charles III signs the visitors' book as Queen Camilla watches at Hillsborough Castle in Belfast on Sept. 13, 2022, during his visit to Northern Ireland. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson previously told Fox News Digital they don’t comment on books.

Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"The King: The Life of Charles III" by Christopher Andersen is out now. (Gallery Books)

Following his mother's death in September 2022, Charles appeared frustrated with a leaking pen during a visit to Northern Ireland. He told an aide, "I can't bear this bloody thing! Every stinking time." A pen was quickly handed to Camilla to complete the signing during the royal ceremony.
Fordwich said the king's reaction to the downpour contrasted with the late queen's reputation for maintaining her public composure. Constant agreed.
Queen Elizabeth II watches from the balcony of Buckingham Palace during the Trooping the Colour parade in London on June 2, 2022. (Jonathan Brady/WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"Queen Elizabeth was much better at embodying the 'keep calm, carry on' tradition, especially in public," she said. "That was never going to be Charles. These moments stand out because they are in such stark contrast to Queen Elizabeth. King Charles is very aware that he is viewed as a transitional monarch, and he wants to leave his mark."
King Charles is seen here with his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, before her death in 2022 at age 96. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
Royal experts agreed Charles has been navigating mounting pressure, as the Caribbean tour unfolded amid renewed calls from regional leaders for the U.K. to address slavery reparations.

On Nov. 3, the king called the transatlantic slave trade a "shameful chapter of history" during a speech at the official opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda. While Charles said it "still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth," he did not apologize, The Associated Press reported.

King Charles III greets locals holding national flags during a visit to Nelson's Dockyard, a historic naval base established in 1725, in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, on Nov. 2, 2026. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

According to The Associated Press, Charles said he was seeking ways to address past wrongs by improving access to education, investing in jobs, encouraging intra-Commonwealth trade and promoting climate resilience.

"We are so used to perfection that the media salivates over leaky pens," royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital about the umbrella mishap.

Britain's King Charles III reacts after joking while delivering a speech at an official dinner and reception during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Soldier's Bay near St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"The thunderstorm, of course, should have been anticipated," he said. "And given that King Charles is fighting cancer, no wonder he needed an umbrella. Queen Camilla realized her umbrella was not large enough to cover the king as well and duly behaved with dignity. Afterward, they both laughed about it, which is very British. Neither would have thought it funny at the time and small wonder. It’s unlikely to be repeated."
The soggy snafu drew international headlines, but Charles refused to let it rain on his parade.
King Charles III and Queen Camilla prepare to depart from VC Bird International Airport in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, on Nov. 4, 2026. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
During a dinner he and Camilla hosted for Commonwealth leaders, Charles joked about the varied climates across the organization's 56 member countries.

"It is one of the few organizations able to unite countries famous for snow, countries famous for deserts, and, most of all, countries whose citizens are utterly convinced they enjoy perfect weather all year round," he said, according to People magazine.

King Charles III and Antigua and Barbuda's Prime Minister Gaston Browne attend an official dinner and reception during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Soldier's Bay near St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"Although perhaps part of my role as Head of the Commonwealth is to provide an umbrella for you all!" he added with a smile.

"Sometimes that requires not talking about it and just moving on through," he said. "And sometimes it requires sitting down and talking about it a little bit, saying, 'Hey, we need to check in a little bit and see where we're at now that everything's changing.'"
He went on to say that "points of change in a marriage" can come "regularly throughout a long marriage," and these can often be "the most dangerous parts, I think, for a marriage."

title: Bridget Fonda spotted in rare LA outing 24 years after her final on-screen appearance
summary: Bridget Fonda was spotted out in Los Angeles 24 years after her last on-screen role, having previously told paparazzi she has no plans to return to acting.
story: The former actress was photographed Nov. 2, while out to lunch in Los Angeles.
Bridget Fonda stepped out for a rare public outing in Los Angeles, 24 years after she last appeared on-screen.
The 62-year-old actress was photographed while out to lunch on Monday, Nov. 2, keeping it casual in black sweatpants and a white tank top, paired with a yellow collared button-up shirt.
She accessorized the look with a black crossbody bag and sunglasses, and styled her hair in a ponytail.

As the granddaughter of Academy Award-winning actor, Henry Fonda, known for his roles in "The Grapes of Wrath," "12 Angry Men" and "On Golden Pond," Bridget made her film debut when she was five years old, appearing alongside her father, Peter Fonda, in the 1969 movie, "Easy Rider."
Bridget Fonda was photographed while out having lunch with a friend in Los Angeles. (The Image Direct)
'80S ICON KRISTY MCNICHOL MAKES RARE APPEARANCE 25 YEARS AFTER LEAVING HOLLYWOOD

She had her breakthrough in 1989, when she starred in the film, "Scandal," and continued to prove herself in films such as "Single White Female," "Point of No Return," "It Could Happen to You" and "Jackie Brown."

Although she found big success as an actress, she slowed down in the late 1990s and into the 2000s. Her final movie role was in the 2001 TV movie, "After Amy," and her final time on-screen was in two episodes of the miniseries "Snow Queen," in 2002.
Bridget's final on-screen role was in two episodes of "Snow Queen" in 2002. (KMazur/WireImage)
According to the Daily Mail, she told paparazzi in April 2023 that she had no plans to return to acting, noting, "It’s too nice being a civilian."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

In addition to her grandfather and her father, Bridget also grew up with Academy Award-winning actress, Jane Fonda, who is her aunt. She explained that coming from an acting family, it was hard not to be compared to one another.
Bridget told The Guardian that the media often put her and her aunt against one another. (Ben Rose/WireImage)

title: Dustin Hoffman had a 'terrible experience' making Hollywood classic 'The Graduate'
summary: Dustin Hoffman reveals in a new essay that he felt "unworthy" and feared being fired every day while filming "The Graduate" with Mike Nichols.
story: The actor shared he didn't feel he was right for the part and felt tension with the film's director, Mike Nichols.
Dustin Hoffman is opening up about the "terrible experience" he had while filming "The Graduate," a film he said "exacerbated all my insecurities from the start."

In a recent essay written for The New Yorker, the 89-year-old actor reflected on his experience making the film, which earned him his first Academy Award nomination and a BAFTA Award win, noting he "felt immediately uncomfortable" and "unworthy" on set.

"Here I was, playing a starring role in a movie by Mike Nichols, who was the director of the moment, but I felt like I had no right to be there," he wrote. "It was a terrible experience making the movie that changed my life."

He went on to explain that a lot of his time on set was spent wondering if director, Nichols, "was angry at me," because he was either "doing something wrong" or had finally noticed what Hoffman and "everybody else already knew, that he had miscast the lead in his film."
Hoffman called working on "The Graduate" a "terrible experience." (Getty Images)
JOHN GOODMAN ADMITS HE FELT 'FRIGHTENED' AFTER THE SUDDEN FAME HE EXPERIENCED FROM 'ROSEANNE'

The "Rain Man" star felt he was wrong for the part from the start, admitting he "didn't even want to try out for the part," saying he thought "it was obvious" to him after reading the novel the film is based on "that I was all wrong for Benjamin."

"A track star and straight-A student, the head of the debate team—this was an affluent, all-American kid, whose surname was ‘Braddock,’" he said. "Why would you cast a person who looks as ethnic as I do to play the ultimate Wasp? It made absolutely no sense."
Hoffman recalled feeling like he was wrong for the part from the beginning. (Screen Archives/Getty Images)
Part of what made the experience so bad for Hoffman was his relationship with the director, who he said was "irritable with everyone," and was "frequently sour" on set.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

The director's attitude often led to Hoffman feel "that I was about to be fired," as the actor found himself "thinking, I have no f- - -ing idea what I'm doing," while filming some of the most well-known scenes in the movie.
Hoffman recalled the director's "frequently sour" mood while on set. (Michael Loccisano/Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Hoffman also recalled feeling as if the director had a "certain sadism" that was directed mostly towards him.

"There was a scene in which Katharine Ross had to slap me, and he made us do twenty-seven takes. The scene has Benjamin run into Elaine’s room, soaking wet from the rain, to tell her that he’s had an affair with an older woman; within seconds, Elaine realizes the woman is her mother," he said. "Mike just kept telling Katharine to hit me, to hit me harder. Katharine worried she would hurt me, and I told her, ‘I’m O.K. Just don’t hit my ear.’ Unfortunately, she missed a few times. I was dizzy by the end of that day, and Mike didn’t even use the slap in the film."
Hoffman was slapped by his costar 27 times for a scene that ended up being cut. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
The next day, Hoffman was scheduled to film a scene underwater, which left him with "blood trickling out of my ear," which later turned out to be a punctured eardrum.

"The Graduate" went on to become one of Hoffman's most well-known films. The movie follows Hoffman's character, Benjamin, a recent college graduate who is struggling to find direction post graduation and is seduced by an older housewife and friend of his parents.

title: 'Blue Lagoon' star Christopher Atkins wanted to be a dad more than 'a drunk' as he nears 40 years sober

story: Christopher Atkins told Fox News Digital at the Chiller Theatre Expo why becoming a dad motivated him to get sober nearly 40 years ago and how his grandchildren keep him committed today.
Christopher Atkins says becoming a father gave him a reason to walk away from alcohol, and nearly four decades later, his grandchildren are giving him another reason to stay sober.

The former Hollywood heartthrob, who rose to fame opposite Brooke Shields in 1980's "The Blue Lagoon," opened up about the turning point that changed his life during an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital at the Chiller Theatre Expo in New Jersey.
"I guess the turning point for me was having children, so I wanted to be a dad more than I wanted to be a drunk," Atkins said.

The actor shares two adult children, Grant and Brittney, with his former wife, Lyn Barron Weber, whom he married in 1985. The couple divorced in 2007.
Atkins previously spoke about how his drinking affected his Hollywood career, including an opportunity to star in the 1984 film "Footloose."

During an appearance at Fanboy Expo Knoxville earlier this year, the actor said he had been considered for the lead role that ultimately went to Kevin Bacon but was drinking heavily when he met with filmmakers.

title: Macklemore claims Free Palestine tour blocked from 9 major US arenas
summary: Macklemore claims Madison Square Garden and the Kia Forum are among nine major U.S. venues that denied his Free Palestine tour benefit shows.

Macklemore is claiming that Madison Square Garden and the Kia Forum are among venues who refused to host his Free Palestine tour.

On Friday, Macklemore, whose legal name is Ben Haggerty, uploaded a lengthy statement to Instagram, claiming it has been difficult for him to bring his Free Palestine tour to the United States. He claimed nine major venues across the U.S. turned him down.

Madison Square Garden, Prudential Center, Barclays Center, UBS Arena, Intuit Dome, Kia Forum, Crypto.com Arena, Chase Center and Climate Pledge Arena were among the venues that said no, according to Macklemore.
He emphasized that their decision came "once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine."

Macklemore shared a lengthy statement on social media about the status of his Free Palestine tour. (Kristy Sparow/Getty Images)

Macklemore explained that activists, poets, entertainers and artists who stood in solidarity with Palestinians have been experiencing this treatment for "decades."

Macklemore said U.S. venues are denying him access for his Free Palestine tour. (Zoe Rain/Reuters)

Macklemore has a long history of using his public platform to amplify activism. (Arnaud Finistre)

"Look at what just happened in Europe. Three sold-out arenas. Tens of thousands of people from different backgrounds, religions and walks of life standing together. More than forty artists and speakers putting their names and platforms behind Palestinian liberation. For all the attempts to paint this movement as one rooted in hatred, what filled those rooms was love," he wrote.

title: Defense attorney in Tupac Shakur murder trial found dead at 55: report
summary: Michael Sanft, the Las Vegas attorney who defended Duane Davis in the Tupac Shakur murder trial, was reportedly found dead days after filing an appeal in the case.
story: Jurors on Monday reached a verdict in the trial of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, who was charged in Tupac Shakur’s 1996 killing.

Michael Sanft, the Las Vegas defense attorney who represented Duane "Keffe D" Davis in the Tupac Shakur murder case, was found dead inside his home Friday morning, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal.
He was 55.
The cause and manner of Sanft's death has not yet been determined. Police told the Las Vegas outlet the death did not appear suspicious.
Michael Sloan, a close friend who rode motorcycles with Sanft, according to the report, confirmed his death and remembered the attorney as a devoted friend.
DUANE 'KEFFE D' DAVIS FOUND GUILTY OF FIRST-DEGREE MURDER IN 1996 KILLING OF TUPAC SHAKUR

Michael Sanft, the defense attorney who represented Duane "Keffe D" Davis in the Tupac Shakur murder trial, has reportedly died at age 55, days after filing an appeal challenging his client's conviction. (David Becker/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"He was one of my best friends and one of the best human beings I knew," Sloan shared.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Clark County Coroner's Office and the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department for comment.
Tupac Shakur was shot in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas Sept. 7, 1996, and died six days later at age 25. (Raymond Boyd/Getty Images)
TUPAC SHAKUR MURDER TRIAL'S FIRST WEEK SEES HEATED TESTIMONY FROM RELUCTANT WITNESSES WITH OLD GANGLAND TIES
Sanft's death comes after a courtroom battle that ended with Davis, 63, becoming the first person convicted in Shakur's 1996 murder.
Duane "Keffe D" Davis was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1996 killing of rapper Tupac Shakur and sentenced to 40 years to life in prison. (John Locher/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
A Nevada jury found Davis guilty of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon in August. He was sentenced Oct. 13 to 40 years to life behind bars, according to The Associated Press.
The verdict marked a significant development in a case that has drawn international attention for nearly three decades.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Shakur was riding in a BMW with Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight near the Las Vegas Strip Sept. 7, 1996, when a gunman in a white Cadillac opened fire.
Knight survived with minor injuries. Shakur, one of hip-hop's biggest stars at the time, died six days later at age 25.
Defense attorney Michael Sanft cross-examines James McDonald during the murder trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis related to the 1996 killing of rapper Tupac Shakur. (John Locher/Pool via Reuters)
Prosecutors argued Davis orchestrated the killing after his nephew was involved in a fight with Shakur and Knight earlier that night.

During closing arguments, prosecutor Binu Palal told jurors Davis obtained a gun and "went hunting" for the two men. Prosecutors also pointed to Davis' own statements placing himself inside the Cadillac used in the shooting.
Sanft disputed the prosecution's case, telling jurors there was no evidence beyond Davis' statements placing his client in Las Vegas or inside the Cadillac.
Jurors deliberated for about three hours before finding Davis guilty.

A 1996 photo of rapper Tupac Shakur, left, and Marion "Suge" Knight is displayed during the Duane Davis murder trial, related to the 1996 killing of the rapper. (Steve Marcus/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
The decision prompted an emotional scene in court, with Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa "Set" Shakur, crying as the verdict was read. Davis' son covered his face with one hand.
The jury consisted of 12 jurors and four alternates. The panel heard testimony over nine days from 24 prosecution witnesses and three defense witnesses.
