title: iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8: Is $2,000 worth it?
summary: Apple's iPhone Duo reportedly outlasted the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 by over three hours in battery tests, but its weight and repair costs raise concerns.
story: Apple's newly unveiled foldable iPhone Duo sparks significant consumer interest despite a hefty $1,999 starting price tag. On 'Varney & Co.', Taylor Riggs explains the premium device's unique dual-screen capability and ultra-thin design. Host Stuart Varney admits he plans to purchase the high-end smartphone, which can cost up to $3,000 for the two-terabyte storage model.

How much would you pay for a phone that turns into a small tablet? Apple is betting the answer is nearly $2,000. After seven years of watching Samsung build folding phones, Apple has finally entered the race with its first-ever foldable iPhone.

The new iPhone Duo, which went on sale Oct. 23, opens like a book to reveal a 7.6-inch screen. Its biggest competitor, Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, offers the same screen size and a remarkably similar design. However, Samsung's phone is lighter and costs about $100 less.

Apple has some interesting advantages of its own, including impressive battery performance and a clever screen designed to reduce glare. But there are compromises on both sides, including a repair bill that might make you think twice about carrying either phone without protection. So, has Apple finally cracked the folding phone formula, or does Samsung still have the better idea?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT
Apple's first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, takes on Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 with longer battery life, a glare-reducing display and a higher price tag. (Annice Lyn/Getty Images)
Apple enters the foldable phone race seven years late

Samsung introduced the original Galaxy Fold in 2019. Those early devices came with plenty of growing pains, including concerns about screen durability. Since then, Samsung has steadily improved its folding technology.

Apple took its time. In fact, we covered one of the company's early ideas in our article about Apple's foldable iPhone patent in 2023. Now the iPhone Duo is finally here, and Apple has made some interesting design decisions. The phone features a polished titanium frame, Apple's A20 Pro processor and a large inner OLED display. It also introduces a redesigned version of iOS built around the folding experience.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 takes a different approach. It uses Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and Samsung's One UI 9 software, which has evolved through several generations of folding phones. That experience gives Samsung an advantage in some areas. However, Apple has already managed to outperform its rival in early battery testing.
iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8 price: Prepare for sticker shock

Let's get the painful part out of the way. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage. The 512GB model costs $2,199, while the 1TB version jumps to $2,599. If you really want to splurge, Apple's 2TB model costs an eye-watering $3,199.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899.99 for 256GB. The 512GB version costs $2,099.99, while the 1TB model reaches $2,499.99. That puts Samsung roughly $100 below Apple at comparable storage levels. Of course, Samsung has another advantage. Its Fold 8 has been on sale since August, so retailers and carriers have had time to introduce promotions.

However, I'd look closely at those deals before celebrating the savings. Some carrier offers require a qualifying trade-in or a lengthy commitment to monthly bill credits. There's also a larger question. When you're already spending nearly $2,000, will saving $100 really determine which phone you choose? I suspect the answer comes down to what happens when you actually hold them.
Apple's folding iPhone has a weight problem

One of the first things you'll notice about these phones is how similar they look. Both fold horizontally like a book, with smaller screens on the outside and expansive displays when opened. But there's a noticeable difference in weight. The iPhone Duo weighs 8.96 ounces, compared with 7.09 ounces for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's almost two ounces heavier for Apple's phone.

If you've ever carried a heavy smartphone in your pocket all day, you know how noticeable that can become. The difference could be even more apparent when you're holding the phone open for extended periods. Samsung also wins on thickness. Its Fold 8 measures about 0.38 inches thick when closed, while the Duo measures 0.44 inches. Apple counters with a rounded titanium design that may feel more comfortable in your hand. Samsung uses sharper edges and a flatter appearance.

There's also something worth thinking about. Both phones have relatively small outer screens. Apple's measures 5.4 inches, while Samsung's comes in at 5.5 inches. Those screens are perfectly usable for everyday tasks. However, they're considerably smaller than the displays on many conventional flagship phones. You could end up spending $2,000 on a device that requires an extra step whenever you want a bigger screen. That's why I'd recommend trying both in person before buying. The phone that feels exciting for five minutes in a store needs to feel comfortable after five hours in your hand.
The iPhone Duo display has a clever trick

Both folding phones open to reveal 7.6-inch OLED screens with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. Each also offers peak outdoor brightness of 3,000 nits. The real difference comes down to how those displays handle reflections.

Apple developed a nano-texture finish for the Duo's inner screen. It creates a matte appearance that helps reduce glare and makes the fold crease harder to see. Anyone who has struggled to read a glossy screen near a sunny window might appreciate this approach.

Samsung's screen has a more traditional glossy finish, which can make colors appear richer. Some early iPhone Duo reviews suggest Apple's matte display sacrifices a little contrast and vibrancy to achieve its reduced reflections. Neither approach will appeal to everyone. However, Apple has another interesting feature coming.
Apple Pencil support could give the Duo an edge

The iPhone Duo now supports the Apple Pencil (USB-C) through iOS 27.2, which Apple released on Oct. 26. That means you can sketch or annotate documents directly on the folding screen. The feature already works in the software's release candidate.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 does not support the S Pen. Samsung removed the feature as it pursued thinner folding designs. There is one catch with Apple's approach. The Duo works only with the USB-C Apple Pencil. Even if you already own an Apple Pencil Pro, you won't be able to use it with this phone.

The USB-C version also lacks the pressure sensitivity available on more advanced Apple Pencil models. Still, this could be useful for someone who regularly signs documents or prefers handwritten notes.
Samsung still understands multitasking better

Here's where those seven years of Samsung experience become apparent. Let's say you're on a video call and someone sends you an important document. You want to review it without interrupting the conversation. Then you need to check your calendar. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 can handle several apps on its larger screen. You can run three apps in split-screen mode, and Samsung also offers pop-up windows for additional flexibility. The Fold 8 supports Samsung DeX, too, giving you a desktop-style experience when connected to compatible external displays.

Apple has introduced Split View on the Duo, allowing two apps to run side by side. That's a first for the iPhone, and it should make the larger screen far more useful. However, Apple's approach remains more restrictive than Samsung's. Split View uses a fixed arrangement, and you don't get the same floating-window flexibility. There's another issue that early iPhone Duo owners are discovering.
Some iPhone apps aren't ready for the bigger screen

Apple redesigned iOS 27 for the Duo, which ships with iOS 27.1. Its own apps have been adapted to use the folding display. However, some third-party apps haven't caught up. Early reviewers found that certain apps display large black bars or awkward layouts when opened on the bigger screen. That could be frustrating when you've paid so much for additional screen space.

Fortunately, developers can update their apps to support the Duo's design. Some popular apps have already received updates, and more are expected. For now, though, Samsung has a more established folding software experience. I would also pay attention to which apps you use most. A larger screen loses some of its appeal when your favorite apps still behave as though they're running on a much smaller phone.
Apple's battery life delivers a welcome surprise

Folding phones have a difficult job. They need enough battery power to run a large display without becoming too bulky. Apple's iPhone Duo uses two internal batteries and an A20 Pro processor designed for efficient performance. Samsung equips its Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a 4,800mAh battery and Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip.

Both processors offer plenty of power for demanding apps. However, early independent testing suggests Apple has a surprising advantage when it comes to battery life. In one battery test involving continuous web browsing over 5G, the iPhone Duo reportedly lasted 13 hours and 20 minutes, compared with 10 hours and 6 minutes for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's more than three additional hours for Apple.

Another independent test produced encouraging results for the Duo. While streaming video over Wi-Fi with the larger screens at maximum brightness, Apple's foldable reportedly lasted 18 hours and 15 minutes, compared with 16 hours and 30 minutes for Samsung. Although the tests used different methods, both suggest Apple has managed to squeeze impressive battery life out of its first folding phone.

Apple officially claims up to 31 hours of video playback using the inner display. However, that figure comes from controlled laboratory testing, so everyday results will vary depending on how you use the phone.

Charging is another consideration. Apple says the Duo can reach 50% in about 20 minutes with a compatible wired charger. Samsung supports 45W wired charging and fast wireless charging. For anyone who spends long days traveling or regularly finds their battery running low before dinner, Apple's early results are encouraging.
THE IPHONE DUO IS OFFICIALLY HERE — GET IT FOR NO MONEY DOWN AT T-MOBILE
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, roughly $100 more than Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, as Apple enters the foldable smartphone market. (Jung Yeon-je/AFP via Getty Images)
A $2,000 folding phone still comes with camera compromises

For nearly $2,000, you'd expect a phone with an incredible camera. And while both of these foldables take excellent photos, there's a catch. Apple's iPhone Duo has two 48MP rear cameras, while Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 has two 50MP cameras. Neither has a dedicated telephoto lens, which means you're giving up some of the zoom capabilities found on other premium phones.

Think about trying to get a close-up shot of your child playing soccer or capturing something interesting in the distance while on vacation. Apple's Duo offers 2x optical-quality zoom by cropping into its main sensor. Samsung uses a similar approach, with digital zoom for subjects farther away. Both can handle everyday photos, but if you love getting those close-up shots, an iPhone 18 Pro Max or Galaxy S26 Ultra may be a better choice.

Here's where Samsung throws another option into the mix. Its Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.99, just $100 more than Apple's Duo at their regular starting prices. For that extra money, you get a 200MP main camera and a dedicated telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom. That's worth considering if you want a folding phone but aren't willing to give up a more versatile camera. And with Samsung already offering discounts on some models, you may not even have to spend more.
Apple has some fun camera features Samsung can't match exactly

Ever try taking a group photo and realize you're the one missing from it? Apple's Smart Take could help with that. Just prop open the iPhone Duo, get into the picture and let its AI recognize when everyone is posing. The phone automatically snaps the photo, so there's no racing against a timer or asking someone else to take the shot.

Then there's Duo Preview, which lets the person you're photographing see themselves on the outside screen. That could save you from hearing, "Wait, let me see that one," after every picture. Apple also came up with Kid Cue, which plays Peanuts animations on the outer display to get children to look toward the camera. If you've ever tried getting a toddler to cooperate for a family photo, you can probably appreciate that one.

Samsung has a few tricks of its own. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 can show people a preview on its outer screen, and you can prop it partially open for hands-free photos. That comes in handy when you want to be in the picture instead of always being the one taking it.
The most expensive iPhone Duo surprise could come after you buy it

Now let's talk about something that deserves far more attention than it usually receives. Repairs. Apple rates the iPhone Duo IP68 for dust and water resistance, while Samsung gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 an IP48 rating. That gives Apple stronger protection against dust under standardized laboratory testing. However, neither rating guarantees that a folding screen or hinge will survive years of rough treatment. These phones also contain more moving parts than conventional smartphones. And if something goes wrong, the repair costs can be substantial.

There's another reason to think carefully about durability. As we reported in our article, Apple confirms iPhone Duo screen problems after launch. Some owners experienced cracks along the inner screen near the hinge within hours or days of purchase, sometimes during initial setup. Apple acknowledged an issue affecting a small number of devices and directed affected customers to contact AppleCare for replacements. The company hasn't identified the cause or disclosed how many phones are affected. An AppleCare+ subscription isn't required to request a replacement for this acknowledged issue. Still, it's something I'd consider before spending nearly $2,000 on a first-generation folding iPhone.

According to Apple's published repair estimates, replacing the iPhone Duo's damaged inner display costs $999 without AppleCare+. That's roughly half the cost of the entry-level phone. Apple also lists an estimated $1,499 charge for certain other damage repairs. There is some relief for minor screen damage. Apple's replaceable inner display cover layer costs $49 to replace without AppleCare+, provided the damage is limited to that layer. AppleCare+ can significantly reduce eligible repair charges. For example, an inner display repair is listed at $99 under the coverage, subject to the plan's terms. Of course, the coverage itself adds to the cost of ownership.

Samsung's folding phones also have specialized displays and hinges that can be expensive to repair. However, repair pricing varies by model, damage and coverage. This is one area where I'd encourage anyone considering either phone to look beyond the advertised purchase price. After all, a $2,000 phone is expensive enough without worrying about what happens if it slips out of your hand and you're suddenly facing a repair bill approaching $1,000.
Another iPhone Duo change could surprise travelers

Apple has made the iPhone Duo eSIM-only worldwide. That means you won't find a physical SIM card slot. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 supports both eSIM and a physical nano-SIM card, although configurations may vary by market.

For most people in the United States, this probably won't be an obstacle. Major carriers support eSIM, and many international providers offer digital plans. However, if you travel frequently and prefer buying physical SIM cards at your destination, Samsung gives you more flexibility. It's worth checking whether your preferred mobile provider supports eSIM before buying the Duo.
iPhone Duo or Galaxy Z Fold 8: Which should you buy?

If you've been waiting years for a folding iPhone, Apple's Duo is an appealing first attempt. It offers excellent early battery performance, an impressive display and the convenience of staying within Apple's ecosystem. However, I wouldn't overlook Samsung. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is significantly lighter, costs a little less and offers more flexible multitasking. Those advantages could become increasingly important once the excitement of owning a new folding phone wears off.

And here's something else to consider. If most of your day involves texting or checking email, you may spend far more time using the smaller outer screen than you expect. The larger display becomes especially useful when you frequently review documents or watch videos while traveling.

Before buying either phone, think about how much time you would realistically spend with it unfolded. Also, if you're considering switching between Apple and Samsung, take a look at our guide on how to transfer data to a new iPhone or Android at CyberGuy.com. It can help make the move considerably easier.
HERE ARE SOME TIPS ON HOW TO ORGANIZE PHOTOS WITH KEYWORDS ON YOUR PHONE

Apple's iPhone Duo and Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 feature 7.6-inch folding displays, but differences in weight, battery life and multitasking could influence buyers. (Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to give Samsung credit. Seven years ago, folding phones seemed like an expensive experiment, and I wasn't convinced they'd ever catch on. But Samsung stuck with the idea, and now Apple has finally joined the party. I like what Apple's done with the iPhone Duo, especially the display and those impressive early battery results. Still, I keep coming back to the price. Nearly $2,000 for a phone that's heavier than Samsung's and doesn't have a dedicated telephoto camera? That's a tough sell. And the possibility of a $999 inner screen repair would certainly make me nervous.

I also wouldn't count Samsung out just because Apple has entered the race. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is noticeably lighter, and Samsung has spent years figuring out how to make that larger screen useful. Being able to run more apps at once is a nice advantage, especially if you're someone who likes getting work done on your phone. And let's face it, a lighter phone is something you'll appreciate long after the excitement of showing everyone how it folds has worn off.

If I were spending this kind of money, I'd want to see how Apple's first folding iPhone holds up after a few months of everyday use. I'd also want to hold both phones before deciding. But here's what I keep wondering. How often would I really open that larger screen? If I ended up using the smaller outside display most of the day, I'd have a hard time convincing myself that spending $2,000 was worth it.
Would you really spend $2,000 on a folding phone, or do you think Apple and Samsung are charging us more to solve a problem we never had? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Florida police unveil $148K flying patrol vehicle
summary: Florida Polytechnic University's Jetson ONE eVTOL police vehicle named Astro still awaits FAA authorization before officers can fly operational patrols.
story: Florida Polytechnic University's Astro flying patrol vehicle takes to the skies above campus as police explore how electric aircraft could support emergency response. (Florida Polytechnic University)

You may be used to seeing police cars cruising through your neighborhood or helicopters flying overhead. But what if an officer could respond to an emergency in a small electric aircraft that looks like a giant drone? That idea is getting closer to reality in Florida. The Florida Polytechnic University Police Department in Lakeland has introduced a flying patrol vehicle that the university has nicknamed Astro. Jetson, the company behind the Jetson ONE personal flying machine, built the single-seat aircraft.

According to the university, it's the first U.S. law enforcement agency to add this type of piloted electric aircraft to its fleet. Jetson calls it a world first. However, Astro still needs FAA authorization before officers can use it for operational police patrols. Here's how Astro works and why police believe this unusual aircraft could change the way they respond to emergencies.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

FLYING SPORTS CAR HIDES ITS WINGS AS PRODUCTION GETS CLOSER
Astro is Florida's new flying patrol vehicle

Astro gets its name from the dog in the classic cartoon The Jetsons. The aircraft even looks like something George Jetson might have parked outside his house. Astro uses electric vertical takeoff and landing technology, commonly called eVTOL. As a result, it can lift straight into the air without needing a runway. Unlike a conventional police helicopter, Astro has a compact frame that folds for easier transport and storage. The aircraft features an open cockpit surrounded by a lightweight frame.

Eight electric motors power its eight propellers. Meanwhile, a four-axis joystick allows the pilot to control its movement. Florida Polytechnic University selected the Jetson ONE to explore its potential for law enforcement. The aircraft arrived during summer 2026. Since then, police personnel have completed flight training, according to Jetson. That includes Police Chief Aaron Murray. Jetson also identifies the aircraft by its registration number, N911FP. The number references emergency services and Florida Polytechnic University. Jetson tells CyberGuy that Astro is a standard Jetson ONE with police lights added. Officers use a handheld radio, and the aircraft has mounts for action cameras. The company says a pilot-controlled searchlight could be added in the future.
How fast can the flying police vehicle go?

Astro may look compact, but its advertised performance is impressive. According to Jetson's published specifications, the aircraft can reach speeds of 63 mph. That's fast enough to cover short distances across a large campus without following roads or dealing with traffic. However, battery life limits how long it can stay airborne. Jetson estimates approximately 20 minutes of flight time per charge, making Astro better suited to short missions than extended patrols. Jetson tells CyberGuy that the aircraft takes approximately 90 minutes to recharge using a 240-volt connection. Charging through a standard household outlet takes about three hours. However, officers can swap batteries between flights. This allows them to return to the air sooner if fully charged replacements are available. Each flight still lasts approximately 20 minutes.

Jetson confirms that the 210-pound maximum includes the pilot, police gear and any emergency supplies. The company says this is a hard limit, which could restrict how much equipment an officer can carry. Jetson also advertises several safety features. The company says Astro can continue flying even if one motor fails. It also has an automatic landing system and a ballistic parachute designed for emergencies. Jetson lists the vehicle at $148,000 before taxes and additional fees, making it a significant investment for a police department.
How police could use Astro during emergencies

Florida Polytechnic University wants to explore whether Astro can help officers respond when roads become difficult to navigate. Consider what happens after a major Florida storm. Roads may flood, debris can block access and emergency crews may struggle to reach certain locations. Once weather and flying conditions allow, a small aircraft that takes off vertically could help officers survey the damage.

Police Chief Aaron Murray believes Astro could help officers monitor the campus and reach places that traditional vehicles cannot easily access. The department also wants to investigate using it to deliver emergency supplies. "Advanced air mobility is a technology on the rise, and we can either choose to be proactive or reactive as it develops," Murray said.

The university also plans to collaborate with regional law enforcement agencies on potential emergency-response missions. However, Astro carries only its pilot. It cannot transport an injured person or bring someone back from a rescue mission. Because the 210-pound limit includes the officer and everything onboard, the amount of emergency supplies Astro can carry depends on the pilot's weight and equipment.
PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE
The single-seat Jetson ONE aircraft can reach speeds of 63 mph and stay airborne for approximately 20 minutes per charge. (Florida Polytechnic University)
The FAA hurdle facing Florida's flying police vehicle

There's an important regulatory issue before Astro can become a regular part of police operations. Jetson developed the ONE as a recreational aircraft designed around the FAA's Part 103 ultralight rules. Those rules allow qualifying ultralight vehicles to operate without traditional aircraft or pilot certification. However, Part 103 limits their use to recreational or sporting purposes. Police patrols fall outside those permitted uses. FAA guidance specifically identifies aerial surveying and patrolling as activities that cannot operate under Part 103.

Jetson says Florida Polytechnic University needs additional federal authorization involving FAA Part 91 rules to use Astro for public-safety missions. When the university announced the aircraft in mid-October, it said the approval process was in its final stages. At that time, officials expected approval in November or December. The university has not publicly confirmed when regular operational police patrols will begin.
Students will help develop the flying police aircraft's future

Astro has another role beyond its potential police duties. It will serve as a hands-on research platform for Florida Polytechnic University students. The university launched an aerospace engineering degree program in fall 2026. As a result, students will have an opportunity to study electric aircraft technology while learning about the challenges of operating it.

Faculty members and students plan to use Astro's flight data for research and senior engineering projects. Reports also indicate that the university is exploring virtual training simulations for police officers. This could provide useful information about how small electric aircraft perform during specialized missions. It may also help future engineers identify limitations that need attention before wider adoption.

Florida is also expanding its involvement in advanced air mobility. The nearby SunTrax transportation testing facility in Auburndale has a dedicated aerial test track for emerging aircraft technology. Testing under Florida's participation in a federal advanced air mobility pilot program is expected to begin by the end of 2026. That statewide testing effort is separate from Astro's pending authorization for police operations.
Could more police departments start using flying vehicles?

Astro raises an interesting possibility for law enforcement agencies looking for alternatives to traditional helicopters. Police helicopters require significant resources to purchase and maintain. A smaller electric aircraft could eventually offer another option for certain missions, especially when an officer needs a quick view of an area from above.

However, Jetson's aircraft also has substantial limitations. Its short flight duration means officers would need to plan missions carefully. Swappable batteries could support repeated flights, but officers would still need to land between missions to replace them. Weather conditions and airspace restrictions could further affect operations. There's also the question of whether a single-seat piloted aircraft provides enough benefits compared with a drone, which can conduct aerial surveillance without putting an officer in the cockpit.

Even so, Jetson sees the police department's purchase as an important step toward expanding personal electric aircraft into professional use. The company says its entire 2026 and 2027 production is sold out. It is now accepting orders for 2028, with a listed price of $148,000. Jetson also expects Astro to appear at the public UP.Summit event at Kennedy Space Center in Florida on November 7 and 8.
A closer look at Astro reveals its compact design, open cockpit and police markings, with eight electric motors powering the $148,000 aircraft. (Florida Polytechnic University)
What this means to you

You probably won't see flying patrol vehicles operating above your neighborhood anytime soon. However, Astro offers an early look at how public-safety agencies might use small electric aircraft. After a major storm, an officer flying over blocked roads could potentially assess damage and help emergency crews understand where assistance is needed. The same technology might eventually support searches for missing people, although Astro's usefulness still needs to be demonstrated during actual police operations.

There's another side worth considering. As police departments explore aerial technology, questions about privacy will become increasingly important. People may want to know when officers can fly above their property and whether aircraft will collect or record information. Those questions deserve attention alongside the aircraft's potential benefits. For now, Florida Polytechnic University has an opportunity to study a new approach to emergency response while working toward the necessary federal authorization.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've been following Jetson's flying aircraft for several years, and seeing one enter a police department's fleet is an interesting development. When I first covered the Jetson ONE, the attraction was the idea of people being able to fly their own electric aircraft. Now we're seeing a possible use beyond recreation. I can understand why a police department would want this technology, especially in Florida, where storms can leave communities cut off from emergency services. But I'm also interested in what happens after the excitement wears off. Twenty minutes of flight time leaves little room for unexpected delays, and there's still the question of whether an officer flying overhead offers enough advantages over a drone to justify the expense. I'm encouraged that the university plans to study those questions before putting Astro into regular service. And I think communities should have a say in how police use these aircraft, particularly when it comes to privacy.

Would seeing police officers flying above your neighborhood make you feel safer, or would you worry about having another set of eyes watching from the sky? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: ChatGPT now lets you lock private chats with a PIN
summary: OpenAI's new locked chats feature lets you protect ChatGPT conversations with a PIN, Face ID or Touch ID, but there are key privacy limitations.
story: OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane addresses the investigation into an OpenAI hack on an Australian government Medicare portal. During an interview with Lawrence Jones, Lehane explains the context of the July security incident and shares findings from their ongoing review. He also reacts to a new Fox News poll showing 71 percent of Americans oppose local AI data centers.

Ever handed someone your phone or let them use your computer to show them something, then suddenly worried about what else they might see? Maybe you've been using ChatGPT to work through a personal issue or plan a surprise for someone. Your conversation history can reveal quite a bit.

Now, OpenAI is giving you a way to keep certain conversations out of sight. The company just introduced Locked Chats, a new feature that lets you protect individual ChatGPT conversations with a four-digit PIN. On supported devices, you can also use Face ID, Touch ID or your phone's unlock method.

That sounds reassuring, especially as more people turn to artificial intelligence for personal advice. However, there are a few privacy limitations worth understanding before you start locking everything down. Here's how the feature works and how to set it up.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay and downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
OpenAI's new Locked Chats feature adds another layer of privacy for people using ChatGPT to discuss personal or sensitive topics. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What are ChatGPT Locked Chats?

OpenAI's new Locked Chats feature allows you to protect selected conversations without deleting them. Once you lock a chat, it moves into a separate area under Projects > Locked chats. The conversation disappears from your regular chat history, pinned chats and standard search results. Its title and contents stay behind your PIN until you choose to open them. You can even continue the conversation later without moving it back into your regular history.

Think about how useful that could be if you share a computer with your spouse or occasionally let someone use your phone. Perhaps you're researching an anniversary surprise and don't want the details popping up in your sidebar. Now, you have a way to keep that conversation separate.

There's one important detail if you already use ChatGPT Projects. Locking a conversation removes it from its original project. As a result, the conversation loses access to that project's instructions, files and memory. Even if you unlock it later, the conversation returns to your regular history rather than its previous project.

The feature is rolling out gradually to ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users. It works on the web, in the iPhone and Android apps and in the new ChatGPT desktop apps for Mac and Windows. OpenAI says ChatGPT for Healthcare does not support Locked Chats.
How to lock a ChatGPT conversation with a PIN
You can lock an existing conversation in a few steps. The process is similar whether you're using ChatGPT on your computer, iPhone, Samsung Galaxy or Google Pixel.
Note: If you don't see Lock chat, the feature may not have reached your account yet. OpenAI is releasing it gradually. Some conversation types also cannot be locked.

Open ChatGPT and sign in to your account.Find the conversation you want to protect.Open the conversation's three-dot menu (•••).Select Lock chat.Select Lock chat again to confirm.If this is your first time, select Create a PIN.Enter a four-digit PIN.Enter the PIN again to confirm it.
Open ChatGPT and sign in to your account.
Find the conversation you want to protect.
Open the conversation's three-dot menu (•••).
Select Lock chat.
Select Lock chat again to confirm.
If this is your first time, select Create a PIN.
Enter a four-digit PIN.
Enter the PIN again to confirm it.
Your conversation will move into Locked chats. The PIN belongs to your OpenAI account, so you can use the same PIN across supported devices where you're signed in.
Note: If you don't see Lock chat, the feature may not have reached your account yet. OpenAI is releasing it gradually. Some conversation types also cannot be locked.
META AI LAUNCHES PRIVATE INCOGNITO CHAT
ChatGPT users can now select "Lock chat" from a conversation's menu to protect it with a four-digit PIN and hide it from regular chat history. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to use Face ID or Touch ID for ChatGPT Locked Chats

Typing a PIN every time you want to open a personal conversation can get tiresome. Fortunately, OpenAI supports biometric authentication on compatible iPhones and device authentication on supported Android phones.

Open the ChatGPT app.Open the sidebar and tap your profile icon to access Settings.Select Security and login.Tap Account PIN.Turn on Use Face ID or Use Touch ID, if available.Follow any prompts to enable authentication.
Open the ChatGPT app.
Open the sidebar and tap your profile icon to access Settings.
Select Security and login.
Tap Account PIN.
Turn on Use Face ID or Use Touch ID, if available.
Follow any prompts to enable authentication.
You can now use supported biometric authentication to access locked conversations on that iPhone. Your four-digit account PIN remains available as a backup.
Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel users follow the same steps inside the ChatGPT app. The available authentication method depends on your phone and its settings.

Open the ChatGPT app.Go to Projects.Select Locked chats.Enter your four-digit PIN when requested.Select Use device unlock when prompted, if available.Follow your phone's instructions to enable authentication.
Open the ChatGPT app.
Go to Projects.
Select Locked chats.
Enter your four-digit PIN when requested.
Select Use device unlock when prompted, if available.
Follow your phone's instructions to enable authentication.

Once enabled, you can use your supported device unlock method to access protected conversations. Depending on your phone, that may include fingerprint recognition or another available authentication method.
This setting applies only to the device where you enable it. Turning on device authentication on your Galaxy or Pixel does not automatically enable it on another phone.
How to open a locked ChatGPT conversation
Once you've protected a chat, you'll probably want to return to it. Fortunately, OpenAI keeps your locked conversations in one dedicated location.
Open ChatGPT.Go to Projects.Select Locked chats.Enter your four-digit PIN or use supported device authentication.Select the conversation you want to reopen.
Open ChatGPT.
Go to Projects.
Select Locked chats.
Enter your four-digit PIN or use supported device authentication.
Select the conversation you want to reopen.

You can continue chatting as you normally would. Opening the conversation temporarily gives you access without permanently removing its protection. You can also start a brand-new conversation directly inside Locked chats. After opening that area with your PIN, simply enter a new message. It will remain in the protected section. However, there's a limitation worth knowing. OpenAI doesn't allow you to archive, pin, move or share a conversation while it's locked. You'll need to permanently unlock it before using those options. Anyone who can open a locked conversation can also copy its contents.
Will ChatGPT lock your conversations again automatically?

Yes, although the timing depends on your device. On iPhone, Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel, OpenAI says access ends automatically after you've been away from a locked chat or the Locked chats area for one minute. The same one-minute rule applies when the app runs in the background.

On the web, refreshing the page or closing the tab ends access. The desktop and web versions also relock after you've been away from the authorized window. If you want to secure everything immediately, select Lock now.

There's another detail worth knowing. A conversation may remain visible in the browser tab immediately after you lock it. Similarly, another device that's already running ChatGPT might temporarily display an older conversation title until it refreshes. So, check your screen before handing over your device.
How to move a locked ChatGPT conversation back to regular history
You may eventually decide that a conversation no longer needs extra protection. You can return it to your normal history without deleting its contents.

Open Projects > Locked chats.Enter your PIN or use device authentication.Open the conversation you want to restore.Select the three-dot menu (•••).Choose Unlock chat , or Unlock on iPhone.Confirm by selecting Unlock chat.
Open Projects > Locked chats.
Enter your PIN or use device authentication.
Open the conversation you want to restore.
Select the three-dot menu (•••).
Choose Unlock chat , or Unlock on iPhone.
Confirm by selecting Unlock chat.
The conversation returns to your regular history and can eventually appear in ordinary search results again.
The privacy limits of ChatGPT Locked Chats

Here's where I want you to pay close attention. Locking a conversation can stop someone casually browsing your chat history. However, OpenAI makes clear that Locked Chats do not provide end-to-end encryption or create a separate encrypted vault. The company also says locking a chat does not change how long it retains your information. Your existing Improve the model for everyone setting remains unchanged, too.

Memory introduces another consideration. If ChatGPT remembered something before you locked a conversation, that information can still exist in regular Memory. Once the chat is locked, new information remembered from subsequent messages stays within the Locked Chats memory area. Other locked conversations can use that information, but regular chats do not receive those new memories automatically. Locked chats can also draw on existing regular Memory when it's enabled.

There's also a potential surprise involving shared links. If you previously shared a conversation through a link, locking it does not revoke that link. Anyone with the existing link may still access the content that was previously shared. You must delete the shared link separately to stop that access.

Files come with their own limitations. Documents and other files uploaded or created inside a locked conversation receive the same protection as the chat itself. However, files already stored elsewhere in ChatGPT's Space or brought in from connected services keep their existing access permissions. Locking a conversation won't automatically protect those separate files.

For workplace accounts, existing organizational retention and compliance policies still apply. OpenAI says Enterprise and Edu conversation logs can include locked chats through its compliance tools. Workspace administrators cannot unlock your chats or reset your PIN, but authorized compliance systems may still access applicable conversation data.

These are important limitations if you're discussing financial information or other highly personal subjects. I would still avoid uploading passwords, Social Security numbers or complete banking credentials to a general ChatGPT conversation.
How to stop ChatGPT from using your new chats for AI training

If you're concerned about how OpenAI handles your conversations, there's another privacy setting you should review. Turning off Improve the model for everyone prevents your new conversations from being used to train OpenAI's models. These instructions apply to personal ChatGPT accounts. OpenAI says content from ChatGPT Business, Enterprise and Edu workspaces is not used to train its models by default.
Here's how to do it.
On the ChatGPT website
Open ChatGPT and sign in.Click your profile icon to open your account menu.Select Settings.Click Data controls.Select Improve the model for everyone.Turn the setting off.Select Done.
Open ChatGPT and sign in.
Click your profile icon to open your account menu.
Select Settings.
Click Data controls.
Select Improve the model for everyone.
Turn the setting off.
Select Done.
On iPhone, Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel
Open the ChatGPT app.Open the sidebar.Tap your profile icon to access Settings.Select Data controls.Turn off Improve the model for everyone.
Open the ChatGPT app.
Open the sidebar.
Tap your profile icon to access Settings.
Select Data controls.
Turn off Improve the model for everyone.

Your new conversations will no longer be used for model training after you turn off this setting. They can still remain in your chat history, so you'll need Locked Chats or another option to keep them out of view. For additional privacy controls across other AI services, see my guide on how to opt out of AI data collection in popular apps.
ChatGPT Locked Chats vs. Temporary Chat: Which should you use?

OpenAI already offers a feature called Temporary Chat, which serves a different purpose. Temporary Chats don't appear in your regular history or create new memories. OpenAI also excludes them from model training while they remain temporary. However, the company may retain temporary conversations for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Depending on your settings, a Temporary Chat can also use existing personalization information.

Locked Chats make more sense when you want to save a conversation and return to it later without leaving it exposed in your normal history. You can keep adding messages, and the conversation stays behind your PIN.

So, if you're having a one-time discussion you don't need to save, Temporary Chat may be the better choice. If you're working through something personal over several days, Locked Chats gives you a way to maintain that conversation with additional access protection.
ChatGPT's Temporary Chat feature keeps conversations out of regular history, offering an alternative for discussions you don't need to save. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What happens if you forget your ChatGPT PIN?

This is one detail I really don't want you to overlook. Resetting a forgotten PIN permanently deletes all your locked chats, along with memories stored only within those chats and files or other content protected only by the previous PIN. OpenAI says the deletion cannot be undone. Even its support team cannot recover that protected content. If you remember your current PIN and simply want to change it, you can do so without losing your conversations.

Open ChatGPT.Go to Settings.Select Security and login.Select Account PIN.Under Change PIN, select Change on the web or desktop, or Change PIN on iPhone or Android.Enter your current PIN.Create and confirm your new four-digit PIN.
Open ChatGPT.
Go to Settings.
Select Security and login.
Select Account PIN.
Under Change PIN, select Change on the web or desktop, or Change PIN on iPhone or Android.
Enter your current PIN.
Create and confirm your new four-digit PIN.

If you've forgotten your PIN, you can also reset it from Settings > Security and login > Account PIN. However, you'll need to verify your identity and confirm the permanent deletion of your protected chats and associated content before creating a replacement PIN.

One more thing: OpenAI doesn't allow every conversation to be locked. The exclusions include Temporary Chats, archived chats, group chats and conversations created from shared links. Chats involving scheduled tasks, meeting recordings or background tasks are also excluded. The same applies to conversations with responses saved as project sources. Some Health, Codex and Work conversations have additional restrictions. If the Lock chat option doesn't appear, your conversation may not qualify.
Kurt's key takeaways

I like that OpenAI is finally giving people more control over which conversations appear when someone opens ChatGPT. As AI becomes a place where people work through personal decisions, there's a real need for some discretion. Being able to hand someone your phone without exposing an entire conversation history is a useful improvement. Still, I would treat Locked Chats as a convenience and access-control feature rather than a guarantee of confidentiality. The four-digit PIN helps keep curious eyes away, but your broader privacy depends on the information you share and the settings you've chosen. And that leaves me wondering whether OpenAI should eventually offer something stronger for conversations people consider deeply private.

Would you trust ChatGPT with your most personal conversations if they were protected by a PIN, or should OpenAI offer stronger privacy protections before you feel comfortable sharing? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Stephen Colbert accused of crossing Harvard picket line before event with Yo-Yo Ma cut short by alarm
summary: Stephen Colbert and Yo-Yo Ma are accused of crossing the Harvard Graduate Students Union picket line before a fire alarm cut their event short.
story: Members of the Harvard Graduate Students Union who are on strike were picketing outside a campus event where Stephen Colbert joined famed cellist Yo-Yo Ma, claiming the pair crossed the picket line. (Harvard Graduate Students Union via Storyful)

Stephen Colbert, who publicly supported striking Hollywood writers in 2023, was accused of crossing a union picket line Thursday to join famed cellist Yo-Yo Ma at a Harvard University event that was abruptly cut short by a fire alarm.

Members of the Harvard Graduate Students Union, which has been on strike since Oct. 27, had urged Colbert and Ma to cancel, postpone or relocate the appearance in solidarity with workers seeking higher wages and stronger workplace protections. The union said it contacted both performers in advance, including through their respective labor organizations, but neither withdrew from the event.

The alarm sounded roughly 40 minutes into the sold-out event at Sanders Theatre, forcing Colbert, Ma and audience members to evacuate, according to Harvard Magazine. The discussion, titled "Arts for Life's Sake," had been scheduled to last 90 minutes but did not resume.
OBAMA FOUNDATION WORKERS MOVE TO UNIONIZE OVER BENEFITS, WORKING CONDITIONS MONTHS AFTER CENTER OPENS
Stephen Colbert speaks onstage at "The Debut" Premiere during the Montclair Film Festival at MKA on Oct. 24, 2026, in Montclair, New Jersey. (Joy Malone/Getty Images)

About 50 union protesters demonstrated outside the theater before and during the event, beating drums, sounding air horns and chanting slogans demanding better pay and working conditions, the outlet reported.
The cause of the fire alarm remains unclear, and the union denied any involvement.
"The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" host Stephen Colbert. (CBS Photo Archive/Getty)
"The alarm was unrelated to HGSU's picketing activity and we have no knowledge of its cause," the union said in a social media statement, adding that members were relieved no one inside was at risk.
The union is seeking annual pay of $55,000 for research assistants and approximately $45,000 for teaching fellows on 10-month appointments, along with 3% annual raises or cost-of-living adjustments.

Other demands include an independent grievance process for harassment and discrimination complaints, legal fee assistance in Title IX cases and financial support for workers who need to leave unsafe laboratory environments.
Students walk through Harvard Yard on the campus of Harvard University in Cambridge, Mass., on April 27, 2022. (AP Photo/Charles Krupa)

The union is also seeking protections for sensitive immigration documents, guaranteed leave for visa delays or immigration emergencies, and a requirement that Harvard notify the union if Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrive on campus. It also wants the university to require a judicial warrant before cooperating with ICE.

The union had highlighted Colbert's support for the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike, during which he joined striking Hollywood workers on the picket line, in its appeal for the performers to reconsider their appearance.
FEDERAL JUDGE TOSSES TRUMP ADMIN HARVARD ADMISSIONS LAWSUIT, LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO FUTURE CHALLENGE

In a statement, the union said it had repeatedly urged Colbert and Ma to avoid crossing its picket line, including through their respective labor organizations, SAG-AFTRA and the Boston Musicians' Association.
Yo-Yo Ma plays the solo as Gustavo Dudamel conducts his last performance at the Los Angeles Philharmonic on May 28, 2026, in California. (Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
"They continued the event inside without regard for the picket line, and refused to speak with union members as they left the event," the union said. "In other words — they crossed our picket line."
Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for both Colbert and Ma for comment, but did not immediately hear back.
Author John Green, meanwhile, moved a scheduled Harvard appearance online to avoid crossing the graduate student union's picket line.
"They're on strike and I had to move a thing to not cross a picket line," Green said in a video shared by the union. "Which was an easy decision… it was not a hard decision for me."

Green also donated proceeds from the event to the union, according to The Boston Globe.

title: Blue Angels pilot removed from team for 'failing to uphold' standards, Navy says
summary: Blue Angels pilot Scott Laux was removed for failing to uphold team standards, forcing the squadron to fly five jets at its Pensacola season finale.
story: Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin speaks with visitors at the Great American State Fair about the U.S. Navy Blue Angels flyover on 'America 250: Celebrating Freedom.' (Courtesy: Freedom 250)
A Blue Angels pilot was removed from the Navy’s flight demonstration team for "failing to uphold" its standards, leaving the squadron with a five-jet show on Friday.

Maj. Scott Laux, a second-year member of the elite team, was identified as Blue Angel No. 6. The Chief of Naval Air Training (CNATRA) confirmed his removal to the Pensacola News Journal, saying the decision was announced Friday before the season finale at home in Pensacola.

"Blue Angel #6 was removed from the team for failing to uphold the standards expected of members of the Navy Flight Demonstration Squadron and will not participate in the team’s remaining performance this season," Chief of Naval Air Training (CNATRA) public affairs office wrote in a statement Friday.
When reached for comment, CNATRA noted Sunday the removal came Nov. 3.
NAVY SAYS NO REPRIMANDS OR FIRINGS AFTER BLUE ANGELS’ LOW PASS OVER BEACHGOERS
Maj. Scott Laux answers media questions at NAS Pensacola on July 16, 2026. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
The Navy has not said exactly what conduct prompted Laux's dismissal. His photo and biography are no longer featured on the Blue Angels’ website's team page.

Laux was absent from the squadron’s NAS Pensacola Homecoming Air Show on Friday and Saturday, where the team performed with five jets instead of its usual six. Laux's role was the opposing solo, which flies with lead solo #5 in the head-on crossing passes and mirror-image maneuvers that fill the gaps between the four-jet Diamond’s routines.
VIRAL VIDEO OF JETS BUZZING DHL STADIUM IN CAPE TOWN PROMPTS AVIATION SAFETY INVESTIGATION
Maj. Scott Laux spent one year as a narrator and most of his second year on the Blue Angels, before being shelved before the final performance of the season this weekend. (Getty Images)
The routines were adjusted to account for the missing jet, according to reports.
The 2026 narrator, Lt. Cmdr. Ronny Hafeza, might replace Laux on the 2027 team. The Blue Angels officers serve three-year terms, one as a narrator as Laux did.
HEGSETH STEPS IN TO ‘FIX’ SITUATION AFTER APACHE PILOTS SUSPENDED FOR ‘SALUTE FROM THE SHORES’ FLYOVER

Marine Corps Maj. Scott Laux was outspoken in defending the July low beach flyover, but he is the one who has conspicuously been removed from the Blue Angels' final performance of the season. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)

Laux, a native of Chantilly, Va., graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 2012 with a degree in Chinese and earned his wings in 2015, according to his bio, which as of Sunday morning could still be accessed on the site despite no longer being listed with the rest of the team. He flew F/A-18 Hornets with Marine Corps squadrons, deployed to Japan and aboard the USS Nimitz and supported three operations during the 2020 carrier deployment: Resolute Support, Inherent Resolve and Octave Quartz.

title: Killer’s chewing gum blows open 40-year-old murders, detective warns there may be more victims
summary: Mitchell Gaff admitted to six rapes during state evaluations, yet a court later freed him. DNA evidence now ties him to two 1984 Everett murders.
story: A 74-year-old man was sentenced to 50 years to life in prison after DNA evidence linked him to the cold case murders of two Everett, Washington, women in the 1980s. (FOX 13 Seattle)
Decades before DNA evidence linked Mitchell Gaff to two Washington cold-case murders, he admitted to six rapes during state psychological evaluations, court records show.
Years later, a judge ended his civil commitment, allowing him to live in the community without the restrictions imposed under Washington’s sexually violent predator program.
Gaff pleaded guilty in April 2026 to the murders of Judith "Judy" Weaver and Susan Vesey. A Snohomish County Superior Court judge sentenced him to 50 years to life in prison in May.
DNA FROM CHEWING GUM NAILS LONGTIME SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES AFTER REIGN OF TERROR: REPORT
Mitchell Gaff is pictured in a mugshot. (Washington State Department of Corrections)
His convictions have raised questions about other victims, given Gaff’s history of sexual violence before a court unconditionally released him from civil commitment in September 2018.
Gaff later lived in Olympia under the alias "Sam Wise Price."
CALIFORNIA SHERIFF FIGHTS PLAN TO HOUSE CONVICTED SEX PREDATOR NEAR GIRL SCOUT CAMP
Dr. Katherine Ramsland, a forensic psychologist and author not affiliated with the case, told Fox News Digital that ignoring a predator's admissions carries dangerous risks.
"Psychologically, if he'd confessed but discovered there'd be no consequence, he'd likely feel emboldened to potentially repeat it," Ramsland said.
CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE
Victims found strangled, sexually assaulted

In June 1984, authorities found Weaver bound, sexually assaulted and strangled inside her apartment off Rucker Avenue in Everett. Investigators determined that Gaff had also sliced her clothing with a knife and set a fire in an attempt to destroy evidence.
Authorities found Judy Weaver's body inside her home on Rucker Avenue in Everett, Washington, after first responders were called to a fire on June 2, 1984. (Everett Police Department)
The investigation initially focused on Bill Richards, Weaver’s fiancé. Weaver’s daughters told investigators that the couple had a volatile relationship, according to KING 5 News.
COLD CASE BREAKTHROUGH SOLVES TEEN KILLING AFTER SUSPECT LIVED FREE FOR DECADES: 'BETTER BE AFRAID'
Richards remained a suspect until his death in 1994.
In November 2023, Everett Police Department Detective Susan Logothetti submitted evidence from Weaver’s case for modern DNA testing, after obtaining a DNA sample through a ruse involving chewing gum.
DISCARDED TRASH UNCAPS 41-YEAR-OLD MURDER CASE IN RITZY SEASIDE RESORT TOWN, AUTHORITIES SAY
Authorities arrested Gaff in May 2024 after obtaining a DNA sample through the gum.
DNA evidence then linked Gaff to Vesey’s murder. Authorities found her beaten and bound inside her Everett home on June 2, 1984, the morning of her 21st birthday.
Susan Vesey was murdered inside her home in Everett, Wash., on July 12, 1980, according to authorities. (Everett Police Department)
FORENSIC GENEALOGY UNMASKS COLD CASE SUSPECT AS STRANGLER, SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES LATER: OFFICIALS
Everett police said Gaff’s statements about the murders matched evidence investigators had gathered.
Court records document a history of sexual violence

In 1979, a jury convicted Gaff of first-degree burglary and second-degree assault after he bound a woman’s hands, repeatedly struck her with a pistol and smashed her head against concrete before she escaped, according to a Washington Court of Appeals opinion.

Gaff received probation and work release. While still on probation in 1984, he broke into an Everett home and raped two teen sisters, ages 14 and 16, at knifepoint. A judge imposed an exceptional prison sentence of 138 months and revoked his probation, requiring him to serve his sentences consecutively.
Before Gaff’s scheduled release from prison, Washington authorities petitioned to commit him to a secure facility as a sexually violent predator.
CONVICTED PREDATORS FACE LIFETIME BARRIER UNDER GOP LAWMAKER’S SWEEPING VICTIM PROTECTION BILL
Mitchell Gaff pleaded guilty to the rapes and cold case murders of Judith Weaver and Susan Vesey in Everett, Wash., according to the Everett Police Department. (KCPQ)

During psychological evaluations, Gaff admitted to making obscene calls and committing sexual assaults, including six rapes. A jury found that he met the legal criteria for civil commitment, and the Washington Court of Appeals upheld the decision in April 1998.
A psychologist who testified for the state diagnosed Gaff with sexual sadism and concluded that he posed a risk of reoffending.
A defense expert, meanwhile, believed Gaff could live safely in the community under controlled conditions.
Gaff moved to a halfway house before his 2018 release

By 2005, state evaluators decided Gaff no longer required maximum confinement and approved his transfer to a less restrictive setting. In 2006, he left Washington’s Special Commitment Center on McNeil Island for a secure halfway house in Seattle’s SoDo district.

The agreement required GPS monitoring and supervision whenever Gaff left the facility. It also required him to give up his right to challenge his sexually violent predator status for eight years.

Gaff remained under the state’s civil commitment system until September 2018, when a court dismissed his sexually violent predator petition and unconditionally released him from civil commitment, according to a 2019 report in The Olympian.
Mitchell Gaff appears in court in Washington. (FOX 13 Seattle)
"It's tricky to hold them beyond their sentence, and sometimes it means having to prove they're an imminent danger, not just a possible one," Ramsland said.

Everett police are now reviewing other unsolved homicides, sexual assaults and cold cases for possible links to Gaff, Logothetti told Fox News Digital.

title: Alexander brothers allegedly paid for coverage of sex-trafficking trial as writers deny favorable treatment
summary: The Alexander brothers each received 30 years in prison, but allegations that they paid journalists for favorable trial coverage add a new twist.
story: Attorney Michael Willemin says private jets, superyachts and powerful connections helped the convicted brothers operate for years and left women fearful of coming forward.

The Alexander brothers allegedly paid independent journalists for writing favorable coverage of their sex-trafficking trial – claims those writers have denied – as the wealthy trio sought to beat the federal charges before they were convicted and sentenced.

Tal Alexander, 40, and his 39-year-old twin brothers, Oren and Alon Alexander, were convicted in March of conspiracy to commit sex crimes, including with minors. They each were sentenced on Oct. 27 to 30 years in prison.
The jet-setting trio was found guilty of working together and with others to engage in sex trafficking, including by repeatedly drugging, sexually assaulting and raping numerous female victims.
Now, the brothers face civil litigation from women who say they were victims.
Oren Alexander, Tal Alexander and Alon Alexander attend Chanukah With The Stars Gala on Dec. 10, 2014, at Harmonie Club in New York City. (J Grassi/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
PRIVATE JETS, YACHTS AND POWERFUL FRIENDS HELPED ALEXANDER BROTHERS LURE WOMEN — AND SILENCE THEM, LAWYER SAYS
But two independent journalists who covered the proceedings also are facing accusations.
Daniel Mael is one of two writers accused in a New York Times piece of accepting payment to portray the trio of brothers in a positive way.
But that’s not true, Mael said in a phone call with Fox News Digital. He simply wrote about his own conclusions, he said.

Mael rejected claims from the New York Times report that he was paid $15,000 for writing "sympathetic posts" about the brothers during their trial. In the report, publisher Frank Parlato was said to have been paid $10,000 for similar writings.
Mael declined to discuss the details of his financial agreement with the Alexanders’ publicist, Juda Engelmayer.

Oren Alexander, center, and his twin brother, Alon, center right, speak to their attorney, Joel Denaro, during their bond hearing after being charged with multiple state and federal crimes, including sex trafficking and rape, at the Richard E. Gerstein Justice Building on Friday, Dec. 13, 2024, in Miami. (Matias J. Ocner/Miami Herald via AP, Pool)
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Engelmayer "offered to help subsidize part of the cost of covering the case, and I accepted," Mael wrote in a statement on X on Nov. 5.
"No one requested favorable coverage, no one dictated a single word, and no one exercised the slightest editorial influence over my reporting."
Parlato also declined to discuss whether he was paid for his writing.
In an email to Fox News Digital, he maintained his coverage was independent.
"I have never spoken to the Alexander brothers," Parlato wrote. "Nobody tells me what to write. Nobody sees my stories before publication.
"I wrote about the brothers from court records, before trial, when they were presumed innocent. I write what I believe is true."
Oren Alexander and Tal Alexander speak at a panel at the Rockstars of Real Estate Event, Sept. 3, 2013, in New York. (Amy Sussman/Invision for Details Magazine/AP Images, File)

"By the time the Alexander brothers went to trial, they had already been convicted in the court of public opinion," Engelmayer told Fox News Digital in an email. "The coverage was extensive, overwhelmingly negative, and largely driven by the allegations against them. There was very little interest in examining anything that might challenge the prevailing narrative."

To make sure the defense's perspective "was at least heard," he contacted independent journalists who might be willing to cover the trial, he said. He sought those who would ask "the questions that weren't being asked elsewhere."
Mael published frequent trial updates on his Substack. And sometimes, he presented evidence that weakened the defense’s case.
A text from Alon Alexander referencing how he "took down a 17 year old," was "perhaps the most damning piece of evidence," Mael wrote in a recap of the trial’s eighth day.

Real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their brother Alon, who were found guilty of repeatedly drugging, sexually assaulting and raping dozens of female victims, listen as their lawyers argue for a lesser sentence on their behalf in New York, Oct. 27, 2026, in this courtroom sketch (Reuters/Jane Rosenberg)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
He bristled at the New York Times’ suggestion that he covered the trial with a bias against witnesses for the prosecution.
"I never ever criticized the motives of the women on the stand," he said. "Ever."
Mael asserted that his writing was independent and accurate, even though it was supported financially by Engelmayer.
Parlato’s online platform, The Frank Report, published articles suggesting the Alexanders’ innocence in July and August 2025.
One of the published pieces, "What If Everything You’ve Been Told About the Alexander Brothers Case Is Wrong? And Other Matters," was written by Engelmayer.
Brothers on trial
The Alexander brothers grew up in a wealthy Miami family.
Oren and Tal were star real-estate agents who sold palatial homes to celebrities and the ultra-wealthy in New York, Miami, Aspen and beyond.
Real estate brokers Tal Alexander, right, and his younger brother, Oren Alexander, outside their Miami Beach home on Feb. 1, 2019. (Getty Images)
Alon worked as an executive at the family’s Miami-based private security company, Kent Security.
Their lifestyle put them on private jets and super yachts, and at exclusive parties. And they used that world as a hunting ground, prosecutors said.

The brothers, who resided primarily in New York and Miami, Florida, used their "wealth and prominence to create and facilitate opportunities to sexually assault women," according to the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York.
For years, they identified women through dating apps, clubs, parties and promoters, then lured them with trips, luxury accommodations, and access to powerful people and Hollywood celebrities.
Once the women were isolated, the brothers drugged them and sexually assaulted them—sometimes together or with other men.
In some cases, they recorded the attacks.

Oren Alexander and his twin brother, Alon, attend a bond hearing after being charged with multiple state and federal crimes, including sex trafficking and rape, at the Richard E. Gerstein Justice Building on Dec. 13, 2024, in Miami. (Matias J. Ocner/Miami Herald via AP, Pool)

Eleven women testified at their trial. Prosecutors said more than 70 women came forward with similar accounts.
With the criminal proceedings finalized, three women are pursuing civil cases against the trio of brothers.

At sentencing in their criminal trial, the brothers denied drugging, raping or trafficking anyone. But they did express regret over their past behavior.
Prosecutors sought life in prison. The defense had asked for the 15-year minimum sentence.

Judge Valerie Caproni also imposed 10 years of supervised release on each brother, with fines of $300,000 for Alon and Oren and $350,000 for Tal.

title: Three teens, adult charged with murder after woman finds her teenage son dead in abandoned home
summary: Austin Payne's mother tracked his cellphone to an abandoned Albany, Georgia, residence after the 15-year-old called to say he had been shot.
story: Three teenagers and a 22-year-old man face murder charges after a 15-year-old Georgia boy was found shot dead in an abandoned home, where his mother reportedly tracked his cellphone after he failed to return home.
Three teenagers and an adult have been charged with murder in Georgia after a mother found her 15-year-old son shot to death inside an abandoned residence following Halloween night.
The Albany Police Department said investigators arrested 22-year-old Detravion Parker, as well as two 15-year-olds and a 16-year-old in connection with the death of Austin Payne, 15.
All four suspects were charged with murder and transported to the Dougherty County Jail, according to police.

Officers responded to the 800 block of Cameo Lane in Albany on Nov. 1, where they discovered Payne dead inside an abandoned home, police said. His mother found him by tracking his location via cellphone after he failed to return home on Halloween, according to WALB.
MARSHALS NAB TEEN WANTED FOR MURDER OF PENN STATE STUDENT 1,700 MILES FROM CRIME SCENE, 2ND SUSPECT IN CUSTODY

Austin Payne, 15, was found shot to death in an abandoned Georgia residence. Detravion Parker, 22, was arrested and charged with murder alongside three teenagers in connection with the death. (Albany Police Department/GoFundMe)
Albany Police Chief Michael Persley said during a Nov. 2 news conference that Payne had contacted his mother after being shot.
"He did make a call to his mother that he had been shot," Persley said.
According to WALB, investigators reviewed surveillance footage, cellphone records and witness statements to reconstruct the events leading up to Payne's death.
Witnesses told investigators that armed individuals approached a group walking with Payne, demanded their belongings and opened fire, the outlet reported.

Payne may have been targeted during an attempted robbery involving a handgun he had recently displayed on social media, according to WALB.
Payne's family has launched a GoFundMe fundraiser to help cover funeral expenses following his death.
A relative said Payne would have turned 16 on Nov. 12.
"Our family is trying to process this heartbreaking loss," the relative wrote.
The fundraiser also noted that Payne is survived by his mother and 17-year-old sister.

title: Two experienced skydivers die after midair collision entangles their parachutes
summary: The two skydivers collided midair at about 150 feet during an organized skydive in Southern California, entangling their parachutes.
story: First responders and investigators work at the scene after a skydiving plane crashed moments after takeoff in northeastern France, killing all 11 people aboard. (Reuters)
Two experienced skydivers died Friday when their parachutes became entangled during an organized dive in Southern California.

Georgia Jean, 56, of Box Elder, S.D., and Levi Pimentel, 29, of Aurora, Ill., both licensed skydivers, began to plummet at about 150 feet above the ground when they collided midair at Skydive Elsinore around noon in Lake Elsinore, about 75 miles southeast of Los Angeles.
The freefall portion of the skydive was normal, as was the opening of the parachutes, Skydive Elsinore said.
FRENCH INVESTIGATORS PROBE FATAL SKYDIVING PLANE CRASH THAT KILLED PILOT AND 10 PARACHUTISTS
A file photo of a person skydiving. (Skydive Dubai/Getty Images)
Jean and Pimentel suffered "traumatic injuries" and were rushed by ambulance to a hospital, the Riverside County Fire Department said on social media.
They were pronounced dead at the hospital.
MISSOURI SKYDIVING PLANE CRASH THAT KILLED ALL 12 ABOARD IS A 'DAVASTATING LOSS,' COMPANY SAYS
Skydive Elsinore is located in Lake Elsinore. (Glenn Koenig/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
"The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground," Skydive Elsinore said in a statement.
Pimentel was a lead skydiving instructor at iFLY Naperville in Illinois, according to her LinkedIn, and Jean had done more than 1,700 jumps, according to her website.
Two U.S. Army skydivers perform a stunt during an air show in Southern California. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images)

The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Ex-police officer accused of stabbing NYC jogger to death appears emotionless in new photos
summary: Sayed Mohassib was seen led away in handcuffs after being charged with second-degree murder in the stabbing death of Brooklyn jogger Katie Suarez.
story: Sayed Mohassib was escorted Saturday from a Brooklyn police precinct. (WNYW)
An ex-NYPD police officer accused of murdering a Brooklyn jogger was seen being led out of the 62nd Precinct police station in handcuffs on Saturday.
Sayed Mohassib has been charged with second-degree murder in the stabbing Oct. 30 death of Katie Suarez at the Shore Parkway Greenway.
He is also charged with tampering with physical evidence and criminal possession of a weapon.
Mohassib, who wore a red Van Dutch jacket, black top and jeans, showed little emotion as he was escorted by police.
NYC WOMAN CRITICALLY INJURED AFTER BEING STABBED MULTIPLE TIMES WHILE JOGGING ALONG BROOKLYN WATERFRONT
Sayed Mohassib showed little emotion as he was escorted away in handcuffs. (WNYW)
He told police that he woke up covered in blood with no memory of the attack, adding that he threw the knife in the garbage, according to the New York Post.
Sayed Mohassib is seen after his arrest. (WNYW)
Suarez, 28, was running along a waterfront path around 8 p.m. when she was stabbed in her neck.
She had been on the phone with her parents before the attack and when they got cut off, they went looking for her along the path where they found her in critical condition.
She died of her injuries at the hospital.
COPS RETURN TO NEW JERSEY MOTHER'S HOME MONTHS AFTER SHE WAS FOUND STABBED AND HUSBAND CALLED 911
The NYPD says Katie Suarez, 28, was stabbed in the neck several times in an unprovoked attack that happened as she was on a run in Brooklyn on a popular jogging and biking path. (NYPD; Google Maps)
Mohassib briefly served with the NYPD before he left for the Marines, where he was deemed unfit for service, the Post reported.
The 27-year-old was most recently working as a public school aide.
The New York City Department of Education told FOX 5 that Mohassib has been suspended and will be fired depending on a conviction.
