In an interview in Kyiv, Zelenskyy acknowledged holding discussions with the Trump administration about targeting oil facilities, attacks President Donald Trump has pinned as being partly to blame for high gas prices in the U.S.
"We had different conversations — different, and several — with President Trump and with his team about attacks on refineries," Zelenskyy said.
"We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system."
TRUMP TELLS ZELENSKYY TO STOP DOING 'ONE THING' DURING ATTACKS ON RUSSIA

During an interview with Fox News, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged President Donald Trump to pursue an energy cease-fire with Russia as Washington pressures Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries. (Fox News)
Ukraine has reported near-daily Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, triggering power outages just as temperatures dip ahead of winter.
"That's why we have to respond. But our response has to be painful for Russian military people," Zelenskyy said. "If we will not respond on energy, they will continue."
U.S.-Ukraine relations took a further hit in October when Trump struck a deal to import millions of tons of Russian diesel to the United States.
ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE
Zelenskyy warned President Donald Trump against helping Russia while praising first lady Melania Trump’s role in securing a humanitarian evacuation from Russian-controlled territory. (Fox News)

Zelenskyy suggested Ukraine might be encouraged to hold off on further attacks on Russian oil facilities if the United States were to deliver more U.S.-made Patriot missile interceptors to protect Ukrainian skies. Pressed by Fox News on whether that might be seen as an attempt to leverage Trump, Zelenskyy said: "I don't have any concerns when I share the truth between partners."
"Our countries are huge partners. American society (is a) huge supporter."
"And that's why I have to share with (the) president the truth, the real situation: that America can't help Russia. (The) president can't help Putin."
US WILL MEDIATE UPCOMING UKRAINE-RUSSIA TALKS IN ABU DHABI, WITKOFF SAYS

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News that Ukraine will continue targeting Russian oil refineries despite objections from the Trump administration. (Pier Marco Tacca; Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Ahead of planned peace talks in the United Arab Emirates, Zelenskyy urged Trump to launch another push for a targeted ceasefire where both Russia and Ukraine refrain from attacks on energy facilities.
"If the American president thinks that this war has influence on the prices," Zelenskyy said, "he can ask, energy ceasefire, during (the) Abu Dhabi trilateral meeting: energy ceasefire."

Zelenskyy spoke with Fox News hours before starved and exhausted residents left the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky and crossed into Ukrainian-held territory under a humanitarian truce brokered by first lady Melania Trump, the first of its kind in more than four years of war.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Zelenskyy welcomed the first lady's initiative, calling the evacuations "a huge result," and adding: "I don't know how many such steps will be available for us, but if the first lady can do it ... it's very helpful. I'm very thankful to her."
Trey Yingst currently serves as chief foreign correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in August 2018.

title: US will mediate upcoming Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi, Witkoff says
summary: U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff announced U.S.-mediated peace talks between Ukraine and Russia on Nov. 10 and 11, focusing on security arrangements and de-escalation.
story: Negotiations to end the war could resume after Russian President Vladimir Putin met with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy tells Brian Kilmeade he is open to freezing front lines in exchange for security guarantees. American Military Project director Will Thibeau provides his analysis on the developments during 'Fox & Friends First.'

U.S. officials will mediate a new round of talks between Ukraine and Russia next week with the goal of delivering "lasting security for generations to come," U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.
Witkoff said the U.S.-mediated negotiations will be held on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates.

"The United States will mediate working-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia on November 10–11 in Abu Dhabi, advancing President Trump’s mission to end the war. Discussions will focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace," Witkoff wrote on X.
INSIDE MELANIA TRUMP'S SECRET DIPLOMATIC ROLE IN THE RUSSIA-UKRAINE CEASEFIRE DEAL
U.S. officials will mediate peace talks between Ukraine and Russia next week. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)
Ahead of next week's peace talks, U.S. negotiators will meet this week in Brussels with representatives from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the EU and NATO.

"Additionally, American negotiators will meet this week in Brussels with representatives from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the EU, and NATO to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe’s post-war security architecture, and economic opportunities to support Ukraine’s reconstruction," Witkoff said.
The negotiations will be held on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates. (Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP)

The push by the U.S. government builds upon earlier diplomatic discussions held in Kyiv, Oslo and St. Petersburg, as the Trump administration continues efforts to broker an end to the war following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said.
TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR
The push by the U.S. government builds upon earlier diplomatic discussions held in Kyiv, Oslo and St. Petersburg. (Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo via AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

This comes after President Donald Trump said last month that efforts to resolve the war were "maybe now the closest we’ve been," adding that he believed both sides wanted an end to the conflict after years of fighting and heavy casualties.

title: Russia plotting 'massive strike' during midterms, Zelenskyy warns, urges US to stop Putin
summary: Zelenskyy says Russia plans a massive attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure while the world watches Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections unfold.
story: Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's response to Russian attacks, warning that strikes on their infrastructure will meet a painful response.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Monday that Russia is preparing a "massive attack" on Ukraine centered on Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States, accusing Moscow of seeking to exploit the historical vote to unleash strikes while the world's attention is elsewhere.

The Ukrainian leader's warning came as voters prepared to decide which party controls Congress, a result that could also influence Washington's future response to Russian President Vladimir Putin's almost five-year war in Ukraine.

In a post on X, Zelenskyy went on to urge the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, warning that Russia could exploit the elections to target Ukraine's battered energy infrastructure and supply routes.
DRONE STRIKE SINKS SHIP IN NATO WATERS AS ZELENSKYY WARNS OF LOOMING ‘MASSIVE STRIKE’
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/Efrem Lukatsky/AP)
"We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics," Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.

"The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked."
Zelenskyy's warning came hours after Russian forces struck a school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a settlement in southeastern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region.
At least 26 people, including police officers and first responders, were killed, five others were injured and others remained missing, according to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda.
ZELENSKYY PRESSURES US AND EUROPE FOR MORE 'AIR DEFENSE' ASSISTANCE AMID ONGOING WAR WITH RUSSIA
Ukraine's largest private energy company reports 90% of generation capacity damaged by Russian attacks, leaving over 1 million without power during freezing temperatures. (Reuters)
In his X post, Zelenskyy urged the U.S. and its allies to warn Putin that continued attacks on Ukraine would bring serious economic consequences.

"We need signals from the world to Russia that will make them feel that terror is no good, that it will bring no gains, and that as long as this war continues, their oil will burn, and they will not be able to make money doing business with the world," Zelenskyy warned.
"We must not play games with Russia's oil or gas revenues," he added.
"We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left talks with President Donald Trump and members of his Cabinet during a lunch meeting at the White House on Oct. 17, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has sought to negotiate an end to the war with the help of special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, both of whom have been involved in diplomatic efforts with Moscow.

Zelenskyy told Fox News in a Sunday interview that Ukraine would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries for a month if Washington provided Patriot missile interceptors during the same period, potentially opening the door to diplomacy.
The State Department approved the potential sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, according to Reuters.
The proposed sale could provide a significant boost to Ukraine's air defenses if finalized, although the delivery timeline is uncertain.
TRUMP SAYS US WILL LET UKRAINE MAKE PATRIOT MISSILES IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT

First Lady Melania Trump, left, and civilians being evacuated from Oleshky, Ukraine, in October 2022 during the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war. (Umit Bektas/Reuters; Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters)
On Monday, Ukraine also accused Moscow of exploiting a U.S.-backed humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, to strengthen Russian military positions.
Nearly 800 people were evacuated during the six-day humanitarian pause, according to first lady Melania Trump, with the White House clarifying that she helped broker the arrangement.
Ukraine's General Staff accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian pause to rotate troops, reinforce their defenses and improve battlefield logistics.

"Under the ceasefire introduced for the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, units of the Defence Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," the General Staff said in a statement on X.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The enemy, by contrast, used the humanitarian pause to improve its positions."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Poland's constitutional crisis deepens as Prime Minister Tusk faces accusations of power grab
summary: President Karol Nawrocki turned his plane around as Poland's Constitutional Tribunal standoff triggered ambassador resignations and clashes.
story: Protesters gathered outside Poland’s top court as a long-running political dispute involving President Karol Nawrocki and Donald Tusk’s government escalated.  (AP Video.)

Friday’s late-night confrontation at Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, which drew riot police and protesters and prompted President Karol Nawrocki to turn his plane around and return to Warsaw, has reignited a bitter debate over whether Prime Minister Donald Tusk is restoring the rule of law or overstepping constitutional limits.

The dispute erupted after the tribunal announced the suspension of its president, Bogdan Święczkowski, a move that supporters of Tusk’s government described as necessary to restore judicial independence, while critics denounced it as an unconstitutional power grab.

Marcin Przydacz, the head of the International Policy Bureau in Nawrocki’s office, took to European TV Monday morning denouncing Tusk’s actions, saying, "Even lawyers who are close to the Tusk government say that there's absolutely no legal basis for such behavior."
POLISH PRESIDENT TURNS PLANE AROUND AFTER 'COUP' AT NATION’S TOP COURT
Donald Tusk, Poland's prime minister, during the Polish Army Parade in Warsaw on Aug. 15, 2025. (Damian Lemanski/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The dispute is also triggering diplomatic fallout, with at least three Polish ambassadors resigning in protest. Przydacz, a former parliament member of the now-opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, says Poland’s permanent representative to the U.N. since 2021, Krzysztof Szczerski, resigned Monday, which followed the resignations over the weekend of the ambassadors to China and Romania.

"This crisis didn’t begin on Friday," said Simone Rodan‑Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. "Poland has been living with a deeply compromised Constitutional Tribunal for more than a decade."

Rodan-Benzaquen said the confrontation cannot be understood in isolation. Parliament has continued appointing judges under Poland's constitution, but several of those appointments have been blocked from taking office amid a years-long standoff between the government, the presidency and the tribunal itself.

Presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki, a conservative historian backed by the right-wing Law and Justice party, second right, greets supporters at his headquarters after the presidential election runoff in Warsaw, Poland, June 1, 2025. (AP Photo/Czarek Sokolowski)

"This isn't simply a case of Tusk deciding to pack a functioning, independent court ahead of an election," Rodan-Benzaquen tells Fox News Digital. "There is a genuine institutional crisis that predates his government, and a legitimate question of how to resolve it."

That underlying conflict exploded into public view Friday after Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska suspended Święczkowski and his deputy, triggering protests outside the tribunal and prompting Nawrocki to abandon a trip to Senegal. Police detained three people after some demonstrators clashed with officers outside the court complex.
HUNGARY AND POLAND DEFEND TOUGH MIGRATION POLICIES AS FRANCE REELS FROM VIOLENT UNREST

Rodan-Benzaquen cautioned that concerns about Friday's actions are not limited to supporters of the opposition, saying they "raise serious questions about the legality and proportionality of the methods being used."

Critics of the government have described Friday's events as an unprecedented assault on Poland's constitutional order. "My former boss, Margaret Thatcher, would have been absolutely appalled by what we're witnessing in Poland," Nile Gardner, director of the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at the Heritage Foundation told Fox News Digital. "This is clearly a crisis for Poland and an attempted coup by Donald Tusk."

"This has all the hallmarks of a Soviet-style coup operation," added Gardner, who said Tusk waited until Nawrocki was traveling out of the country, accusing the prime minister of undermining the tribunal and further destabilizing Poland ahead of next year's election. "It's the sort of thing you'd expect actually from a third world dictator."
Protesters gather outside the headquarters of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw after police blocked access to the court building on Oct. 30, 2026  (Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images)

Others reject the coup characterization. Boštjan Udovič, chair of international relations at the University of Ljubljana, says the dispute centers on the government's attempt to restore judicial arrangements that critics of the previous PiS government say were inconsistent with both Poland's constitution and European legal standards.
"Tusk wants to restore the situation as required by the constitution and the international institutions," Udovič said. "I think that he hoped the transition would be easier."

Tusk defended his government's actions as part of an effort to restore the rule of law, accusing both the president and the tribunal of improperly blocking judges elected by parliament from taking office. "The solution to the conflict is simple," he said on Monday. "The president recognizes the judges legally elected by [parliament], because that is what the Constitution stipulates." He accused Nawrocki of "choosing forceful confrontation, which could cost Poland very dearly. A democratic state under the rule of law cannot yield to violence."
POLAND ARRESTS RUSSIAN ALLEGEDLY HIRED TO KILL UKRAINIAN-AMERICAN WHO WAS 'INCONVENIENT TO THE PUTIN REGIME'

"Restoring the rule of law is essential," Rodan-Benzaquen says, warning against viewing the dispute purely through a partisan lens. "But the legitimacy of that restoration depends not only on its objectives, but also on the legality of the means used to achieve it."
The divide in Poland has increasingly been reflected abroad, with European institutions and political leaders offering sharply different interpretations of the crisis.
Protesters rally outside Poland’s top court as tensions between President Karol Nawrocki and Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government intensify. (AP)

The European Commission has largely backed the Polish parliament's authority to appoint judges. European Commissioner Michael McGrath said selecting new judges lies within the powers of Poland's parliament.

French opposition leader Marine Le Pen, meanwhile, accused Brussels of applying a double standard. "One cannot claim to defend democracy and the rule of law while remaining silent when the constitutional balance of a member state is gravely threatened," she posted on X. "The proliferation of such strong-arm tactics within the European Union itself is beginning to raise serious questions."

"America is on Poland’s side," U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose posted to X, urging restraint. "Our concern is for the stability, security, and democratic future of a country we are proud to call our friend and ally… Poland has come too far and accomplished too much to let political differences, no matter how strongly felt, put any of that at risk."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Police were deployed outside the Constitutional Tribunal after Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, elected by the Parlament in March 2026, issued an order suspending Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and Vice President Bartlomiej Sochanski from their duties for one month. (Kai Taller/Arena Akcji/Sipa USA)

For Rodan-Benzaquen, the larger issue extends far beyond the events of Friday night. "One side claims to be defending constitutional order against the abuses of the other, while the institutions that should arbitrate the dispute have themselves become the object of the dispute," she said.
With parliamentary elections in Poland only a year away, the battle over who gets to define the rule of law may prove more consequential than the confrontation that unfolded this weekend.

Calling Tusk’s tactics "straight out of the Putin playbook," Gardner warns Poland is in "an incredibly dangerous situation right now, and the blame is squarely at the door of Donald Tusk and his government."
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: Gov. Josh Shapiro urges Democrats to prioritize healthcare, food assistance
summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January, though he urged them not to forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.
story: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January, though he urged them not to forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I hope one of the first things that the Congress does is to stop these Medicaid cuts, stop the SNAP cuts, roll back the cuts, the effective cuts in the Affordable Care Act,” Shapiro said in an interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that aired Sunday.
Shapiro noted that in Pennsylvania alone, 510,000 people are losing healthcare and 143,000 more are losing SNAP or food assistance due to cuts approved during President Donald Trump’s second term.

“In general, though, I think Democrats need to have an aggressive agenda that cuts costs, that ends the war, that gets put on the president’s desk,” he said. “Hopefully, he will sign it because it’ll be common-sense stuff that makes people’s lives better.”

Trump has said that he intends to work with Democrats when Congress begins its new term, though he has also touted a new “VETO”-branded hat since Republicans lost the majority in the midterm elections.
Shapiro said that if Trump chooses to veto Democrats’ legislation, “it’s yet another signal to the American people the president actually doesn’t care about their well-being.”
While the governor stressed the importance of revitalizing Medicaid and SNAP programs, he also said Democrats shouldn’t forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I think the Congress needs to be responsive to where voters are on corruption, and there has to be real accountability for this administration,” Shapiro said, adding that Democrats need to “walk and chew gum at the same time” to pass effective legislation and also “have real accountability for the corruption that exists in Washington.”
“It can’t be either/or,” he said. “It has to be both/and.”

Shapiro added that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker of the House, “has made very clear that both are going to be on the agenda for the first 100 days and for these next two years.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The governor said that he doesn’t think Democrats should be thinking about the 2028 elections yet. Instead, “we should be thinking about how to make people’s lives better in 2027,” he said.
“It’s incumbent upon the Congress to now do that, and it’s incumbent upon governors now to continue to lead the way in our states,” Shapiro said.
Shapiro, who has been floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, did not commit to running.

Asked whether he is more likely to run than not, Shapiro answered that his focus was on “figuring how we advance policies like raising the minimum wage and many other things that have been blocked by Republicans,” as Pennsylvania Democrats won a majority in the state legislature Tuesday.
He also did not directly answer whether he was committed to serving his full four-year term.

“Well, I committed to run for governor, and that’s the work I’m focused on doing,” Shapiro said. “And if I’ve got something to say about my future, I’d love to come back on your show and talk about it.”

title: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says he is a ‘hard yes’ on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he is a “hard yes” on supporting impeachment efforts against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
story: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he is a “hard yes” on supporting impeachment efforts against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which are expected to be brought to a vote this week.
Asked in an interview on ABC’s “This Week” whether he would support Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., in his efforts to impeach Hegseth, Jeffries confirmed he supported the push.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”
“Pete Hegseth has got to go,” he added.

Jeffries’ support marks a major endorsement of impeachment efforts against Hegseth and signals how other House Democrats could ultimately vote on the measure. The impeachment push also tests how far lawmakers are willing to go to oust the top Pentagon official after voters have given low marks to the administration’s handling of the war in Iran, which factored into midterms.

Asked on ABC whether Jeffries believed all other House Democrats would support the impeachment resolution, he said that they would “have that conversation Tuesday morning.” The House is back in session this week, and the impeachment resolution is expected to be filed early this week with a vote to follow.

Massie has been a vocal critic of Hegseth and the war in Iran. He previously filed a resolution to impeach Hegseth in September, but Republican leaders canceled planned votes and the House left early, pushing the vote to after the election.
For Subscribers

NBC News reported last week that President Donald Trump has told allies that he was considering replacing Hegseth. Trump, though, has publicly denied that he is planning to replace the secretary, telling reporters last week that Hegseth was “doing a very good job.”
For Subscribers
At the same time, Hegseth has forcefully pushed back on Massie’s impeachment plans, referring to the congressman in a social media video last week as a “disgruntled, defeated congressman.”
“It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said in the video. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Massie, though, said in a social media post last week that his “Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress.” Democrats, Massie said, would “have hearings & trials.”

title: Tensions rise in Philadelphia over boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants
summary: A bike ride organized to promote a boycott of several Jewish-owned restaurants drew opposing demonstrators to Philadelphia on Sunday, with people waving Palestinian and Israeli flags exchanging heated words.
story: A bike ride organized to promote a boycott of several Jewish-owned restaurants drew opposing demonstrators to Philadelphia on Sunday, with people waving Palestinian and Israeli flags exchanging heated words.
NBC Philadelphia witnessed several verbal confrontations between the groups in the city’s Rittenhouse Square.
A line of Philadelphia police officers worked to keep the groups separated as tensions continued to build before the bike ride had even begun.
At least one physical altercation occurred, with NBC10 witnessing police pull one protester away from another. It was unclear whether anyone was arrested in connection with that incident.
At least one person was arrested amid the crowd. The circumstances surrounding that arrest were not immediately known.
Meanwhile, some of the restaurants targeted by the boycott were seeing long lines of customers supporting.
The demonstration was organized by Philly Bike On Your Left, a group that describes itself as an “anti-fascist, anti-Zionist social cycling collective.”
On Oct. 31, the group announced plans to boycott what it called “Zionist establishments” in Rittenhouse Square in solidarity with the Palestinian community.
The restaurants named in the boycott include Mac Mart, K’Far Café, Huda, Goldie, Schlesinger’s and Dizengoff.
Half of the establishments targeted are owned by Philadelphia restaurant group CookNSolo, whose Israeli co-owners have publicly supported and fundraised for Israel’s military efforts.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The restaurant group has already been the target of a local “Boycott CookNSolo” campaign that says it protests the restaurateurs for “materially and ideologically support[ing] the ongoing occupation and genocide of Palestinians.”

“We stand with the organizers of the Boycott Ride, a small group of bicyclists against genocide who have been doxxed and villainized by social media Zionists and self-serving politicians,” Boycott CookNSolo wrote in an Instagram post this weekend.
The planned event drew widespread criticism, including from Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker and Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday, who condemned the boycott on social media.
The Anti-Defamation League also encouraged people to show their support by dining at the targeted restaurants and other Jewish-owned businesses.

“This protest is an attempt to intimidate a Jewish community that has faced generations of violence, exclusion and antisemitism. It’s the latest in a string of incidents that hold Jewish businesses responsible for events in the Middle East,” the ADL wrote. “That’s antisemitic, plain and simple. But we refuse to let hate win.”
Billboards urge Philadelphians to ‘boycott the boycott’
In response to the planned ride, nonprofit organization JewBelong installed billboards at 14 locations across Philadelphia urging people to support Jewish-owned businesses.
The billboards read, “Running over Jewish businesses isn’t a peace plan,” and encourage residents to “boycott the boycott ride.”

The demonstration also falls on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht, or the “Night of Broken Glass,” when Nazi-organized antisemitic attacks targeted Jewish communities in Germany, Austria and Sudetenland on Nov. 9 and 10, 1938.
In a statement posted to Instagram, Philly Bike On Your Left said the ride had been “grossly misrepresented.”
“We stand firmly against racism and oppression of all forms, including fascism, antisemitism, islamophobia and colonialism.”
It added that the ride was planned “around people’s schedules”and that any implications “about the timing of our ride are simply false.”

“There are business owners in our community who have raised funds for the Israeli military, hosted Israeli soldiers, were praised by Benjamin Netanyahu, or expressed support for Israel,” the organization wrote. “How we spend our money is a reflection of our values.”
Ahead of the bike ride, Governor Josh Shapiro on Friday joined in on the condemnations.

“Hate and antisemitism have no place in our Commonwealth,” Shapiro wrote on X. “And I’m grateful to state and local law enforcement who will work to make sure our neighborhoods remain safe this weekend.”

title: James Talarico kicks off ‘SNL’ days after historic Texas Senate win
summary: James Talarico, a Democrat whose U.S. Senate victory this week was once thought improbable in the Republican stronghold of Texas, made a surprise appearance to help kick off the latest episode of “Saturday Night Live.”
story: James Talarico, a Democrat whose U.S. Senate victory Tuesday was once thought improbable in the Republican stronghold of Texas, made a surprise appearance to help kick off the latest episode of “Saturday Night Live.”

The state lawmaker and seminarian’s defeat of Attorney General Ken Paxton was one of a slew of victories for Texas Democrats, who claimed every statewide office up for grabs, including state Rep. Gina Hinojosa’s gubernatorial win, after a decades-long drought.

“SNL’s” cold open featured New York’s Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (played by Kenan Thompson) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (Sarah Sherman) celebrating Tuesday’s wins, which helped to set up Jeffries as the likely House speaker in January.
Sherman’s Schumer introduced the pair as “establishment Democrats” and asked, “Do we even know how to lose?”
Thompson’s Jeffries answered: “Yes.” Still, he suggested a toast to victory.
“We flipped the House, we flipped the Senate, and how did we do it?” he said.
“Me!” said a party crasher, President Donald Trump, played by James Austin Johnson.
He called the Democrats’ victory wave a “blue Toonami,” referring to Cartoon Network’s late-night block of anime shows, and he indicated he wouldn’t challenge the midterm election’s results.
“I accepted the results, which is almost scarier in a way,” he said. “It’s like, ‘What the hell is he planning?’ I’ll tell you what I’m planning: Ballroom.”
Trump said he hopes voters enjoy the results of the election, including the victory in Texas by the man he calls “Talafreako.”
The real Talarico then moved into the spotlight in front of Trump to loud applause from the show’s New York City studio audience.
“Hi, America,” he said. “I’m James Talarico, the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for $5.”
Trump responded, “In this economy, who can blame you?”
Talarico, who campaigned on battling wealth disparity and political corruption, suggested working with the Republican president to “make life better for everyday Americans.”
“It’s clear people want something new,” the senator-elect said. “They want something different. I’m talking, of course, about ‘SNL’s’ cold opens.”
He suggested voters were tired of the comedy show’s political cold-open sketches, asking, “How many of these Trump freezers are they going to do?”
“Infinity,” Trump responded.
Both then joined voices in uttering the show’s trademark introduction, “Live from New York ... ”
“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

title: We want to hear your experience with changes to student loan repayment plans
summary: If you’re a student borrower who was required to transition to another plan this year, share your story.
story: President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” has transformed the sprawling federal student loan system — and student borrowers are feeling the effects of the most consequential changes.
For Subscribers

This year, the approximately 7.5 million student borrowers under the Biden-era Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE, plan had to select a new one. So far, about 2 million borrowers have done so, after the Education Department warned that the SAVE plan was “illegal” and would be discontinued. The remaining borrowers who did not select a new plan were set to start receiving notices this month informing them that they missed a final deadline and were automatically moved to a new plan.
For Subscribers

The Trump administration has said ending the SAVE plan would help streamline repayment programs while ensuring borrowers are paying off what they owe to the federal government. But student advocacy groups fear lower-income borrowers who had benefited from smaller monthly payments — or even qualified to make no payments at all based on their income — will end up with significantly higher bills under the other available plans.
We want to hear from you, whether you’re in this situation or are facing another challenge related to the recent student loan changes. Please share your experience by filling out the form below.

title: The human touch: Luxury brands embrace craftsmanship as ‘AI slop’ floods the internet
summary: Artists say brands are embracing traditional art forms and making a point to show off the human labor behind their campaigns.
story: The sound of pencil putting lines to paper. The geometric shapes of a cartoon animal before it comes to life on the page.

Those were the opening shots of a teaser for Prada’s 2026 holiday campaign, which introduced a series of films made “using the anachronistic craft of hand-drawn animation,” working with longtime Disney animator John Pomeroy.
“I learned my craft with pencil and paper, old-school analog drawing with pencil and paper,” Pomeroy, who left Disney in 2003, says in the teaser video.

It’s that kind of skill that some artists say has become a greater asset than ever. In the age of widespread and accessible AI, artists say they’ve noticed more brands leaning into handcrafted art as a selling point.
In recent weeks, the luxury fashion houses Prada and Hermès touted their human-made art projects in social media campaigns — even tagging the artists behind the work to showcase their authenticity.

Alina Golovlova, a stop-motion artist in Prague, said that recently, she has felt that her work is actually “appreciated more than in previous years” as brands try to separate themselves from the AI content flooding the internet.

“In previous years, I felt like I was just some hired content creator. No one really cared to tag me or make a [collaborative post],” Golovlova said. “And I think now for brands, it becomes valuable to bring the artists together with the brand to show that they are working with real people.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Golovlova directed a short film for Anthropologie last month, featuring a needle-felted bunny, embroidered stars and stop-motion movements — all designed and put together entirely by hand by a team of artists.
And the choice proved to be an effective marketing strategy, as support rolled in from commenters online.
“Beautiful! Love the creativity and seeing something human made and NOT AI 👏❤️,” a user wrote on Anthropologie’s post, accruing thousands of likes.
“AI = Broke, cheap, lazy,” another user posted in response to Prada’s campaign. “Art from human hands = High-end, luxurious, high quality.”

Animator Jon Densk, who worked on the hand-drawn Prada campaign under Pomeroy, said that while he suspects AI still has a way to go before it can be used successfully in animation, he has seen signs of it in commercials. Coca-Cola, he said, comes to mind as a major company that has leaned into AI for its advertisements.

“After the first one I saw two years ago, I was like, I’m not buying Coke until they stop it. I still haven’t bought a Coke in two years,” Densk said. “So having a stance against [AI], I think, is a smart move for brands.”

Coca-Cola’s use of AI stirred some controversy, as attitudes about the technology remain divided over labor and environmental concerns, as well as fatigue over the swath of mass-produced content commonly described as “AI slop.”
Still, Densk said he wasn’t expecting the explosion of support that Prada’s hand-drawn campaign would attract online.

“I think people that see people like us who are still drawing things, and even people working in CG animation, as true craftsmen, because that stuff really does take hours and hours and hours of practicing to get to a proficient level,” Densk said.

title: Democrats won big on Election Day. But can they agree on AI?
summary: Democrats campaigned on concerns about AI and data centers, but competing priorities and opposition from the Trump administration could complicate efforts to enact new regulations.
story: Democrats across the country who swept into power amid growing voter skepticism about AI and data centers are now reckoning with knotty discussions about how to tackle AI regulation and which technological impacts deserve their attention first, according to AI experts, strategists and legislators themselves.

Dusted with confetti and batting away Election Day balloons, midterm victors touched on everything from data centers — Sen.-elect Chris Pappas of New Hampshire railed against the facilities that “harm our communities and our well-being” — to healthcare, as Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota committed to restricting the use of AI systems in insurance decisions.

The renewed calls for AI regulation are at odds with President Donald Trump’s insistence that Congress must limit AI-focused regulation or risk hampering American AI innovation. Trump has repeatedly referred to AI as a “golden goose” and data centers as sound economic investments.

It is unclear whether Tuesday’s results could create a new opening for meaningful bipartisan AI legislation — with representatives mindful of voters’ AI hawkishness — or instead result in messy infighting within the Democratic Party, Congress and Washington.

“Every Democrat in the House I’m speaking to wants to see AI regulation,” said incoming representative Scott Wiener, who pioneered California’s state-level regulation about AI and will represent San Francisco. “There may be different ideas about what that should be, but I think there’s broad support to take action.”

Some Democrats, like Ohio’s Sherrod Brown, have focused their attention on data centers, often viewed as the physical manifestation of nebulous AI worries and which have stressed electrical grids and water supplies in some areas. “I do not work for data centers,” he said Tuesday night in a state that has one of the highest concentrations of the facilities in the country.

Others, like re-elected Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, have also highlighted the technology’s catastrophic risks. “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction,” he said in his victory speech.

Polls and pundits agree that AI played a significant role in the election. “Six months ago, if you had told me that 56% of voters would have left their polling places stating that concerns about AI were crucial or important to their vote, I would have looked at you like you had 10 heads,” said Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of the Tech Oversight Project, a Washington, D.C.-based watchdog and advocacy group.

Yet some AI experts predict that the variety of Democrats’ AI priorities could lead to fractured policy approaches and watered-down legislation, while other party leaders on AI predicted a more cooperative result.

“I think the Democrats are going to have a hard time wrangling their own perspectives on this,” said Samuel Hammond, director of AI policy at the Foundation for American Innovation, a right-leaning Washington, D.C., think tank. He highlighted the distance between proposals like the one championed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., to ban artificial superintelligence — referring to systems smarter than humans at all cognitive tasks — and more prosaic efforts to update permitting guidelines to build power plants and other AI-related infrastructure.

Alex Bores, a New York Assembly member who authored one of the country’s most substantial pieces of AI legislation — the RAISE Act — disagreed. He framed candidates’ differing priorities as an asset that will allow Congress to tackle many critical AI policy initiatives simultaneously.

Multiple policy approaches are “good and healthy as long as we’re working together to ensure that we are protecting the American people from the many different ways that this technology could harm people,” he said. “There is so much that we have to do in AI, foundational to who gets to decide what we’re building.”
For Subscribers

Bores also said that pro-AI funding had proved toxic to some candidates, pointing to significant losses for candidates supported by pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future. The organization also spent heavily against Bores in his own primary campaign for Congress earlier this year, which he narrowly lost.
For Subscribers
AI experts also predicted that Washington’s previous AI proposals would likely be significantly reimagined under the new political order.

Before the election, a bipartisan bill co-sponsored by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., called the FRONTIER Act had worked its way through Washington as one of the most likely pieces of legislation to pass.

The bill would require increased independent testing and oversight of the most advanced AI systems and mandate that leading AI companies create and publish safety-focused plans. However, Obernolte has faced an unusually competitive re-election battle. As of Sunday morning, his race had not been decided, according to NBC News.

Congress has not passed a significant AI law in recent years, in large part because Trump has opposed regulation. The president and his allies, many of whom hail from Silicon Valley’s tech circles, have insisted that legislation will stifle America’s economy and the AI industry.
“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post in late August.

The Trump administration has repeatedly endorsed federal bills that would pre-empt, or override, state-level legislation. David Sacks, the former White House AI czar and current chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, has said that state laws would lead to a harmful “patchwork” of legislation.

Yet Tuesday’s results point to increasing bipartisan interest in passing meaningful AI legislation, according to the Foundation for American Innovation’s Hammond. “AI is not nearly as left-right polarized as most other issues,” he said.
“Post-midterms, I think Republicans will feel less pressure from tech money and have, at least in the short run, greater degrees of freedom to express their parallel concerns about AI,” he added.

title: Arrest made following shootings that killed 1 and injured 3 others on Winston-Salem State University campus
summary: Authorities have made an arrest in connection to one of two shootings on Winston-Salem State University’s campus that killed one person and wounded three others Saturday.
story: Authorities have made an arrest in connection to one of two shootings on Winston-Salem State University’s campus that killed one person and wounded three others Saturday.

Ziyaire Antonyo Spinks, 20, was arrested in connection to a shooting that killed 19-year-old Peyton Izaia Patterson, Winston-Salem Police Department said in a statement Sunday. Spinks is facing charges of murder, assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill inflicting serious injury, and felony possession of a firearm on an educational campus.

Officers who responded after hearing shots fired found Patterson suffering from a gunshot wound. The officers and emergency medical services attempted life saving measures,  police said, but he did not survive.
The shooting injured Alyssa Janae Ellerbee, 19, who was treated at a hospital and later released, police said.
Police have determined this shooting to be an isolated incident, not connected to a separate shooting that also occurred on campus Saturday night.
Spinks is being held without bond, according to police. Court records show he has a pending case involving a concealed weapon and marijuana possession charges from an arrest in March.

The lawyer representing Spinks in the March case, which is in Randolph County, told NBC News Sunday that he was unaware of the new charges in Forsyth County. It is unclear if Spinks has retained a separate attorney.

The shooting stemmed from an altercation between two groups, according to Jason Swaim, assistant chief of the Field Services Bureau for the Winston-Salem Police Department. An additional arrest was made against Cequon Warren Brower, 18, in connection to fighting.

“One thing I’ll add about the homicide on campus — because I know this has been a question — is that the arrestee that’s been charged with murder, Mr. Spinks, he was not a student of Winston-Salem State University, and neither was Cequon Brower,” Swaim told reporters Sunday.
That shooting occurred at 9:46 p.m. and another shooting was reported on campus at 10:22 p.m, Swaim said.

Two people were found with gunshot wounds by the responding officers. A vehicle related to that incident was identified and later stopped by West Side police officers. No arrests have been made in that case as of Sunday afternoon, according to Swaim.
Saturday was homecoming game day at the historically black university, with the WSSU Rams facing the Fayetteville State Broncos earlier in the day.

Winston-Salem State University Police Chief Amir Henry assured the public that the campus was secured. He noted that this was typically a time for the university’s community to come together in “shared pride and connection.”
“Tragically, this year, this celebration has been overshadowed by the loss of life and the injuries resulting from two separate shootings on our campus,” Henry said.
Emergency services audio obtained by NBC News showed officers reporting one victim suffered a gunshot wound to the head. Another recording showed an officer calling for a second ambulance.

Remaining homecoming activities scheduled for Sunday were canceled, including an event at the Emmanuel Baptist Church, according to a statement from Winston-Salem State University Chancellor Bonita J. Brown.

Brown expressed her condolences to the family of the deceased victims and said she was praying for the recovery of those who were injured. She also acknowledged that members of the campus community “may have witnessed or experienced things that no one should have to endure.”
She urged people to utilize the university’s counseling services and continue to follow police instructions as the investigation in the shootings continued.

“Throughout our history, Winston-Salem State University has faced challenges, but we have always found strength in one another,” Brown wrote. “That is what it means to be part of the Ramily and to be Ram strong.”

title: Gov. Josh Shapiro urges Democrats to prioritize healthcare, food assistance
summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January, though he urged them not to forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.
story: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January, though he urged them not to forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I hope one of the first things that the Congress does is to stop these Medicaid cuts, stop the SNAP cuts, roll back the cuts, the effective cuts in the Affordable Care Act,” Shapiro said in an interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that aired Sunday.
Shapiro noted that in Pennsylvania alone, 510,000 people are losing healthcare and 143,000 more are losing SNAP or food assistance due to cuts approved during President Donald Trump’s second term.

“In general, though, I think Democrats need to have an aggressive agenda that cuts costs, that ends the war, that gets put on the president’s desk,” he said. “Hopefully, he will sign it because it’ll be common-sense stuff that makes people’s lives better.”

Trump has said that he intends to work with Democrats when Congress begins its new term, though he has also touted a new “VETO”-branded hat since Republicans lost the majority in the midterm elections.
Shapiro said that if Trump chooses to veto Democrats’ legislation, “it’s yet another signal to the American people the president actually doesn’t care about their well-being.”
While the governor stressed the importance of revitalizing Medicaid and SNAP programs, he also said Democrats shouldn’t forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I think the Congress needs to be responsive to where voters are on corruption, and there has to be real accountability for this administration,” Shapiro said, adding that Democrats need to “walk and chew gum at the same time” to pass effective legislation and also “have real accountability for the corruption that exists in Washington.”
“It can’t be either/or,” he said. “It has to be both/and.”

Shapiro added that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker of the House, “has made very clear that both are going to be on the agenda for the first 100 days and for these next two years.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The governor said that he doesn’t think Democrats should be thinking about the 2028 elections yet. Instead, “we should be thinking about how to make people’s lives better in 2027,” he said.
“It’s incumbent upon the Congress to now do that, and it’s incumbent upon governors now to continue to lead the way in our states,” Shapiro said.
Shapiro, who has been floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, did not commit to running.

Asked whether he is more likely to run than not, Shapiro answered that his focus was on “figuring how we advance policies like raising the minimum wage and many other things that have been blocked by Republicans,” as Pennsylvania Democrats won a majority in the state legislature Tuesday.
He also did not directly answer whether he was committed to serving his full four-year term.

“Well, I committed to run for governor, and that’s the work I’m focused on doing,” Shapiro said. “And if I’ve got something to say about my future, I’d love to come back on your show and talk about it.”

title: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton says he’d be disappointed if Democrats focus on investigating Trump
summary: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said that he hopes to prioritize lowering costs and that he would be “deeply disappointed” to spend two years investigating Trump.
story: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, who flipped deep-red Kansas for Democrats, said Sunday that he hopes to prioritize lowering costs for his constituents in the next Congress and that he would be “deeply disappointed” to spend two years investigating members of the Trump administration.

“The bigger priority for me, and I think for most people in America, especially people living paycheck to paycheck, is ‘please help us with the cost of living,’” Hamilton told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.”
Specifically, he said the new Congress should immediately focus on ending the war in Iran and “claw[ing] back tariffs policies.”

“If I spent the next two years — my first two years in the Senate — in investigations, I’d be deeply disappointed. I want to get to work helping the people in my state and helping the people across the country,” Hamilton said.

After Democrats’ landslide victories Tuesday, which granted them control of the House and Senate in the next Congress, newly elected leaders and those who were re-elected are turning to focus on their priorities for the next two years.

Many are calling on colleagues to focus on an affordability agenda, but some senior leaders have said that they’ll also prioritize oversight and investigations into possible corruption by President Donald Trump and his allies.

“Whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court and entangle him in legislative razor wire,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters Wednesday.
For Subscribers

Several Democrats, including Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who served as an impeachment manager for one of Trump’s impeachments during his first term, have floated potentially impeaching the president for a third time.
“I’m not as interested in impeachment as setting up guardrails,” Hamilton said Sunday, though he added, “I understand the move and the desire to do this.”
Instead, the senator-elect said his party should concentrate on making life more affordable for Americans.

“Let’s focus on helping the American people,” he said. “And I’ll tell you, the Democrats, if they don’t, if we don’t figure that out and get to work on helping people, this is going to be a one and done, kind of, you know, kind of blue wave.”
For Subscribers
Appearing later on the program, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., agreed with Hamilton.

“I think the senator-elect Hamilton made a good point,” Sanders told “Meet the Press,” adding: “We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump. We have to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.”

With Democrats winning in 54 Senate seats and two more Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled, Schumer could be poised to take over as Senate majority leader in the next Congress if a majority of the Democratic members of the Senate vote in his favor.
Hamilton has said that he doesn’t plan to support Schumer’s bid to be majority leader.
On Sunday, he said he has “no disrespect for Chuck Schumer,” but “I just really don’t [want him as majority leader], and I’ve told him that as well.”

The senator-elect cited the volume of TV ads during the campaign linking him to Schumer, which he said addressed the fact that “a lot of people in Kansas feel, who may not know Chuck Schumer personally, who don’t know him personally, but you know that that they perceive him to be further to the left, and somebody who’s a divisive figure.”

He demurred when asked who he might support over Schumer, saying, “I know probably 10 senators personally, and even those I only know from brief conversations. So, you know, I’m not at a place where I can tell you, ‘these are, this is my short list.’”
Hamilton added: “There are a handful of people that I think are probably, you know, lead more from the center, but I don’t know enough yet to be able to say, ‘these are the people I would endorse.’”

title: Parents, sister of far-right Kraków shooter found dead in family home
summary: Three bodies found in the home of the 24-year-old shooter in the Saturday’s rampage in the heart of Kraków belonged to the gunman’s family, police said.
story: Three bodies found in the home of the 24-year-old shooter in the Saturday’s rampage in the heart of Kraków belonged to the gunman’s family, police said.

Investigators are looking at the deaths of the shooter’s parents and sister as they unravel events surrounding the random violence in the Polish city’s historic center, Main Market Square, around 3 p.m. on Saturday.
The relatives, who lived about 90 miles from Krakow, likely died from gunshot wounds, according to police.
Authorities said the shooter, who survived a shootout with police and remains in the hospital, wore a bulletproof vest during the attack.

The identifications were made as world leaders paid tribute to victims and Poland declared two national days of mourning after a shooter motivated by far-right ideologies killed six people in Kraków on Saturday, in what the country’s defense minister characterized as a “terror attack.”

Victims of the attack included a man from the United Kingdom, a woman from Austria and four Polish nationals, according to regional official Krzysztof Jan Klęczar. The injured included visitors from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria, according to the Associated Press.
St. Mary’s Basilica in the square paused its hourly trumpet call overnight in honor of the victims. It was the first time the historic church had done so since World War II.

The gunman, described by officials as having “ultranationalistic” beliefs, is reported to have opened fire in Kraków’s main market square. Four women and two men were killed in the midday attack, the country’s deadliest shooting in decades, while a policeman who confronted the gunman is in critical condition.

The suspect is being investigated on suspicion of murder in connection with the six deaths, Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said on X Sunday, adding that he “acted with the aim of seriously intimidating a large number of people, making this a terrorist offence.”

The same suspect is facing a separate murder charge over killings in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyskie, Żurek said, a town some 93 miles northeast of Kraków where three of the man’s relatives were found dead in his home.

“Establishing all the circumstances of these tragic events, determining the full sequence of the perpetrator’s actions and securing evidence are currently the priorities of the investigation,” which is being led by terror offense specialists within the prosecutor’s office, he said.
Krakow‘s prosecutor Eryk Stasielak said the shooter was in critical condition and victim autopsies were set to start on Monday, according to PAP, a Polish news service.
“Tomorrow we will be deciding the fate of the attacker, if he survives, because he remains in critical condition,” Stasielak said, according to a translation of the report.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński did not name the suspect but identified him as a Polish national in his mid-20s from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyskie. He used an automatic rifle, Kierwiński said Saturday, describing him as having “ultranationalistic” views.
“Everything indicates he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” he said.
The suspect was shot by police at the scene and taken to the hospital around 3 p.m. local time. He remains in critical condition, regional governor Krzysztof Klęczar told a news conference Sunday.
A man and two women later found dead in an apartment are believed to be the suspect’s parents and sister, according to Andrzej Fijołek, deputy inspector of Police National Headquarters.
Two national days of mourning on November 8 and 9 were announced by the Interior Ministry on Sunday.

Pope Leo XIV issued a message to the archbishop of Krakow on Sunday expressing sadness over the tragedy. The Pope “implores the gift of Christian hope for the families overwhelmed by grief and joins with all those experiencing these days of mourning,” the message read, according to a translation.
Żurek, the justice minister, said on social media early on Sunday that Senior Constable Jakub Kulik “is fighting for his life in hospital” after he confronted the shooter.
“One of his lungs is not functioning, and he needs every drop of blood he can get,” he posted on X.
Police later said that blood banks in Kraków were full and thanked those who donated.
“Senior constable Jakub Kulik and senior constable Artur Moranski are true heroes,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, referring to both policemen.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Klęczar said that without “the efficient and selfless intervention” of the officers, “the number of victims could have been significantly higher.”
“The condition of the two police officers remains serious,” Klęczar said Sunday, though Kierwiński later said the two men had been brought out of comas.

Video posted on social media shows what appears to be an injured police officer firing at the gunman before dropping to his knees and rolling over onto his back. The officer, who did not appear to have backup nearby, is seen struggling to reload his firearm and appeared to be clutching his right arm.

Four of the dead in the city center attack have been identified, though their names have not been released. They include four Polish nationals, a British national, and one non-Polish woman whose nationality has not yet been publicized, Klęczar said.
All those wounded were alive on Sunday, he said, adding that 11 of the 16 injured people are Polish and two of the individuals are police officers.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the U.K. government “deeply mourns the British national and other victims” who died in the shooting.
“The U.K. stands resolutely in solidarity with the people of Poland,” he said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said Saturday that his country “stands in solidarity” with neighboring Poland, calling the shooting a “shocking crime.”
The U.S. State Department said it was not aware of any American citizens harmed in the violence.
“The profound depth of Poland’s shock at the horror of yesterday’s appalling mass murder in Krakow is truly remarkable to behold,” U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said in a post on X.

Noting how rare the incident was in a “extraordinarily safe” country like Poland, he added: “There’s something profoundly precious about being in a country where such evil remains so foreign to everyday life, where an entire nation recoils in horror at the mere thought of it, and where the depth of grief reveals the true goodness of its people.”
Part of Main Market Square in Kraków and surrounding streets reopened Sunday, but cordons remain in place while police carry out forensic work, the city has said in a statement.
Several makeshift memorials with flowers and candles appeared across the city on Sunday.
Tourists caught up in attack
Many of those caught up in the attack were tourists visiting the city.

Taylor Dorfmeister, a 21-year-old American student studying in Italy who was visiting Poland, was in the square with his roommate when gunfire erupted. Dorfmeister said there was a delay before the crowd reacted and then everyone began to flee the area. He said he took shelter in a building.
“We ran up the stairs in the building to hide and it was a dead end, which is when I was the most terrified since the gunshots were [loud] and near,” Dorfmeister told NBC News.

It sounded to Dorfmeister like the gunfire was coming from the first floor of the building where he hid. The student from Santa Cruz, California, was “fully prepared for the worst” based on the proximity of the noise, he said.
“This is it,” Dorfmeister thought. “Like, there’s nowhere to go, nowhere to hide.”
Marie-Ange Collaer was visiting with her family from Brussels.

“We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around,” she wrote on Facebook. “Lying on the floor in a shop like in a bad police movie whilst you hear bullets everywhere.”
Collaer said her family was shaky and “quite in shock” after returning to their hotel but everyone was grateful to be alive.
“We saw a few that did not make it, true horror,” she wrote.
U.K. resident Neil Thaxton and his wife, Nicky, also survived the attack.

“We had just walked through the main square and heard the gunshots,” Thaxton wrote on Facebook. “We thought it was fireworks then people started running, we went into a gift shop and the staff took us in the back of the shop and locked the doors and turned the lights off.”

title: James Talarico kicks off ‘SNL’ days after historic Texas Senate win
summary: James Talarico, a Democrat whose U.S. Senate victory this week was once thought improbable in the Republican stronghold of Texas, made a surprise appearance to help kick off the latest episode of “Saturday Night Live.”
story: James Talarico, a Democrat whose U.S. Senate victory Tuesday was once thought improbable in the Republican stronghold of Texas, made a surprise appearance to help kick off the latest episode of “Saturday Night Live.”

The state lawmaker and seminarian’s defeat of Attorney General Ken Paxton was one of a slew of victories for Texas Democrats, who claimed every statewide office up for grabs, including state Rep. Gina Hinojosa’s gubernatorial win, after a decades-long drought.

“SNL’s” cold open featured New York’s Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (played by Kenan Thompson) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (Sarah Sherman) celebrating Tuesday’s wins, which helped to set up Jeffries as the likely House speaker in January.
Sherman’s Schumer introduced the pair as “establishment Democrats” and asked, “Do we even know how to lose?”
Thompson’s Jeffries answered: “Yes.” Still, he suggested a toast to victory.
“We flipped the House, we flipped the Senate, and how did we do it?” he said.
“Me!” said a party crasher, President Donald Trump, played by James Austin Johnson.
He called the Democrats’ victory wave a “blue Toonami,” referring to Cartoon Network’s late-night block of anime shows, and he indicated he wouldn’t challenge the midterm election’s results.
“I accepted the results, which is almost scarier in a way,” he said. “It’s like, ‘What the hell is he planning?’ I’ll tell you what I’m planning: Ballroom.”
Trump said he hopes voters enjoy the results of the election, including the victory in Texas by the man he calls “Talafreako.”
The real Talarico then moved into the spotlight in front of Trump to loud applause from the show’s New York City studio audience.
“Hi, America,” he said. “I’m James Talarico, the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for $5.”
Trump responded, “In this economy, who can blame you?”
Talarico, who campaigned on battling wealth disparity and political corruption, suggested working with the Republican president to “make life better for everyday Americans.”
“It’s clear people want something new,” the senator-elect said. “They want something different. I’m talking, of course, about ‘SNL’s’ cold opens.”
He suggested voters were tired of the comedy show’s political cold-open sketches, asking, “How many of these Trump freezers are they going to do?”
“Infinity,” Trump responded.
Both then joined voices in uttering the show’s trademark introduction, “Live from New York ... ”
“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

title: Man arrested outside LeBron James’ L.A. home claiming to be his son
summary: A man found outside LeBron James’ Los Angeles home was arrested on suspicion of felony stalking, police said.
story: A man found outside LeBron James’ Los Angeles home was arrested on suspicion of felony stalking, police said.

Police were called to the scene just after 9:30 p.m. Friday on a report of a possible burglary suspect at the basketball legend’s home in the affluent neighborhood of Brentwood on the city’s west side, Los Angeles police said.
Security personnel had spotted a man on surveillance cameras and called police, law enforcement sources told NBC Los Angeles.
For Subscribers
Responding officers located the man, who claimed to be James’ son, sources told NBC Los Angeles.
For Subscribers
The man was arrested on suspicion of felony stalking, police said. Authorities did not identify him.
James was not home at the time. He was in Cleveland playing for the Philadelphia 76ers.

title: UFC’s Dana White says he will meet Trump on Monday to discuss press secretary offer
summary: President Donald Trump said that he’d offered the job of White House press secretary to the CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, Dana White.
story: President Donald Trump on Saturday said on Truth Social that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship.
“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” the president wrote.
Trump suggested in his post that White should bring several UFC fighters, including Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje and Amanda Nunes, as assistants to defend against the “Lunatic Left.”
“Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” he added.
White said at a boxing event in London Saturday evening that he was heading to Washington, D.C., that night and had a meeting scheduled with the president Monday.
Asked whether he could speak about conversations he has had with Trump so far, White declined.
“We have a meeting on Monday, so sure, I’ll have more to talk about after that,” White said.
When Trump posted on Truth Social earlier Saturday, it was unclear whether his offer to White was a serious one.
Shortly after Trump posted, White posted on Instagram what appears to be an AI-generated image of himself behind the podium in the White House briefing room, captioned, “On to the next chapter.”
White also added a screenshot of Trump’s post to his Instagram story.
Trump and White have long been friends and the president has attended many UFC fights while serving in the White House.
Earlier this year, White also organized a UFC fight on the South Lawn of the White House, an event that was part of a slate commemorating the United States’ 250th birthday.
Many Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers attended the fight in July.
A spokesperson for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The position has been vacant since Katie Zacharia departed the role after just five days in October.

Zacharia had replaced Karoline Leavitt, who served as White House press secretary since Trump returned to office in January of last year. Leavitt announced in August that she would leave her post to spend more time with her family.
The White House had another staff shake-up on Friday, when Chief of Staff Susie Wiles said she would be stepping down from her post. Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as her replacement.

Wiles’ departure made her the seventh woman to leave the Trump administration this year. So far, all of the women who have left have been replaced by men, with the exception of Zacharia and Leavitt, as a press secretary has not yet been named.

title: 1 dead, at least 12 injured after elderly driver plows into group of cyclists in North Carolina
summary: One cyclist was killed and at least 12 others were injured after a driver, suspected to be impaired, plowed into a group of cyclists in North Carolina.
story: One cyclist was killed and at least 12 others were injured after a driver, suspected to be impaired, plowed into a group of cyclists in North Carolina.

Donald Robert Morris-Jones, 76, was driving on Optimist Farm Road in Wake County on Saturday morning when he crossed the center line and struck the group of cyclists, the North Carolina State Highway Patrol said. The incident unfolded about 14 miles southwest of Raleigh.
After striking the group, the vehicle traveled away from the scene then ran off the left side of the roadway and crashed into a ditch a half a mile away from the cyclists, officials said.
The North Carolina State Highway Patrol responded to the scene just after 9:30 a.m.
One cyclist died as a result of the crash and at least a dozen more were hurt, authorities said. Their injuries range from minor to serious, and several were transported to hospitals for treatment.
Highway Patrol identified the deceased victim as Patrick Allen Turner, 63, of Cary, North Carolina.
For Subscribers

Morris-Jones was arrested and charged with death by vehicle, seven counts of serious injury by vehicle, eight counts of hit and run, driving while impaired, reckless driving and drive left of center, according to Highway Patrol.
For Subscribers
“Impairment is suspected to be a factor in the crash,” the agency said.
Morris-Jones was being held in the Wake County Detention Center on $1 million bail.

The Infrared Sauna Blanket was the very first product that HigherDose released, and of the devices we tested for this guide, it has the broadest appeal: It’s simple to use, effects are quickly noticeable and it’s easy to fit in your day-to-day routine.

According to experts in our red light therapy guide, infrared light therapy has been used to treat joint pain for years. Laid flat, the blanket looks like an oversized black sleeping bag made of vegan leather. It plugs into the wall and connects to a small handheld controller with a dial that lets you adjust the heat across eight levels, so you can start low and work your way up as you get used to it. The brand recommends preheating it for about 10 minutes, then zipping yourself in for a 30- to 45-minute session. When you’re done, you let it cool, wipe it down, fold it up and tuck it under a bed or in a closet, which makes it much easier to store away than a full-size sauna.

The purpose of the sauna blanket is to soothe aches and pains and wind down. NBC Selected editorial operations associate Jem Alabi says this product “changed [her] life,” and she regularly falls asleep when using it because she’s so relaxed. “Since I’ve been using it, I’ve been able to [reduce] the soreness I experience after a long work day and commute. I hop in the shower right after and head straight to bed,” she says.

It’s also designed for post-workout recovery: Lauren Swanson, NBC Selected editorial director, used the sauna blanket while training for the New York City marathon two years ago. Though she didn’t notice a measurable difference in her performance, she liked using it as a way to unwind after training. “While I don’t have hard proof that it helped my pace, I did enjoy those 15 minutes of lying down and sweating after a long run,” she says.

Like the sauna blanket, the mat uses infrared heat, but because you lie on top of it rather than zip yourself inside, the experience is less intense and sweaty. Along with infrared, it has pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy, which sends low-level electromagnetic waves through your body and has been studied for pain and recovery. However, evidence for many of the broader wellness benefits associated with PEMF products is still limited.

“I’ve been using this mat a few times a week at night to help relax me before bed,” says Alabi, who notes it’s particularly good for times you want to avoid getting sweaty or only have a limited amount of time to use it. “Unlike the sauna blanket, this one doesn’t make you sweaty or require time to heat up, so you can just lie down for as long as you like.”

However, since the mat has 20 pounds of amethyst and obsidian crystals built in, lying down directly on it may feel uncomfortable, so Alabi puts a thin blanket down. You can also buy a cover for the mat directly from HigherDose.

The mat is also fairly large and heavy (it’s around 6 feet long and weighs 43 pounds), which can be cumbersome to roll up and put away. If you’re short on space, HigherDose’s smaller Go Mat has the same technology, but is about half the size and much lighter.

The flexible silicone mask straps over your face, using red and near-infrared light (the biggest difference between the two is how deeply they can penetrate skin) to even out skin tone and reduce inflammation without any heat or mess involved, according to the brand. There is also a neck attachment you can purchase separately to extend those benefits to your neck and chest area. The convenience really sets this face mask apart from other red light masks: You can easily wear the mask while scrolling on your phone or watching TV, and sessions typically run just 10 to 20 minutes.

To use the mask, you want to make sure you have clean skin because products like SPF and heavy moisturizers can block the light, according to HigherDose. The actual mask is made of medical-grade, flexible silicone that contours to the face and a head strap keeps it secure. You can choose a 10- or 20-minute session (HigherDose suggests using it for 10 or 20 minutes three to five times a week). When it runs out of juice, you can recharge it with the included USB-C cable.
